### 2026-09-01 to 2026-09-20 — full narratives (digested 2026-09-14; rolling since). Header corrected 2026-09-18: it read "to 2026-09-16" while the batch already held entries through 2026-09-18, so it is now DERIVED from the batch's own span rather than hand-maintained — re-check it with the reconciliation in `npm run docs:budget`.


**2026-09-20 (second) — CDS (II) 2026 English ships: 120 q, the 20th CDS English paper, and the first in that corpus with a PUBLISHED UPSC key. A blind pass scored 119/120 against it. The point of deriving at all was NOT to audit the key — it was the only detector this corpus has for its own mis-slotted-option defect.**

**The paper.** `QP-CDSE-II-26-ENGLISH-140926.pdf`, the raw UPSC booklet: 32 pages, **zero extractable characters**, embedded scan 2368x3118 (~300 DPI), T.B.C. `BFVS-F-GNE`, **Series A**, "120 items", 100 marks, two hours, one-third penalty — all read off the cover rather than inherited from the corpus. Content ends at Q120 on printed page 26; indices 26-31 measure **~0.2% dark pixels**, i.e. the "SPACE FOR ROUGH WORK" header and a page number and nothing else, which is how "the paper ends here" was established rather than assumed. CDS English 2,280 -> 2,400 PUBLIC; bank 72,306 -> 72,426; the corpus now backs **20** timed mocks.

**Thirteen sections, and not one new section type.** `SECTION_CATALOG` already held all thirteen (word-pair-meaning, synonyms, single-word-meaning, paragraph-rearrangement, spotting-errors, idioms, antonyms, fill-blank-grammar, homophones, sentence-relationship, match-list, and two reading-comprehension sets). For a corpus whose catalog grew on almost every previous paper — 27 types accumulated across 19 booklets — a twentieth paper adding none is a small result about the catalog having converged, and it is worth recording because the next paper adding one is then genuinely news.

**WHY DERIVE AT ALL, WHEN FOR ENGLISH THE KEY OUTRANKS OUR JUDGEMENT ANYWAY.** This is the entry's real content. On a mock, the official key *defines* the right answer for judgement items — idiom shades, S1/S2 relationships, rearrangements — so scoring a derivation against it is not an audit of the key in the way the CDS Maths 2026-II exercise was, where exact rational arithmetic could prove the key wrong. What the derivation buys here is different and specific: it is **the only available detector for this corpus's documented defect class**, in which the transcriber copies the CORRECT option's text into the WRONG letter's slot and then keys that letter. The answer is right as content and wrong as a letter. That class cost 19 wrong keys when the mocks were built, and the README already proves a blind re-derivation cannot catch it alone — run `bank-paper:cds-english-blind-2026-08-23` has 89 rows all `confirmed`, one of which (2021-2 Q59) was later disproved from the printed page. An official key breaks that circle because **its letter is defined against the booklet's PRINTED option order**. So a key/derivation disagreement is evidence about the TRANSCRIPTION first, the derivation second, and the key last — and `score.ts` prints that suspect order above its findings so the next person does not reach for the key first.

**Blindness is ORDERING, and that is weaker than what CDS Maths had.** A single agent cannot be two parties: once the key is read, every later judgement is contaminated. So the guarantee here is sequence — transcribe, derive all 120, write to disk, **git-commit** (`20d2ff9d`), and only then open the key PDF. `score.ts` is the only thing in the pipeline that touches `Paper.answerKey`. This is genuinely weaker than the dual-reader reconciliation `scripts/cds-maths/` uses, and the same caveat applies to the two key reads, which are two passes with different crop strategies by one reader, not two readers. Both caveats are written into `data/2026-2.blindscore.json` rather than left to be forgotten, because the tempting thing to write later is "blind, verified", and that would overstate it.

**THE SERIES IS THE TRAP, AND IT WAS CHECKED, NOT ASSUMED.** The key PDF is four pages, one per series. Pages 0-3 were read individually and are A, B, C, D; our booklet's cover says A, so page 0 is the one. This matters because UPSC shuffles question order between series, so the wrong page yields a **well-formed, entirely plausible key that is mostly wrong and reads as a collapsed derivation rather than as the wrong page** — the failure the CDS Maths run documented and the reason `Paper.series` is now a config field that `score.ts` refuses to proceed without. The header also states **0 questions dropped, 120 taken for scoring**, which was read rather than presumed: a dropped question changes the whole downstream marking.

**Result: 119/120, and the confidence flag pointed at nothing.** All **15 MED rows agreed** with the key; the single miss was a **HIGH**. That is worth stating plainly because the pipeline's standing advice for the 19 unkeyed papers is to prioritise re-checking non-HIGH rows, and on this paper that heuristic would have found the error in exactly zero of its passes. Confidence was well calibrated in the aggregate (105 HIGH / 15 MED / 0 LOW, against 30-60 MED on earlier papers, consistent with a much cleaner scan) and useless as a pointer to the one thing wrong.

**The one disagreement, adjudicated in the documented order.** Q96: S1 "The Indian team won the championship", S2 "They were struggling in the preliminary rounds"; derived B (contrasts with), key D (qualifies). Step one was **option ORDER**, re-read from a 4x crop of the printed page — it matched the transcription exactly, so this was not a mis-slot. Step two found the derivation at fault, and the discriminator was sitting inside the same section all along: it keys "contrasts with" only where **two different subjects** are set side by side (Q93 Mohan vs Sohan, Q98 the city vs its villages) and "qualifies" where the **same subject** gets a tempering detail (Q91 the students, Q99 the train, Q100 the vaccine). Q96 is the same team across two times. The pass had already applied that rule to Q91, Q99 and Q100 and simply did not carry it to Q96, where winning-versus-struggling read as oppositional. Answer flipped to D; every answer in the paper is now key-backed.

**Adjudicating a disagreement DESTROYS the measurement, so it is pinned.** Flipping Q96 means a later `score.ts` run reports 120/120 and says nothing whatever about how the blind pass did. `data/2026-2.blindscore.json` records the 119/120, the per-confidence split, the adjudication and the frozen derivation commit, with the command to reproduce it (`git show 20d2ff9d:...questions.json`). That reproduction was run and agrees — 119/120, Q96 the sole miss — and the file's own claim is asserted against the frozen tree rather than typed from memory.

**Layout care, in the three places this corpus has been burned.** (1) **match-list Q101-110** was read from 4x column crops, never the page render, because the documented root cause of 10 corrupted rows is two-column flow: Q104's lists END the left column and its `Code:` table sits at the TOP of the right column, where it belongs to Q104 and not to the question printed beside it. Q103's (b) is `3 4 2 1` and Q104's is `3 4 1 2`, so the two are not interchangeable and a careless read swaps them. All fourteen code tables on three pages were verified at 4x. (2) **Q38's S1** sits at the foot of the left column with its remaining sentences in the right. (3) **sentence-relationship Q91-100 does NOT use a uniform option set** — Q92 offers "negates", Q97 and Q98 "affirms", Q98 "quantifies" — so each set was transcribed per item. Pasting a uniform set would have produced four plausible-looking rows with wrong option text, which is precisely the defect class in a new costume.

**Two subtopics were filed under the wrong chapter and would have fragmented a cleaned taxonomy.** `perQuestionSubtopic` sections take a per-question subtopic, and that subtopic must belong to the **section's own chapter**. The first draft used "Preposition Usage" for two Spotting Errors items (it is a *Grammar* subtopic) and "Vocabulary in Context" for a Grammar item (it is a *Reading Comprehension* one). `commitStaged` auto-creates taxonomy, so nothing would have errored — it would have minted duplicate subtopics under the wrong chapters, in a bank whose taxonomy cleanup is closed at 13/13 subjects. Caught by listing the live chapter-to-subtopic map and checking each name against its own chapter before committing.

**The `--allow-unpublish` guard fired, and it was right to.** `commit.ts --apply` inserted all 120 and then REFUSED, because migration 0022 makes `visibility` default to PUBLIC, so the rows landed PUBLIC and the script's next step would have set the whole paper PRIVATE. For this paper PUBLIC was the destination anyway, so the refusal cost nothing; the state was then verified directly rather than inferred — 120 rows, all PUBLIC, `pyq`/`mcq`, 480 options, exactly one correct each — and `flip-public.ts` was still run for its structural gate (OK, no duplicate options).

**Two probes that would have lied, and the canaries that caught them.** (1) `score.ts --inject=7=A` initially printed `forcing key Q7 to undefined` and changed nothing: the value contains an `=`, and splitting on every `=` and taking `[1]` yields the question number with no letter. The canary existed precisely to prove the probe could go red, and its first run proved the opposite — fixed to take everything after the first `=`, after which it correctly turns the green run red. (2) A scoped underline probe written as a **shell heredoc** died on mangled backslashes, exactly as the standing note predicts (heredocs eat backslashes and hit PROBES, not data); rewritten with the Write tool, given its own canary, it reports 80 underline segments (20 single + 30 homophone + 30 error-parts, which is the arithmetic the sections predict), all in the docx bypass form, 0 unbalanced delimiters.

**The mock needed no code.** CDS sittings are DERIVED from `scripts/cds/config.ts` PAPERS by `cdsSittings.ts`, so registering the paper there was enough — `--only=cds-2026-ii-english --apply --publish` built and published it, and `verify-mocks.ts` confirms `✓ cds-2026-ii-english published 120q / 100m` across 56 CDS mocks. Note `--apply` without `--publish` writes `status='draft'`, so the first run left it unpublished.

**Standing probes, scoped.** `audit:text` on the source: clean across all seven classes. `audit:provenance`: 0 gap rows, 0 denylist leaks; "CDS (II) 2026 — English" is 24 characters and so publishes as a sitting identifier, which is the intent. `npm run stats`: CDS English 2,400, bank 72,426.

**What it changes for the other 19 papers: nothing, and that is the honest answer.** Their answers remain LLM-derived and unverified, and this paper does not transfer accuracy to them. What it does establish is that **from 2026-II onward no CDS English sitting need be unkeyed** — UPSC now publishes a key within days — so the cheap, strong method is available for every future paper, and the tooling to use it (`keyLib.ts`, `score.ts`, the `answerKey`/`series` config fields, `blindscore.json`) now exists rather than having to be invented under time pressure at the next sitting.


**2026-09-20 — CDS Elementary Mathematics 2026-II ships: 100 q, the 21st sitting, and the FIRST paper in this bank with a PUBLISHED UPSC key. A single blind pass scored 99/100 against it, and the one disagreement is the KEY'S error.**

**The paper.** `QP-CDSE-II-26-ELEMENTARY-MATHEMATICS-140926.pdf`, the raw UPSC bilingual booklet: 40 pages, **zero extractable characters measured across all 40**, booklet `BFVS-T-TME`, Series A. Page-selection pre-pass resolved to the same convention as 2026-I but was VERIFIED rather than inherited — p01 is Q1-Q6 in Hindi, p02 the SAME Q1-Q6 in English, printed page = index + 1, English on even indices 2..34, and Q100 completes on p34 (printed 35-A). Indices 35-38 are rough work and 39 is the cover scanned last, so a naive "all even pages" rule would have fed two blanks to a transcriber. CDS Mathematics 1,996 -> 2,096 PUBLIC; bank 72,306.

**ZERO FIGURES, and that is the unusual part.** Checked on all 17 English pages and at full resolution on the three where geometry and DI sit; all five transcription bands independently confirmed it. Every geometry item is prose-described and the DI is tables, so the snap-crop -> verify-figures -> attach-images stage did not run at all — which deletes the most error-prone stage in this pipeline, the detached-label trap that has hit 14 of 17 figures corpus-wide. The standing lesson is symmetric: "a maths paper has figures" is not safe in EITHER direction, so check.

**WHY SINGLE-BLIND + AN OFFICIAL KEY BEATS THE DUAL-BLIND IT REPLACED.** Dual-blind's own documented ceiling is that it observes AGREEMENT and never correctness: two passes wrong the same way are indistinguishable from two passes right, which is exactly why `score.ts` prints "AGREED, BUT DISAGREE WITH THE KEY" rather than "correlated errors". A published key breaks that ambiguity outright. The 2020 pair could not — they are PREP-HOUSE keys measured at roughly 2 errors per 100, where the adjudication prior runs the OTHER way (3 of 4 disagreements there were the key's).

**Q25 IS AN ERROR IN THE OFFICIAL PROVISIONAL KEY, proved rather than asserted.** Alloy X is gold:silver 1:2, Y is 2:3, Z must be 4:7. The key gives B (2:1); in exact rationals B yields **16:29 against a required 16:28** — near, and not equal, which is precisely why it is a plausible setter's slip. Only 6:5 gives exactly 4:7. All four alternative readings of the stem were tested (either source ratio reversed, the target reversed, all three reversed): **B matches under NONE of them**, and the one alternative that resolves at all still gives D. The bank ships D. Three agents had separately predicted Q40, Q43 and Q77 as the likely key-error candidates (each a discarded-root-is-a-printed-option trap); the key agreed with us on all three, so the prediction was wrong and the real defect was somewhere nobody flagged.

**THE KEY IS A SCAN, ONE PAGE PER SERIES, AND THE WRONG PAGE IS A SILENT CATASTROPHE.** Series A's Q1 is B where Series B's Q1 is D, and the sequences diverge throughout, so reading the wrong page produces a well-formed key covering 1..100 that disagrees with the derivation on roughly three quarters of rows — which reads as "the derivation collapsed", not "wrong series". Nothing downstream can tell those apart. Hence `KEY_READ_BRIEF.md` and the `keyread` lane: TWO independent vision reads, each confirming the Series box off the page itself, reconciled by `reconcileKeyReads`, which emits a cell only where every reader agrees and **never votes** — two-against-one is not a majority on a table anyone can re-read, and a tie-break rule quietly converts "we are unsure" into "we are sure". Both reads agreed on all 100 cells and both read the header independently as Total 100 / Dropped 0 / Scored 100.

**BLINDNESS WAS MADE STRUCTURAL — AND THE QUARANTINE STILL LEAKED ITS OWN NAME.** The existing guarantee was instructional only ("stop if you see a key"), which is weak when `data/` holds `sourcekey.json` beside `derive.json`. So every key artifact was physically moved OUT of the repo for the derivation window. But it was moved into the SHARED agent scratchpad, and a deriver listing that directory saw `KEY_QUARANTINE/` plus `*_keyread1.*` and ~20 key crops BY NAME. It opened none, the listing post-dated its written and validated output, and it reported the sighting unprompted — the instruction working as designed. The lesson is exact: **moving a secret out of the repository is not moving it out of reach**, the scratchpad is part of a subagent's world, and `KEY_QUARANTINE` is a signpost rather than a hiding place.

**THREE PRINTED DEFECTS, ALL VERIFIED AGAINST THE SOURCE AND ALL ANSWER-NEUTRAL, transcribed as printed and never repaired.** Q47 prints options (a) and (c) both as a bare "2" (answer is (b) 3/2, so the duplicate never competes); Q60 prints (d) as "14 cm" beside 1.0/1.2/1.4 (answer is (c) 1.4, confirmed: 4.4 / (2200/7) = 0.014 m); Q86 prints (c) as the unreduced "3 : 3" (answer is (a) 3:5); Q98 prints its x column out of order, which cannot move a mean. Q47 forced a real design decision, because BOTH the commit gate and the publish gate refuse duplicate option text — the check that caught 19 wrong keys on the sibling CDS English corpus. The allowance added is narrow and its permission is COMPUTED, not asserted: a question must be declared in `SOURCE_DUPLICATE_OPTIONS` (one map in `config.ts`, read by both gates so they cannot drift) AND the correct option must not be one of the duplicates, or it is refused regardless — a question whose key is duplicated cannot be answered by choosing a letter. Pinned by four tests, including one asserting a declaration cannot leak to a different question.

**Two bugs the work surfaced in the gates themselves.** (1) `flip-public` read `question_number` raw from the database, where it is TEXT, against a numeric allowlist — so `.has("47")` silently missed and the gate refused a row it had been told to allow. Sharing one map across two gates does not prevent drift when the callers read different REPRESENTATIONS. (2) `score.ts` hardcoded the phrase "scoring against a PREP-HOUSE key", which became a false statement in the most load-bearing place the moment an official key existed; it now reads the provenance out of the key file. Also noted and deliberately NOT changed: `buildRecords` accepts a `keyed` option it never reads, and computes an `agreed` variable it never uses — pre-existing dead parameters touching all 21 papers.

**CALIBRATION IS UNTESTED ON THIS PAPER, and the README says so.** All 100 rows came back HIGH, so the confidence band carries no discriminating power here and the usual "HIGH runs ~98.5% while errors sit in MED" reading cannot be checked. The one error was the key's, not the pass's, so this is not evidence of inflated confidence either — it is simply not a test of it. On 2020-I the same method produced HIGH 96 / MED 4, so the all-HIGH split is flagged to watch on the next sitting.

**A README sentence was falsified and rewritten rather than left standing.** It read "There is no third keyed sitting. The remaining 18 papers cannot be scored at all, and this bound is the whole of the evidence they will ever rest on." True when written; false two days after this exam. The replacement records what actually changed: from 2026-II onward **no future CDS sitting needs to be unkeyed**, because UPSC publishes a provisional key within days. CLAUDE.md's exam table carried the same claim ("No official key is published") and was corrected too.

**Verification.** 100/100 transcribed across five bands (0 errors, 1 warning, that warning being Q47 and source-verified twice); 273 math zones through KaTeX clean; option fidelity independently corroborated on 56 options across 14 questions against a full-resolution reading taken BEFORE any agent ran — the one defect class a blind derivation structurally cannot catch; commit inserted 100 / skipped 0 (no content-hash collision, re-confirming UPSC does not reuse Maths items across NDA and CDS); `audit:text` 7 classes clean; `audit:omml` 0 failing zones; `audit:provenance` 0 gap rows and 0 leaks; all five publish gates pass. Two new probes were built and CANARY-PROVED to fire before any clean run was trusted: `audit-answers-file.ts` (the student-facing solution audit one stage EARLIER than the DB-reading one, which is too late for the leak that put reviewer notes on 419 of 800 published rows) and `merge-pass-parts.ts` (coverage, overlap and shape across the range slices).

**Environment, reported not fixed: drive C: is 100% full** (a few hundred MB free of 476 GB). Two agents hit "No space left on device" mid-run and recovered by deleting their own crops. Only scratch that was safely reclaimable was removed; the underlying disk is the user's to decide on.



**2026-09-19 (fourth) — the provenance bracket on every question card was publishing the question's SOURCE to anonymous visitors: the founding tenant's name on 7,359 rows, a third-party publisher on 26,745, and our own derivation method on 5,171. Redacted in the read layer; superadmin keeps the raw column.**

**WHAT WAS ACTUALLY ON SCREEN.** The card footer renders `formatProvenance()` as `[questionNumber · disambiguator · year]`, and the disambiguator is `pyq_month` for NDA and `pyq_note` for every other exam. There was no gate on that span of any kind — anon, student, teacher and superadmin all saw the same string. Every one of the 72,206 PUBLIC rows carries a `pyq_note`, and a scan of them found: 7,359 naming `LWS` (`NDA English (GAT) mock — LWS English Mock Test (Dinner 4)`, `NDA Mathematics mock test 3 (LWS test series)`), 26,745 naming a third-party publisher (`Oswaal 10 Mock Test Papers, Mock Test 9`; `(Balbharati textbook, Part 2 Geometry)`; `ParikshaGruh 13136`; `Allen "Compound Angles" module exercise (Nurture course)`), and 5,171 disclosing our method to students on a public page (`No official answer key is published for this paper. The answer and solution here were derived independently by two blind passes…`, 237 characters of it). The LWS ones are precisely the branding-bug class CLAUDE.md already names — a tenant string rendered to anon — and they had been shipping on 317 indexed `/questions` pages.

**WHY A BLANKET STRIP OF `pyq_note` WAS THE WRONG FIX, AND WAS THE FIRST PLAN.** The column is one field doing two unrelated jobs. It carries either a SITTING IDENTIFIER — `10th May Shift 1`, `21 Jan 2026 Shift 1`, `CDS (I) 2017 — English` — which is load-bearing for a student because one MHT-CET month holds 14 distinct papers and this string is the only thing that says which one a question came from; or a SOURCE BLURB, which is the leak. Roughly 19,000 rows are the former and 43,000 the latter. Dropping the column wholesale would have deleted the JEE and MHT-CET shift disambiguators — the part of the line a student actually wants — to fix a problem those rows do not have. The user's instruction was to keep the question number and year and lose the blurb, and that is only expressible if the two populations can be told apart.

**LENGTH CANNOT TELL THEM APART. `question_kind` CAN.** The obvious separator is size, and it fails on inspection: `CC Botany HT — ParikshaGruh 13159` (practice, a leak) is 33 characters while `CDS (I) 2017 — Elementary Mathematics` (pyq, wanted) is 37. The bands overlap. A publisher-name denylist was the other candidate and is worse — an enumerated grep under-matches silently the first time a new corpus lands, a failure mode this project has already paid for. What does separate them is an axis that already exists. Measured on the live bank: of 34,851 `question_kind='pyq'` rows, **9** name a source and **0** say "practice"; of 37,355 `practice` rows, **22,019** name a source and 28,350 say practice/mock/worksheet/textbook. Every Oswaal, Balbharati, LWS, Cadetprep and ParikshaGruh row is a practice row by construction, because that is what those corpora are. So the rule rides on structure and never on spelling.

**THE TWO CLASSES `question_kind` MISSES, AND THE GAP THAT CATCHES THEM.** Two populations are genuinely `pyq` yet still narrative: the CBSE-12 and MH-HSC-12 board notes (`chapterwise compilation, March 2016-February 2025; no 2021, exams cancelled`) and 9 JEE questions reprinted from an Allen module. A length cap catches those, and the cap is safe because of a measured gap rather than taste: after stripping a trailing `[…]` bracket, `pyq` notes are either **≤38 characters (30,332 rows, every one an identifier) or ≥93 (4,519 rows, every one narrative)** — nothing lands in between. The cap is 48, sitting in 54 characters of empty space. The bracket strip is anchored to the END on purpose: a bracket mid-note is part of a label (a paper code, a set letter) and must survive, and the cap is measured AFTER the strip, since the CDS General Knowledge notes are 237 characters raw and ~32 once the disclosure comes off — measuring first would have silently dropped all 2,280 of their sitting labels.

**PROVEN BY ENUMERATING THE SURVIVORS, NOT BY GREPPING FOR NAMES I PICKED.** The first verification was a count of `oswaal`/`balbharati`/`lws` against the rule — all three went to zero, and that check is nearly worthless, because it can only confirm the names already on it. The check that holds up is the inverse: list every distinct string that still publishes and read it. There are **200 of them, covering 30,332 rows**, and every single one is a date, a shift, a paper number, or an official session label (`NDA 1`, `Paper 26`, `NEET (UG) 2023 — 07 May 2023`, `Re-NEET (UG) 2024 — 23 Jun 2024`). Not one names a publisher, a brand, or a method. A publisher can now only slip through by being disguised as a date, which the enumeration rules out. Two harmless things surfaced from reading the set: `Shift ||` (147 rows, pipes instead of Roman `II`, an old ingest typo now visible on cards) and `Paper 1`…`Paper 26` (~1,500 JEE rows, uninformative but not a leak).

**REDACTED IN THE READ LAYER, NOT AT RENDER, AND THAT IS THE LOAD-BEARING CHOICE.** A render gate would have hidden the bracket while leaving the blurb in the RSC payload of every ISR-cached page, readable from page source — one cached copy is served to everyone. Doing it in `queryQuestionsByIds` means the string never leaves the server for a non-superadmin. `includeRawProvenance` is default-OFF so a new caller that has not thought about this gets the safe behaviour, and the cached routes cannot opt in by accident (they have no identity to resolve during a prerender anyway). `publicPyqNote` likewise fails closed on an unknown `question_kind`, so a caller that has not plumbed the column through redacts rather than publishes. `pyqYear` is deliberately NOT stripped — `/formula` sorts and filters on it.

**SUPERADMIN PASSTHROUGH IS ONLY POSSIBLE WHERE THE SERVER KNOWS THE VIEWER.** `/browse`, `/saved` and the paper editor resolve identity during render and pass the flag; `/questions`, `/formula`, `/guide` worked examples and the `/notes` print sheet are cached and stay redacted for everyone, which is fail-closed and correct — reading identity on those routes is what de-cached the entire site once before. Two traps in the plumbing: `canEdit` could NOT be reused as the signal (it is superadmin on `/browse` but plain org-member on `/saved`, so reusing it would have leaked to teachers), and on `/saved` a superadmin holds no `org_members` row at all, so `getSessionSuperadmin()` had to be added alongside the membership lookup. `loadWorkedExamples` feeds BOTH `/guide` and the notes print sheet through the shared `WorkedExample` type, so one fix covered two surfaces.

**THE WIRING TEST EXISTS BECAUSE THE HELPER TEST CANNOT SEE THE DEFECT.** 33 unit tests prove the rule and would all pass if `queryQuestionsByIds` had never called it — the failure mode here is an omission at the call site. So a separate suite inserts real `practice` and `pyq` fixtures, reads them back through the real query, and asserts what the page would receive. It was then fault-injected: reverting the mapping to `r.pyq_note` made exactly the two redaction assertions fail, confirming the test detects the omission rather than passing on the shape of the data.

**VERIFIED ON ARTIFACTS AND ON THE RUNNING PAGE.** Build output: 1,437 prerendered `.html` files (caching intact, not 0) with **0 provenance leaks** across `.html` and `.rsc` — the 6 surviving "Balbharati" hits are question content (a Class-9 History question whose option IS "Balbharati") and solution prose (a teaching note about what the Std XII chapter covers), neither of which is an attribution. `/browse` is a dynamic `ƒ` route the build never renders, so it was fetched live and confirmed to have compiled (`Compiling /browse` in the dev log — a 200 alone proves nothing on a middleware-matched route). On the page from the original report, `[3.1 SolvedEx.1 · Maharashtra State Board (Class 9) — Triangles (Balbharati textbook, Part 2 Geometry)]` now renders `[3.1 SolvedEx.1]`; MH-HSC-12 board rows render `[Q. 5 · 2026]` in place of a 261-character narrative; and the disambiguators that had to survive did — `[Q93 · 26 April Shift II · 2025]`, `[Q40 · 23 January 2025 · 2025]`. The SUPERADMIN view is auth-gated and therefore NOT proven headlessly; that check belongs to a human in a browser.

**THE STANDING PROBE EXISTS BECAUSE THE GAP IS A PROPERTY OF DATA.** `npm run audit:provenance` re-runs the enumeration and reports two things the gate chain is blind to: rows landing between the cap and the narrative floor (a new corpus at 55 characters would lose its sitting id in silence, and nothing else would notice), and a weak denylist backstop that is documented as weak. Triage, exits 0, deliberately not in prepush because its findings move on an ingest rather than on a push. First run: 30,332 published across 200 distinct notes, 41,874 redacted, **0 gap rows, 0 leaks**.

**2026-09-19 (third) — `answer_correct` had a label, a CHECK-constraint slot and zero rows since migration 0052. It also described itself as something it had never been. Mocks now record a RECOVERY, and the definition of "correct" turned out to be the trap.**

**THE DEFECT WAS NOT "NO EMITTER" — IT WAS A DEFINITION THAT HAD NEVER BEEN TRUE.** `/drill` does emit `answer_correct` (shipped the day before), so the 0 rows meant only that nobody had taken a drill yet. What was actually wrong sat in the kind's own description: `events.ts` said *"got a question right in a **graded mock**"* and `shape.ts` labelled it *"Mock question correct"* — while the sole emitter was the drill. `answer_wrong` fired from mocks; its mirror never had. The asymmetry was undeclared anywhere, and both comments asserted the opposite of the code.

**SYMMETRY WAS MEASURED AND REJECTED, WHICH IS WHY THIS IS CONDITIONAL.** The obvious fix — emit on every correct mock answer — costs **20,250 rows** (more than doubling `user_activity`) to change the drill pool by **484 questions, 4.7% of the 10,395 ever missed**. The ratio is that poor because students rarely meet the same question twice: only 2,056 of ~31,000 answered instances were repeats, and a correct answer to a never-missed question cannot remove anything from a pool it was never in. So the rule became: record a correct answer ONLY where the student had already missed that question. **537 rows instead of 20,250, for the identical outcome.** The cost is stated in three places, because it is a real one: `answer_correct` is now CONDITIONAL and a count of it is NOT "questions answered correctly" — its only honest denominator is `answer_wrong`. The label became **"Question recovered"**.

**GRACE IS SCORED AS CORRECT, AND THAT NEARLY POISONED THE WHOLE BACKFILL.** `verdictFor` returns `1` for a grace question — one the paper officially forgives — *regardless of whether the student answered at all*. A naive `verdict === 1` rule would have written "you recovered this" for questions nobody attempted, and two such rows RETIRE a question out of the drill permanently. Found by reading `verdictFor` before writing the rule rather than after; the existing wrong-answer emitter skips grace for the mirror reason, and a test now pins it. **The same trap ruled out the cheap backfill**: deriving correctness by joining `attempt_answers` to `options.is_correct` in SQL is blind to grace AND to JEE Section-B numeric answers. The evidence it mattered is quantitative — that SQL predicts 559 rows where the real grader produces 537, and those 22 are exactly the rows it would have got wrong. Hence `regradeAttempt`, which replays the live `getMockById → loadAnswerKey → loadSavedAnswers → gradeMock` chain.

**CHRONOLOGY IS LOAD-BEARING IN THE BACKFILL.** "Previously missed" means *as of that attempt*, so attempts are walked OLDEST FIRST with the missed set growing as the walk proceeds. Asking "has this student ever missed this?" against today's data would let a September mistake justify a July recovery — a claim about the past that was not true when it was made. Rows are backdated to the attempt's `submitted_at`, the same discipline as the expiry sweep earlier the same day.

**Verified against a captured before-state, including the invariant rather than just the count:** 0 → **537 rows, 29 students**, oldest 2026-07-18, newest 2026-09-12, **0 stamped today**, and — the check that actually matters — **0 recoveries lacking a prior recorded miss of the same question by the same student**. Idempotency was PROVEN, not claimed: a second full `--apply` left 537 rows, 537 distinct dedupe keys, 0 duplicates. Both the live emitter and the backfill write `answer_correct:<attemptId>:<questionId>`, because keying only the backfill would double-write for anything graded between deploy and run. Drill effect visible on the heaviest student: `due` 223 → 220, with 8/8 still getting a full five.

**One risk measured and accepted rather than guarded:** 52 questions reach two recoveries and would be retired, of which only **4** rest on same-session evidence (both corrects under an hour apart). Four out of 10,395 did not justify a gap rule that would complicate the ladder.

**2026-09-19 (second) — 118 mock attempts had been stranded mid-paper since July, because the only thing that ever expired a timer was a browser tab. The sweep ships, the backlog clears, and the backdate is the part that matters.**

**THE LEAK.** `submitAttempt(id, "expired")` has existed since the mock runner shipped and does everything an abandoned attempt needs — grades it, writes the section breakdown, emits `mock_submitted` plus one `answer_wrong` per missed question. The only caller that ever passed `"expired"` was `MockRunner.tsx`, client-side, **with the tab open**. A student who closed their laptop mid-paper left the row in `in_progress` permanently: no score, no result page, no findings card, and not one of their mistakes reaching the engagement spine. Nothing server-side ever noticed, because nothing was looking — no script in `scripts/mocks/`, no scheduled workflow. Measured 2026-09-19: **118 attempts, 1,285 answered questions, 84 students, oldest 2026-07-10, and still accruing** (the newest was the day before). Six weeks of silent loss, and the count had never been reported anywhere because `in_progress` reads as "in progress".

**THE STAMP IS THE DESIGN, NOT THE SELECTION.** Selecting expired attempts is trivial; deciding what timestamp their submit carries is not. `submitAttempt` stamped `submitted_at = new Date()`, so grading a July attempt in September would have recorded it as *sat in September*. That is not a cosmetic lie: `readReportCandidates` selects on `submitted_at >= SINCE`, so the whole backlog would have become email candidates and **82 students would have been mailed a cheerful report about a mock they walked away from in July** — the first thing to happen when the dormant email channel is switched back on, which is the very next item on the list. Backdating to the attempt's own `expires_at` drops that exposure to **2**, both of which expired within the last day and for which a report is the feature working correctly. The same stamp reaches the drill: `buildActivityRow` writes an explicit `created_at` and `logActivityBatch` already accepted a `nowMs`, so a July mistake now sorts in the drill ladder as a July mistake. **Verified rather than assumed** — `created_at` is exactly the column `lib/drill/query.ts` reads.

**THE AUDIT FIELD IS NOT THE CLAIM FIELD, and I got this wrong first.** The initial patch backdated `updated_at` alongside `submitted_at`. `submitted_at` is a claim about when the *student* stopped and belongs in the past; `updated_at` is a row-audit field and the row was genuinely being touched *now*. Backdating both erased the only trace of when the sweep ran — and the symptom was immediate and self-inflicted: the verification query, which filtered on `updated_at >= now() - 2 hours`, returned **zero rows for a sweep that had just graded 118 attempts**. Every other write site in the same file, including one twelve lines up, already used real-now. Fixed in code and repaired on all 118 rows. **The general shape: when a backfill rewrites time, sort the columns into "claims about the world" and "records of what we did", and only backdate the first.**

**WHY A SCHEDULE AND NOT A READ-PATH HOOK** (the user's call, from three options). Grading lazily when something next loads the attempt is cheaper and needs no infrastructure — and would never have fired for a single one of these 118, because the defining property of the backlog is that nobody ever opens those attempts again. Only something that goes looking finds them. Hourly, 30-minute grace; `submitAttempt`'s `status='in_progress'` guard makes the grace belt-and-braces rather than load-bearing, and makes the job safe to re-run.

**Result, verified against a captured before-state:** `in_progress` 118 → **0**; `expired` 77 → 195; `mock_submitted` +118; `answer_wrong` +184; students with any drill fuel **132 → 152**, so roughly twenty students now have a weak-area drill that did not exist for them yesterday. 116 of the 118 correctly excluded from the email cutoff, 2 correctly inside it. `drill:smoke` still 8/8. Backup taken and verified first (43.9 MB, 87 tables) — the threat model for a bulk write is our own scripts.

**Two smaller things.** The identifying signature for "which rows did the sweep touch" turned out to be `activity.created_at = attempt.submitted_at` **exactly** — a live submit stamps the row and logs a few milliseconds later, so exact equality is the backfill's alone. And `lib/mocks/service.ts` kept its `server-only` guard rather than following the project convention of dropping it so a `tsx` script can import the module: that guard protects the code that decides students' scores, so the resolver is satisfied script-side instead (`scripts/lib/serverOnly.ts`). The convention is right in general and wrong for this module.

**2026-09-19 — `/drill` ships: the first reader `answer_wrong` has ever had. No migration, no new table, and the live smoke caught a defect the unit tests could not.**

For fourteen months the engagement spine recorded every question a student missed in a timed mock and showed them to nobody. By the time this was built that was **10,401 `answer_wrong` rows over 132 students, an average of 79 recorded mistakes each**, and every reader of them was staff-side — /dashboard/pmf, the student detail page. The 2026-07-12 Phase-A note said the spine existed so a mechanic could be added later without re-deriving behaviour from scattered tables. This is the first mechanic to take it up, and the claim held: it needed no schema change of any kind.

**NO MIGRATION, VERIFIED RATHER THAN HOPED.** `drill_completed` and `answer_correct` were already in migration 0052's CHECK constraint — both reserved from the start, both emitterless, both sitting on the explicit UNBUILT list in `tests/pmf-snapshot.test.ts`. `drill_completed` had even carried the PMF label "Weak-area drills" since 0103, a feature name for a feature that did not exist. Shipping the drill emptied that list, and the test keeps its teeth: the next kind added to ACTIVITY_KINDS without a surface still fails there.

**NO NEW TABLE, AND THAT IS THE DESIGN.** A question's state is a FOLD over its own ordered wrong/correct events, so "what is still broken" is derived on every read and never stored. A `drill_state` column would be a second copy of an answer the events already give, free to drift from them — the same rule `question_item_stats` follows in refusing to store a pooled number it can compute at read time.

**THE LADDER IS THE USER'S CALL, AND THE REASON IS THE GUESSING FLOOR.** Wrong puts a question in the pool; one correct answer puts it to SLEEP for ten days; a second correct answer, on the far side of that gap, retires it; a wrong answer at any point sends it straight back with the streak reset. A four-option MCQ answered right once, a day after being missed, is weak evidence of durable recall — one student in four who had learned nothing would manage it. The offered alternative of retiring on the first correct was rejected for exactly that, and the stricter two-in-separate-sessions reading is what shipped.

**GRADING IS SERVER-SIDE AND THE PAYLOAD CARRIES NEITHER KEY NOR SOLUTION.** This is not ceremony about a secret — the answer to any PUBLIC question is one click away on /browse. It is that the verdict is written into `user_activity` and *that row decides whether the question is ever served again*. A client-asserted verdict would let a browser retire its own questions, which turns the whole spaced-repetition ladder into decoration. So `/api/drill/answer` reads the key at grade time from the row being graded, and the key and solution reach the client for the first time in that response, after a choice is committed. The drill payload follows `getPublicQuizBySlug`'s posture: stem and options only.

**THE BEST-EFFORT WRITE IS SAFE HERE, AND IT IS WORTH SAYING WHY RATHER THAN INHERITING IT.** `logActivity` swallows its errors by design, which would normally be a poor fit for a write this load-bearing. It is fine because the direction it fails in is the safe one: a lost `answer_correct` leaves the question DUE, so the student simply sees it again. There is no way for a dropped write to retire a question that was not actually fixed. Extra practice is the worst case, and that is not worth blocking an answer over.

**THE SMOKE FOUND A REAL DEFECT THAT 24 PASSING UNIT TESTS DID NOT.** The first interleaver grouped on the (chapter, subtopic) PAIR — which is how the rest of this repo keys a subtopic, correctly, since a subtopic name is unique only within its chapter. As the single rotation axis it is wrong: a chapter with several weak subtopics wins the rotation repeatedly. `npm run drill:smoke` over the eight heaviest students showed one drawing **three of five from Grammar** (Sentence Completion, Discourse Markers, Correct Sentence Identification) plus two from one geography chapter. Technically five distinct subtopics, and unmistakably blocked practice — the precise thing interleaving exists to prevent. The rotation is now two-level: chapters outside, subtopics within a chapter's turn, one `roundRobin` helper applied at both. The same student now draws five different chapters. **The unit test that "passed" asserted five distinct SUBTOPICS, which is exactly the assertion the bug satisfied** — a reminder that a property test is only as good as the axis it names.

**Mobile-first, because the user said so mid-build.** One question per screen, full-width option targets, the single forward control pinned to the bottom of the viewport, no palette (five questions need no navigation, and a palette invites skipping ahead). An answer cannot be changed after it is committed: a question you can re-pick after seeing the answer measures nothing.

**WHAT IS NOT PROVEN.** `/drill` is auth-gated `ƒ` AND its runner is behind a tap, so it is doubly unverifiable from here — the build proves compilation, 24 + 11 unit tests prove the ladder and the boundary, and `drill:smoke` proves the read chain on live data (8/8 heaviest students get a full five, all MCQ, all four options, no `is_correct` in the payload). None of them renders markup, the smoke reads service-role where the page uses the student's JWT, and nothing here writes — so the grade → record → question-goes-quiet loop is closed only by a person taking a real drill on a real phone.

**Deliberately NOT done:** a primary-nav tab (that nav is public and most traffic is anon, who have no drill), a count on the /me card (computing it honestly costs the whole drill read; the cheap version can only overstate, and the true number is one tap away on /drill itself), and the "3 more like it" transfer half, which needs an unseen/difficulty-matched picker and is the deferred sibling of this pass.

**2026-09-18 (tenth) — the mock result screen stops being a dead end: the per-attempt diagnosis now renders where the student already is, and `AttemptsList` stops prefetching the page that got expensive.**

Measured before building anything. 619 finished mocks in production, and the result page's entire forward path was a score, three tallies, a **Retake** button and a link to the catalogue. `/performance` — the same diagnosis in full, shipped hours earlier under migration 0110 — was linked from exactly one place in the whole product: the UserMenu popover. CLAUDE.md's engagement gate says in as many words that feedback fires at the TRIGGER SURFACE and never on a dashboard the student has to go and find, so this was not a missing nicety, it was the gate's own rule being broken at the one moment the product had the student's full attention.

**THE CARD IS THE EMAIL'S FINDINGS, FROM THE EMAIL'S OWN CORE.** `buildMockReport` already decides all of this and its GRAIN SPLIT is load-bearing: per-question facts are scoped to THIS attempt because a question is a fact needing no sample size, while subtopic picks are POOLED across every paper because one sitting gives a chapter a median of three questions and 29% exactly one. A second derivation on the page would have agreed on the day it was written and drifted afterwards — the failure mode this repo has already paid for twice with `parseTableBlocks`. So the page calls the same function, and the headings match the email's wording (`Easy marks you dropped`, `Easy ones you looked at and left`, `Pacing`, `Where your next marks are`, and the pooling sentence "Across every paper you've sat, not just this one"). What the card adds is the one thing an email cannot: links. Each question anchors to `#q<position>` on its own review card further down the same page, and each subtopic opens `/go/practice` on that topic.

**THE PREFETCH HAZARD WAS THE REAL PREREQUISITE, AND IT WAS FOUND BEFORE SHIPPING RATHER THAN AFTER.** The card's data is `get_own_performance` — the student's whole answer history, and the *same RPC shape* that took `/dashboard/students/[id]/performance` down on 2026-09-15 (5 concurrent calls fine, 9 → 7 failed, 12 → 12 failed with 57014). `AttemptsList` renders one `<Link>` per attempt and is rendered on `/me` and `/mock/attempts` with no `prefetch={false}`, which cost nothing while the result page was cheap. The moment the card landed it would have meant a student with ten sittings firing ten full-history reads on page load, from links nobody clicked. `prefetch={false}` went on first, pinned by `tests/mock-result-no-prefetch.test.ts` — a separate file from the existing `dashboard-students-no-prefetch.test.ts` because that one scans whole directories and this one follows a specific expensive ROUTE, and it uses the same count-based technique for the reason the sibling documents (JSX attributes wrap across lines and contain `>` inside arrow functions, so a tag-parsing regex is a probe that can silently stop matching).

**NO PEER PERCENTAGES, AND THE REASON IS RLS RATHER THAN TASTE.** `question_item_stats` carries a single SELECT policy — `current_user_org_id() IS NOT NULL OR current_user_is_superadmin()` — so a student, who has no org row by construction, cannot read it at all. The page therefore passes an EMPTY `PeerMap` and the card shows no "x% of students got this right". Reaching for it would have meant a service-role read on a student-facing page plus a product decision about showing one student how the cohort did, which is the kind of peer comparison the engagement gate is deliberately careful about. **The honest cost, recorded so it is not rediscovered as a bug:** `rankWrong` sorts on peer evidence first, so without it the on-screen picks fall back to dwell-then-position and can name different questions than the email would for the same attempt. That divergence is currently theoretical — the report email is forward-only and dry-run by default, and has sent nothing — but it is real and it is the thing to fix first if peer evidence is ever opened up.

**THE FIXTURE FOUND A LIVE PROPERTY WORTH KNOWING.** The first test of the pooled picks returned an empty list, and the cause was not the code: `buildPerformance` drops any attempt answering less than `ENGAGEMENT_FLOOR` (20%) of its paper before a lane exists, and the fixture declared a 120-question paper with four facts. The fixture was fixed rather than the floor, and the behaviour it exposed is the live one — **a barely-engaged sitting gets no subtopic picks at all**. `npm run findings:smoke` over the twelve most recent production attempts shows exactly that shape: **12 of 12 render the card, but only 3 carry subtopic picks**, because most of that sample never reached 20% of the paper. For those students the card leads with pacing (`you never reached 108 questions`), which is the correct finding for someone who answered twelve of a hundred and twenty.

**Two duplications closed on the way**, both of the kind that would have drifted: `focusAreas.ts`'s private `practiceHref` became a call to a shared, tested `goPracticeHref` in `links.ts` (which also names `UNCLASSIFIED` — the RPC's coalesce label that can never resolve to a taxonomy row, so every link builder has to drop it), and the email template's private `where`/`marks` formatters moved into `mockReport.ts` as `formatWhere`/`formatMarks` so the two surfaces cannot start rounding the same marks differently.

**WHAT IS NOT PROVEN, stated rather than implied.** The result page and `/me` are auth-gated `ƒ`, so `next build` never renders either: the gate proves compilation, the 5,556 unit tests prove the rules, and `findings:smoke` proves the data chain — none of them prove LAYOUT, and the smoke reads with the service role where the page uses the student's JWT, so the RLS path is untested here too. The browser pass is owed and only a person can do it. Prerendered `.html` count 1,426 before and after, so nothing was de-cached.

**2026-09-18 (ninth) — the context budget itself: eight already-archived digests evicted from the Decisions log, MEMORY.md brought under a ceiling, and a reconciliation that says which entries an archive sweep would DELETE rather than move.**

The brief was "how do I minimise context pollution", answered from measurement rather than advice: CLAUDE.md at 127.9 KB and MEMORY.md at 20.5 KB are both loaded before a session does anything, so the fixed cost was ~38k tokens, every session, whatever the task. The Decisions log sat at 99% of its own ceiling.

**THE EVICTION DELETED NOTHING, AND THAT WAS ESTABLISHED PER TAG RATHER THAN ASSUMED.** The rule in CLAUDE.md is that an entry is archived by MOVING it. The cheaper version of that — delete the digest, because the long form is already in DECISIONS_HISTORY.md — is only safe if the long form really is there. It was, for all eight: 2026-09-17 (second) and everything older. Verified twice, once before removing and once after against `git show HEAD:CLAUDE.md`, and the archived versions are strict supersets (the 2026-09-15 (seventh) narrative carries seven sub-bullets against the digest's four). The cut boundary is therefore not a date somebody liked the look of — it IS the archive's coverage line.

**BOTH POINTER HEADERS WERE STALE, IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS, AND NEITHER WAS READABLE AS WRONG.** CLAUDE.md's note said the September narratives lived under `### 2026-09-01 to 2026-09-14`. The archive's own header said `to 2026-09-16`. The batch actually held entries through 2026-09-18. Three claims, no two agreeing, and every one of them plausible in isolation — the only way to catch it is to diff the tags a header claims against the tags it contains. The header is now derived from the batch's real span and says so.

**THE FINDING THAT CHANGED THE SHAPE OF THE WORK: the two-places convention has NOT been holding.** Having established the eight were safe, the natural next claim was that the remaining eleven were the newest and therefore unarchived. Written into the note, and wrong — a grep for `- **<tag>` missed that the archive mixes TWO heading shapes, a bulleted entry and a bare `**tag — ...**` paragraph. Four of the eleven had narratives after all; seven did not. So the honest statement is neither "all are archived" nor "none are": it is a per-tag question nobody can answer by eye, and the first two attempts to answer it by eye were both wrong. A routine sweep of those seven would have destroyed them silently — the exact outcome the MOVING rule exists to prevent.

**Hence `reconcileArchive`, which is the durable artifact and the reason this entry is not just a cleanup.** It parses both heading shapes, compares tags WHOLE (substring matching reports "2026-09-18" as present inside "2026-09-18 (third)" — that false positive is what made the first hand-check wrong, and it has its own test), and names the entries with no long form behind them. `npm run docs:budget` now prints those seven by name. Warning-only: it reports a debt in the writing convention, not a defect in the tree, and failing a push over it would block unrelated work. It reproduced the hand reconciliation exactly, which is the only reason to trust either.

**MEMORY.md was 16% of CLAUDE.md's cost and bounded by nothing.** `docs:budget` existed precisely because an always-loaded file is a runtime cost rather than a docs-tidiness question, and then measured only one of the two always-loaded files. Ceiling set at 24,000 bytes against a live 20.1 KB, the same "headroom, but it still binds" posture as the other two.

**ABSENT IS NOT ZERO AND NOT A PASS.** MEMORY.md lives under `~/.claude`, outside the repo, so it is present on this machine and absent in CI. Failing there would block every push over a file the repo does not own; passing there would let a green OK imply a budget nobody checked. It reports NOT MEASURED, prints the path it looked at, and the token line says which files it counted. The pure core takes `string | null` and distinguishes `""` from `null` deliberately — an empty index is a real measurement of zero, and a truthiness check would file it as unmeasured; that distinction has its own test.

**The path derivation is allowed to fail, and did, visibly.** Claude Code slugs a project by its absolute path with the drive colon, both separators and underscores folded to "-". The first attempt missed backslashes (Windows `cwd()` uses them) and the lowercased drive letter, and resolved to `C:\Users\vilas\.claude\projects\C-\Users\...` — which the NOT MEASURED branch printed in full, naming its own bug. That is why the branch prints the path rather than a bare "not found". If the slug scheme ever changes, the gate degrades to NOT MEASURED instead of lying.

**Result: 34,869 tokens per session against ~38,000, with the Decisions log at 67% of its ceiling instead of 99%.** The honest framing is that the eviction bought ~3k tokens and the gate bought none at all — what the gate buys is that the next sweep cannot quietly delete seven entries. Gate green: 349 files, 5,544 tests.


**2026-09-18 (sixth) — the daily quiz recorded nothing for a signed-in student, and had not for the 15 months it has been live. `quiz_taken` gets its emitter, `/quiz/attempts` its reader, the reveal gate a sign-in door, and the results share the tags it never had.**

The brief was three questions about the quiz funnel: should the gate ask for a signup instead of name and phone, how does a signed-in user see their score, and how does anyone see past performance. The second and third turned out to answer the first.

**A SIGNED-IN STUDENT'S QUIZ WENT NOWHERE.** `resolveQuizGate` returns "skip" for them, the authed branch of the submit route grades and returns, and no lead is written — deliberately, since signed-in students are meant to stay out of the sales funnel. But nothing was written in the lead's place either. The score lived in React state and died on refresh. There was no `/quiz/attempts` to mirror `/mock/attempts`, and nothing to build one from.

**A KIND WITH THREE LABELS AND NO EMITTER.** `quiz_taken` has been in `ACTIVITY_KINDS` and in the 0052 DB CHECK since the spine was built, and renders a label in three separate surfaces — "Quiz taken" in `activity/shape.ts`, "Daily quiz" in `pmf/snapshot.ts`, "Took a quiz" in `students/profileView.ts`. A grep for emit sites across `src/` and `scripts/` returned none, and prod agreed: zero rows, ever. Meanwhile `/dashboard/pmf` rendered "Daily quiz" with a real-looking zero. This is the fourth instance of the class 0107 (guide reveals) and 0108 (board reveals) were written about, and the first where the surface was missing from `SURFACE_COVERAGE` altogether rather than described wrongly — the header of that array claims it was "Audited 2026-09-17 against the route handlers".

**THE GUARD THAT SHOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT WAS ONE-DIRECTIONAL.** `tests/pmf-snapshot.test.ts` asserted that every kind *named by a surface* is a real activity kind. Nothing asserted the reverse. A funnel the map never mentioned therefore could not fail anything — the map was not wrong about what it said, it simply did not say. The new assertion walks `ACTIVITY_KINDS` and requires each to be claimed by a `SURFACE_COVERAGE` row or to sit on an explicit `UNBUILT` list. Two qualify: `answer_correct` (reserved beside `answer_wrong`, of which only the wrong half is emitted, as drill fuel) and `drill_completed` (a future phase). Both were verified emitterless rather than assumed, and the exemption is symmetric — a kind on that list must NOT be claimed by a surface either, so the list cannot quietly become a dumping ground.

**THE SIGNUP QUESTION, ANSWERED FROM THE DATA RATHER THAN FROM TASTE.** Cross-referencing `quiz_leads.mobile` against `student_profiles.mobile`: **5 of the 13 distinct lead mobiles already belong to an account**. Those students were signed out, re-typed a number we already hold, and were filed as anonymous sales leads — getting no history, while the dashboard gained a duplicate. That is the real defect the question was circling. A signup WALL is still the wrong answer: `/quiz` exists for cold traffic, [[signup-gate-placement]] says gate the reward and not the door, and an account carries no mobile (it is optional on `student_profiles`), so replacing the phone gate would make the sales funnel strictly worse. The fix is a second door, not a taller one.

**AND THAT DOOR WOULD HAVE EATEN THE QUIZ.** Answers are React state only; the existing `qb:lead:v1` key stores the visitor's IDENTITY, not the attempt. A plain link to `/login` would have destroyed a quiz the student had just finished answering — invisible in review, obvious to the first student who tapped it. `lib/quiz/resume.ts` writes the answers to sessionStorage first, and reads them back as UNTRUSTED input, because the user can edit that store: non-object payloads, non-letter values, keys that are not question positions and an entry count above 100 are all dropped, and an empty result after filtering returns null rather than bouncing the student to a review screen with a blank answer sheet. The key is consumed whether or not it parsed, so a corrupt blob cannot resurrect itself on every later visit.

**THE SHARE WAS NOT UNMEASURED — IT WAS MISATTRIBUTED, WHICH IS WORSE.** The results screen has shared a bare `window.location.origin` URL with no campaign tags since 2026-06-09. I assumed those arrivals were invisible; reading `parseAcquisition` showed otherwise. WhatsApp strips the referrer, so the click arrives with no tags and no referrer host, falls through to the `if (!refHost)` branch, and is stored as `source: "direct"`. Every signup the quiz loop has ever produced was credited to nobody. Two organic leads landed during this session, both with `utm_source` null. `lib/quiz/share.ts` mirrors `lib/mocks/share.ts` rather than importing from it: that module shipped the day before, reworking it is out of scope here, and what the two share is a canonical host and three query params. Consolidation is logged as a backfill candidate.

**WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT.** No per-question review on the history page: a signed-in taker's answers are not stored anywhere (`quiz_leads.answers` exists only on the anon path) and an analytics log's schemaless jsonb is the wrong home for them — mocks have `mock_attempts` for exactly this. The page says so rather than leaving the omission looking like a bug. No `share_events` row for a quiz share either: that needs a migration to widen a CHECK constrained to `'mock'` plus a route change, and the inbound tag is the larger half of the value. The score still leads the quiz share message, unlike the mock share which defaults to the paper — a real inconsistency, but a product call rather than a defect, and it belongs in its own change.

**VERIFICATION.** 100 unit tests across the seven affected suites. Probe rows inserted into prod `user_activity` and read back through the loader and the shaping core — including a deliberately malformed row whose `"seven"` score came through as null rather than NaN and whose absent `ref_id` came through as an unlinked entry — then deleted. Both probes confirmed to have reached the code by the `Compiling /api/public-quiz/submit` and `Compiling /quiz/attempts` lines in the dev log, after the server bound to port 3003 rather than 3000. `quiz_leads` grew by two during the session; both rows were checked and are organic. **NOT verified: the authenticated POST actually writing a row.** There is no session cookie available from this machine and the repo has no jsdom or Playwright, so the emitter's wiring rests on typecheck plus the unit tests plus a hand-inserted row proving the DB accepts it. The gate sheet and the results link are click-gated inside a modal and are likewise unproven at the layout level.

**2026-09-18 (fifth) — the mock result screen gets a share button and `/mock/[slug]` gets a link-preview card (migration 0109 `share_events`). The brief was "how do I get 10,000 users in a month"; the funnel said the product works and nothing carries it anywhere.**

The numbers that chose this work, read before any of it was written: 348 accounts, 236 of them in the last 30 days, the weekly trend 25 → 43 → 73 → 72. 183 of 348 students (53%) have sat a mock, 733 attempts, four per student. That is not a leaky product — it is a product with no distribution. And 733 finished mocks had produced **zero** outbound events, because the only share affordance in the entire app was `ShareMock`, which is staff-gated (`{member && <ShareMock/>}`) and lives on the catalogue page rather than the result screen.

**THE RESULT PAGE IS NOT SHAREABLE, AND THAT SHAPES THE WHOLE FEATURE.** `/mock/attempt/<id>/result` is per-attempt, auth-gated and `robots: index:false`; a recipient opening it is redirected to `/mock`, never to a test. So the thing being shared has to be `/mock/<slug>`, the public instructions page — which turned out to have `generateMetadata` with a title and description and **no `opengraph-image` at all**. Every mock link ever pasted into a WhatsApp group has previewed as bare text. The quiz funnel's card has existed since 2026-06-09 and its own comment puts the effect at roughly double the click-through; the share button makes the mock page the highest-volume link this app emits, so the card is arguably more than half the value of the day's work.

**THE SCORE IS OPT-IN AND OFF BY DEFAULT — the one genuine product decision here.** The obvious build is "I scored 186/300, beat that". Two things are wrong with it. The first is volume: a score-forward share only fires for students who did well, so the loop samples the top of the distribution and loses most of its traffic. The second is that it is a leaderboard wearing a different hat. The engagement-principles gate in CLAUDE.md forbids leaderboards specifically because they "demotivate the bottom half in a known-peer setting", and a class WhatsApp group is the most known-peer setting there is — scores broadcast into it rebuild the ranking the gate exists to prevent. Defaulting the message to the PAPER lets a student who scored 61/300 still pass it on, and the checkbox keeps the louder version available to anyone who wants it. `included_score` is stored so the choice can eventually be measured rather than argued.

**A TABLE, NOT AN ACTIVITY KIND.** `user_activity` is a closed, learning-anchored allowlist — every kind in it is something a student learns from — and `export_events` (0104) already set the precedent in its own header for exactly this situation. Filing a share there would put it in `FEATURE_LABELS` and the per-feature retention-lift table as though sharing were a feature students learn from, diluting both readings. It would also have tripped the bijection test added the day before.

**WHY MEASURE THE OUTBOUND SIDE AT ALL, given 0106 already attributes the inbound?** Because zero signups from shares is ambiguous on its own: it reads identically whether nobody tapped the button or plenty did and nobody clicked through, and those call for opposite fixes (change the affordance vs change the card). The two together give the ratios that actually describe a loop — shares per attempt, signups per share. What a row does NOT prove is that anything was sent: `navigator.share()` resolves when the OS sheet closes and never reports the chosen app, and a `wa.me` tap can be abandoned. The table records INTENT TO SHARE and the migration header says so.

**THE UTM TRIPLE NEEDED NO NEW CODE.** `parseAcquisition` (0106) already reads `utm_source`/`utm_medium`/`utm_campaign` and already classifies `whatsapp` and `telegram` as channels, so a tagged inbound click attributes itself end to end. That is not a nicety — **WhatsApp strips the referrer**, so without the tag every arrival from this loop would be indistinguishable from direct traffic, and "direct is not a first touch" means 0106 would have stored nothing at all. The channel is named honestly: only the explicit WhatsApp button claims `whatsapp`; the OS sheet is `share`, because it never tells us where it went. Same rule as the 0107 surfaces — an unknown value is stated as unknown, never defaulted to a plausible one.

**TWO VERIFICATION TRAPS, ONE OF THEM MINE.** The first: the OG route curled a clean `500` three times before the dev log showed the server had bound to **port 3002**, ports 3000 and 3001 being occupied — the curl had been hitting an unrelated process, and that 500 said nothing whatever about this code. Textbook "probe must reach the code": check the log for the compile line before believing any status. The second, once the probe did reach it: a real `500` from `@vercel/og` on a mangled font path — the bundled TTF's file:// URL is turned into a relative Windows path and then not found. The discriminating test was to curl the **shipped, production-working quiz card** — which fails identically. Both routes share the same bundled font loader, so the fault is in what they share and the new route is neither implicated nor proven. What WAS proven: the loader, against live data (`NDA` 120 q / 300 marks / 150 min, `CDS` 120 q / 100 marks / 120 min, an unknown slug returning null for the generic fallback), and that the snapshot column never comes back.

**`getMockCardBySlug` exists because of a fix made eleven days earlier.** `getMockBySlug` carries `questions` — the ordered snapshot — and the listing query was rewritten on 2026-09-07 precisely because dragging that across the network to render facts is a measured 53x overfetch. Printing a title and three numbers onto a card is the same mistake, so the OG route got a listing-columns read of its own.

**Also checked, because the cost of not checking is the whole site:** prerendered `.html` count 1,426 before and 1,426 after, so neither new route de-cached anything; `share_events` appears in the security advisors under `rls_enabled_no_policy` at INFO, alongside `export_events` and `rate_limits`, which is the intended posture and not a finding. The three probe rows inserted to prove the CHECK constraints were deleted the moment they had done their job — a fixture left in prod is the 2026-08-06 incident.

**What is NOT verified and needs a browser:** the share card's own render. The result page is auth-gated `ƒ` and the card is behind a click, so it is doubly invisible to the build gate, and the repo has no jsdom or Playwright to substitute. Compile and logic are proven; layout is not.


**2026-09-18 (fourth) — the /board reader was being measured as /browse. `question_practiced:board` (migration 0108) splits it out; the hook that hid it now refuses to guess.**

The question that started it was "aren't we tracking the board page for PMF?", asked the day after 0107 split `/guide` out of the bank's feature row. The answer was yes and no, and the "no" half is the interesting one.

**It was never dark.** `BoardReader` has called `useRevealMeter` since 0105 — the same hook `/browse` uses — so every answer reveal in the textbook reader was written to `user_activity` from the day the beacon shipped. What it never carried was a surface: `PRACTICE_SURFACES` was `["bank","guide"]`, `useRevealMeter` passed no third argument, and `recordPractice` defaulted to `bank`. Every board reveal was therefore recorded correctly as an act and filed under the wrong product.

**That is a harder defect to see than an un-instrumented surface**, which is why it survived a pass that was explicitly looking for exactly this. Everything observable from outside was right: the events were in the log, `SURFACE_COVERAGE` carried a "Board reader (/board)" row claiming partial tracking via the beacon, and the sentence in it ("answer reveals are recorded (signed-in only)") was TRUE. Only the call site showed the argument was missing. 0107 fixed a surface that emitted nothing; this fixed one that emitted into someone else's row, and the visible symptom of the second is nil.

**The real fix is the required argument, not the migration.** `useRevealMeter(surface: PracticeSurface)` now has no default, so the next surface to adopt the hook must state which product it is. A default is precisely what let the board reader inherit `bank` in silence, and it is a compile-time problem with a compile-time fix. The WIRE-level default in `parsePracticeBatch` stays `bank` and must not be confused with it: that one exists because a tab opened before a deploy still `sendBeacon`s the old `{questionIds}` body on page-hide, and those reveals genuinely were bank reveals.

**Nothing is backfillable.** All 63 existing `question_practiced` rows (37 of them from self-serve students, the rest staff) carry no surface at all, and `COALESCE(metadata->>'surface','bank')` puts them — including the board's share — in the bank's key permanently. The distinction was never recorded, so there is nothing to recover it from. The coverage row now says the board's row counts from 2026-09-18 rather than leaving a reader to infer a start date from a shape.

**A second overclaim fell out of it.** The features table badges a zero-event row "no events ever". For a surface-split key that is a statement the log cannot make: the key counts only from the day its surface began being written. Changed to "no events recorded" — one word, and it applies to the guide row shipped the day before as well.

**The durable artifact is a bijection test.** `SurfaceCoverage` gained a `practiceSurface` field that exists to be asserted rather than rendered, and `tests/pmf-snapshot.test.ts` now requires that every coverage row claiming `question_practiced` declares a distinct `PracticeSurface`, that the declared set equals `PRACTICE_SURFACES` exactly, and that each one renders a human label rather than a raw composite key. Two reveal surfaces went missing in two days by skipping exactly those steps; a fourth now fails the spec instead.

**One surface was found and deliberately NOT added.** `/notes` `PracticeSet` has a per-rep "Reveal answer" button too, but its reps are authored editorial `PracticeProblem` objects — prompt and answer strings with no bank row behind them. The act exists and the referent does not, so recording it would mean inventing a synthetic id. That is a different problem from this one and a surface value cannot solve it. `/books` was excluded for the plainer reason that it is superadmin-only.

**Verified:** the RPC was diffed before and after against live data — 10 feature rows became 11, the new `question_practiced:board` row reads 0/0, and every pre-existing row is identical (`mock_submitted` 142/611, `answer_wrong` 130/10232, `question_bookmarked` 50/1111, `note_checkpoint` 26/116, `chapter_mastered` 5/56, `question_practiced` 4/37). The beacon firing with `surface: "board"` is NOT proven by any gate here: the hook has no test (no jsdom in this repo), `/board` is dynamic, and the reveal is click-gated — compile and pure logic only, with the browser pass handed over.

**2026-09-18 (third) — NCERT Class 10 Mathematics complete: 14 chapters, 587 questions.**

The full narrative for the digest in CLAUDE.md.

**Scope.** All 14 chapters of NCERT Class 10 Mathematics, ingested into the `cbse-10`
exam over two sessions. 587 PUBLIC rows, 46 figure crops, 15 MCQs. The two
appendices (jemh1a1 Proofs in Mathematics, jemh1a2 Mathematical Modelling) were
ruled OUT of scope by the user at the start and remain so.

Per chapter, with each chapter's OWN key denominator — the number that matters,
because it swings from 24% to 100% inside one book:

| Ch | q | key coverage | note |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 Real Numbers | 27 | 5/10 | pilot; Ex 1.2 has no key block at all |
| 2 Polynomials | 18 | 18/18 | shortest chapter; 2 crops |
| 3 Pair of Linear Equations | 51 | 41/41 | §3.3 splits 3.3.1/3.3.2 |
| 4 Quadratic Equations | 39 | 30/30 | every item computable |
| 5 Arithmetic Progressions | 114 | 98/98 | biggest; Optional Ex 5.4; 2 MCQs; 5 crops |
| 6 Triangles | 55 | 7/29 (24%) | weakest key in the book; 32 crops |
| 7 Coordinate Geometry | 34 | 24/24 | 3 crops |
| 8 Introduction to Trigonometry | 59 | 38/47 | 8 MCQs; 5 crops |
| 9 Some Applications of Trigonometry | 22 | 15/15 | single exercise; 3 crops |
| 10 Circles | 23 | 12/20 | 4 MCQs; 4 crops |
| 11 Areas Related to Circles | 21 | 19/19 | 1 MCQ; 4 crops; ONE textbook key defect |
| 12 Surface Areas and Volumes | 24 | 17/17 | preamble hazard |
| 13 Statistics | 30 | 22/22 | 45 GFM tables |
| 14 Probability | 70 | 25/25 | made `cbse-10` mixed-format |

**Zero errata** against the book key across every chapter that has one, from
independent sympy derivation off the STEM in every case — never our answer
compared to the key, which lets a shared error hide.

**What the key's partial coverage actually is.** Not a gap: a genre. The unkeyed
items are always "prove that", "show that", or a construction, because no answer
key can adjudicate a proof. Ch.8's 9 unkeyed items are exactly its 9 proofs
(Ex 8.1 Q6 plus all eight of Ex 8.3 Q4); Ch.10's 8 are its 7 proofs plus one
"Draw a circle and two lines..."; Ch.6's 22 are all "prove that". This is why
every chapter has to report its own denominator instead of inheriting a
book-level number — and why Ch.6's 7/29 is not a defect in Ch.6.

**MCQs: fifteen, not two.** The lane was scoped expecting the Ex 8.2 Q2 four and
the head of Ex 10.2. Found: Ch.5 Ex 5.2 Q2 (two), Ch.8 Ex 8.2 Q2 and Ex 8.3 Q3
(eight), Ch.10 Ex 10.1 Q3 and Ex 10.2 Q1-3 (four), Ch.11 Ex 11.1 Q14 (one).

Ch.10 Ex 10.1 Q3 is the one worth remembering. It is unannounced — Ex 10.2's
three are introduced with "In Q.1 to 3, choose the correct option", but Q3 of
Ex 10.1 just sits between a fill-in-the-blanks and a construction with four
options, and in a text dump the only tell is the answer key's bare "3. D".

This matters because `flip-public.ts` flips `question_format='subjective'` ONLY
and reports success either way. On Ch.14 it flipped 69 of 70 and left the MCQ
PRIVATE with no error at all. Every chapter carrying an MCQ from Ch.5 onwards ran
`--with-mcq`, and the counts were checked against the row count each time.

**Two durable tools, each built because the same defect struck twice.**

1. `scripts/ncert/key-items.ts` — reconciles the key's item numbers against the
   transcription's, BOTH WAYS. Built after two dropped items that a page-scoped
   read could not see: Ch.3 Ex 3.2 Q3's sixth sub-part sits alone atop the next
   page, and Ch.7 Ex 7.1's Q9 and Q10 sit above the next section heading on the
   following page. Both exercises read as finished lists. The KEY is what
   disagreed, by listing answers for items with no row.

   Proven by fault injection rather than asserted: truncating Ch.7 back to Q8
   makes it report "KEY HAS, TRANSCRIPTION LACKS: Q9, Q10".

   Three false-positive classes were found and fixed while building it: "(x)" the
   VARIABLE read as a roman label (the key writes "Age of Nuri (x) = 50"); a
   sentence-final "18." read as an item number; and a strict +1 run that stopped
   dead at a key's first skipped item. The gap allowance ended at 6, which is the
   widest real gap in this book (Ex 10.2 keys 1,2,3,6,7,12).

   It is TRIAGE and always exits 0 — a chapter legitimately has unkeyed items.

2. `scripts/ncert/fig_bounds.py` — measures crop bboxes by caption, carrying the
   three rules each of which cost a bad crop before it was one: SOLID INK ONLY
   (prose fraction bars and square-root vincula are hairlines — this is Ch.6's
   "prose carries vector ink" finding, and it swallowed the whole left text column
   on Ch.5 Fig 5.7); PAGE FURNITURE IS NOT ART (the running-head rule is 0.84 page
   widths); TEXT MUST BE CONTAINED, not merely overlapping (a prose line starts at
   the left margin and overlaps every figure on its row — three Ch.7 crops). It
   later gained a y-floor (Ch.9 p9 stacks Fig 9.12 above Fig 9.13) and an x-floor
   (Ch.10 p8 prints Fig 10.12 and Fig 10.13 side by side).

   It also builds the CONTACT SHEET, which is the part that is not automatable.
   On Ch.5 the geometry reported success and the sheet found 3 of 5 crops wrong;
   on Ch.6 it found 6 of 22. Geometry proposes; the eye disposes.

**The one real defect in the book's own key**, found in the last chapter:
Ex 11.1 Q8(ii) prints "58.875 cm²". The value is right; the unit is not — the
field is a 15 m square and the ropes are 5 m and 10 m, so the increase can only
be in square metres. Flagged `[Textbook: ...]` in the solution rather than
silently corrected, per the errata convention.

**Structural findings worth keeping.**

- Class 10 has no Miscellaneous exercises anywhere, but Ch.5 carries an
  "EXERCISE 5.4 (Optional)*", footnoted "not from the examination point of view".
  It got its own `section_group` with `kind:"exercise"` — deliberately NOT
  `miscellaneous`, which would invent a block the book does not print.
- Two chapters have a taught section with no worked examples (Ch.6 §6.2,
  Ch.10 §10.2), so their `/board` outlines are odd-numbered.
- This 2025-26 reprint has no "Trigonometric Ratios of Complementary Angles"
  section (Ch.8) and no "Area of a Triangle" section (Ch.7); older editions do.
- Ex 11.1 opens with a standing "Unless stated otherwise, use π = 22/7" that six
  of its items then override in their own stem — the constant is per-question.
- Figures split cleanly into DATA-BEARING and ILLUSTRATIVE. Ch.7 Ex 7.1 Q5 names
  four seats and gives not one coordinate; Ch.9's three all carry every number in
  the stem. The crop-only strategy is right either way, but the two are not the
  same risk.

**Not done / still open.**

- Layout of `/board/cbse-10/...` is unverified. The gate proves compile,
