- **2026-09-16 — CDS Elementary Mathematics gets its FIRST /notes chapter: Number System, 12 subtopics / 71 concepts / 218 q / 100% tagged, and `/notes/cds` stops being a coming-soon hub. The brief was "use the learnings of NDA Maths"; the learnings transferred and the content did not.**
  - **The syllabus overlap is ~15%, not the ~80% the shared subject name suggests.** Only 4 of CDS Maths's 26 chapters share a name with an NDA Maths chapter (Quadratic Equations, Statistics, Circles, Logarithms), and even those sit at a different level — CDS "Triangles" is Pythagoras/centres/BPT/Apollonius while NDA "Properties of Triangle" is the sine-cosine rules. **All five top-weightage CDS chapters are CDS-only**, so there was no `_data` to fork: ~85% is genuine new authoring. What transferred was the template, the workflow and the conventions. A pleasing detail found in `scripts/cds-maths/README.md`: the CDS catalogue's algebra/trig/stats section was itself **seeded from NDA Mathematics**, so the real NDA lineage is in the taxonomy, not the teaching.
  - **Zero plumbing, and that was verified rather than assumed.** `EXAM_REGISTRY` already carried `cds` with a `notesPath`; `notesNav` derives hubs from the registry. The genuine hazard was that the DB subject name is **`Mathematics`, identical to NDA's** — but `subtopicSlugRegistry` has been keyed by (exam, subject, chapter, subtopic) since the 2026-08-21 fix and `taxonomyCache` by (exam, subject), so CDS resolves independently. Slugs are still prefixed `cds-ns-` / `cdsns-`, because four of this exam's chapter names collide with shipped NDA ones.
  - **The reshape had to be TWO-SIDED, and the reason is documented in the pipeline's own source.** `catalog.json` was seeded from three OTHER banks' taxonomies to **classify a paper**, never to sequence teaching — which is exactly why the names are technique-canonical yet the cut is wrong for notes. Reading all 218 solutions (not the names) found the 71-q "Divisibility and Remainders" bundling **four unrelated technique families** — rules, congruences, factorisation, and remainder recipes that are really HCF/LCM — while two subtopics held ONE question each, one of them **mislabelled**: the lone "Trailing Zeros" row is solved by parity, while the real Legendre cluster sat under Primes. Reading the names alone, I had concluded "no catch-alls"; the solutions overturned it. So 12 classification subtopics became 12 teaching subtopics, 212 rows reparented, **plus `catalog.json` plus the 20 `<paper>.questions.json` files** — because `lib.ts` states the trap outright: subtopic is SOFT-validated and AUTO-CREATED, so after a cleanup pass an unlisted name "splits one chapter's corpus across two subtopics with no error anywhere." A DB-only reshape would have been silently undone by any re-commit.
  - **The guard went on `commit.ts` only, not `merge.ts`, and was fault-proven before being believed.** The soft default is *correct* at merge time, where an unlisted subtopic on a fresh paper is extension work rather than a typo; the hazard is re-fragmenting the **bank**, which happens at commit. Strict there is precisely targeted and preserves the transcription workflow. Proven by injecting a stale name: `Q1: subtopic "Divisibility and Remainders" is not listed under "Number System"`. Relatedly, the 50 `b*.json` **bands are deliberately NOT rewritten** — they are transcription evidence, and editing them to match a later taxonomy decision would falsify the record; they are also compact on disk, so a re-dump would inflate 39.7 KB to 47.5 KB and bury the change. The gate covers the gap instead.
  - **A stated invariant in NOTES_WORKFLOW.md turned out to be wrong, and is now corrected there.** `set_id` carries **two structurally different meanings** in this corpus. A shared-**premise** set ("Consider the following for the next two items… Let P be the smallest…") is a genuine passage group and MUST be co-located, because the second question is unanswerable without the first's setup. But CDS wraps each ten-question **data-sufficiency block** in one `set_id` whose context is only the rubric, and **those blocks span six chapters each** — so co-location there is not merely undesirable but *impossible*, since concept tags live inside one subtopic. The discriminator is mechanical: `count(distinct chapter)` per `set_id`. A premise set spans exactly one.
  - **Three of my own hand-authored answers were wrong, and no gate in this repo checks arithmetic.** Caught by re-deriving every one before wiring up: a repunit count that read 6 when it is 8 (the `X+3Y=33` case was missed), a digit-sum practice answer of 3 that is 13, and a muddled modular argument. The workflow's warning that "a fresh worked example is only as correct as your verification" is load-bearing, and the honest report is that the first pass failed it three times.
  - **`tests/notes-nav.test.ts` had encoded "CDS has no notes" as an invariant — for the SECOND time.** Its own comment recorded being moved off `jee-mains` in July for exactly this reason. Rather than move it to the next exam that will eventually gain notes, it now **derives** a note-less exam from `EXAM_REGISTRY` minus `NOTES_CHAPTERS`; it picks `foundation-course` with 9 more in reserve, and if that pool ever empties the assertion fails with an instruction instead of passing vacuously. Fault-checked by confirming it selects a real subject.
  - **Near-zero diagram load is the decision rule working, not a shortfall.** Number System is non-spatial almost throughout, so only 2 SVGs earned a place — `cds-unit-digit-cycle-wheel` (drawn as a loop so "remainder 0 lands on the LAST node" is visible, which is the commonest error in the subtopic) and `cds-rational-irrational-line` (a zoom showing decimals bracketing root 2 ever more tightly without landing). The chapter leans on **reference-variant** ConceptUnits instead — divisibility rules, unit-digit cycles, primes below 100, square endings. Stated plainly at plan time: this chapter does **not** prove the diagram pipeline, which is what Mensuration 2D (33 of the corpus's 80 figures) is for.
  - **12 rows carry a recorded defect or ambiguity and are excluded from `pyqExampleId` duty** (a transposed-digit denominator, a plank problem with no correct option, an impossible LCM:HCF ratio, a "100th place" on a 95-digit number, and others). The one exception is deliberate: the concept whose entire subject is *spotting inconsistent data* features such a row, because there the defect is the lesson.
  - Authored **serially, not via the parallel-agent batch** `NOTES_WORKFLOW.md` suggests for a chapter this size, because this session was instructed not to use subagents unless asked. Gate: `GATE_RESULT: PASS` (typecheck, lint, notes:lint **0 errors** across 367 notes, notes:latex, 5,058 tests, build). `notes:coverage` clean on 10 of 12 subtopics with the two flags pure notation (`\operatorname`, `\ge`); `quiz:coverage` **85 traps** against a >=12 gate, its two formula flags both on reference-variant concepts that have no `formula` slot by type. All 13 routes prerender as static HTML, and both diagrams were grepped out of the served markup.

- **2026-09-15 (ninth) — the NCERT CLASS 10 lane opens: a new `cbse-10` exam (the 14th) and its pilot chapter, Ch.1 Real Numbers, 27 q PUBLIC. The pipeline was already built; the EXAM was the new thing, which is what chose the pilot.**
  - **The pilot was picked to prove the NEW THING, not the hard thing.** Ch.1 has ZERO figures, tables and MCQs, so it exercises none of this book's three hazards — and that is correct here, because `scripts/ncert/` is proven across four subjects while `cbse-10` had never existed. Ch.6 / Ch.13 / Ch.12 prove the hazards before any wave.
  - **`board:lint` reported GREEN on 27 rows it could not see.** It iterates `BOARD_EXAMS` from the registry, so until the registry entry landed the new exam was outside its scope entirely — 6 exams / 15,622 rows, then 7 / 15,649. **A gate scoped by a registry is blind to anything not yet in that registry**, and its pass says nothing about it.
  - **The key is partial PER QUESTION and tracks how PROOF-BASED the chapter is** — 5 of 10 items here (Ex 1.1 skips both "explain why"; **Ex 1.2 has no key block at all**, all three being "prove … is irrational"). Measured book-wide: Triangles 31%, Circles 53%, everything else 89-100%. So every chapter must report its own denominator.
  - **Two registry tests encoded "CBSE Class 10 has no corpus" as an invariant** and failed on the data landing, not on a code defect. Updated to keep the real invariant ("a class with no corpus resolves to null") with Class 9 as its remaining case. Cross-check: 5 of 5 keyed items agree, zero errata, derived in sympy against the key read off the RENDER — the text layer gives `2² × 5 × 7` as `22 × 5 × 7`.
  - _(Digest-only: this entry was written as a digest in CLAUDE.md and archived here verbatim on 2026-09-16; there is no longer-form post-mortem.)_

- **2026-09-15 (eighth) — the 28-file control-byte backfill, and a covering index for the bank-weightage scan. Both were authorised follow-ups; both found that the ledger describing them was wrong.**
  - **The backfill's own ledger mis-described what it was backfilling.** It recorded "every one is the SAME pattern — a NUL used as a composite-key separator". Measured before editing: **68 bytes, EIGHT distinct values** (0x00 x24, 0x01 x10, 0x08 x5, 0x0B x11, 0x0C x5, 0x0E x4, 0x1F x8, 0x7F x1) across **three** classes — key separators, control-char DETECTOR regexes (`/[\u0000-\u0008\u000B\u000C\u000E-\u001F]/`), and deliberate test FIXTURES (`"has a \u0001 byte"`, `"\u000Brac"` standing in for an eaten `\frac`). Escaping is behaviour-preserving for all three, but only the first was the class the ledger named.
  - **THE GUARD I SHIPPED THE DAY BEFORE HAD BEEN FAILING CI, AND THE LOCAL GATE COULD NOT SEE IT.** 16 of its 28 baselined paths were gitignored scratch files (`scripts/*/_*`) that exist only on this machine. Its "every entry still exists and still offends" assertion therefore passed here and failed on a clean checkout, from the commit that introduced it. Proven rather than inferred by moving those 16 aside and re-running. **A list of PATHS is a claim about a working tree, not about the repository** — if a baseline is ever needed again, assert its entries are git-tracked. Clearing the backfill deleted the allowlist and the trap with it.
  - **Verified rather than asserted, because the risk was concentrated in one file.** `lib/quiz/atoms.ts` joins on that separator inside a **stored** sha1, so `fingerprint()` was run over 7 inputs before and after: byte-identical. The detector regexes were checked by rebuilding all **13** character classes from both the escaped and the raw form and comparing their match sets over all 256 byte values: identical. Two intermediate probes of my own were WRONG first — one flagged 7 false mismatches by treating array literals as character classes and by assuming a detector must not match tab, when `[\u0000-\t...]` has always included it.
  - **`wt` was cached with an INDEX, not a materialized view, and that was the whole decision.** The CTE takes no `p_user_id` — it scans 34,676 rows and returns the same answer for every student, on every page view. A matview refreshed after ingest was the obvious fix and was rejected: 0100 derives this live *precisely* so it cannot go stale, and nda-tracker's hand-transcribed copy of these same counts has drifted to **78.1% resolution**. A covering partial index on `(question_kind, subject_id, exam_id, chapter_id, subtopic_id) WHERE visibility='PUBLIC'` makes it an **Index Only Scan with Heap Fetches: 0**: **10,519 -> 191 buffers** in isolation (55x), and **62,269 -> 51,974** for the whole function.
  - **And the honest half: END-TO-END LATENCY DID NOT MOVE.** Median of 10 sequential round-trips reads **543 ms** against a ~503-523 ms baseline — inside the noise. The earlier "wt costs 123 ms of 367 ms" came from isolating the CTE, and isolating a CTE changes its plan (the real function auto-materialises `keyed`, referenced 5x), so those per-CTE timings were never additive. Kept anyway, at a cost of 1.1 MB: 10,300 fewer buffers per call is I/O the disk does not serve, and buffer traffic under concurrency — not wall time on an idle database — is what made this query fatal on 2026-09-15.

- **2026-09-15 (seventh) — the projected score read 94 of 300 for a student whose best-ever was 86.69 and whose mean was 75.03. Three independent defects in one formula, all inherited from nda-tracker, found by asking "is this fair?" of one card.**
  - **THE HEADLINE DID NOT MATCH ITS OWN ROWS.** 94 summed over chapters, 86.55 over subtopics, one `projection.total` rendered above both toggles. The 0100 entry had explicitly set out to prevent "two supplied totals disagreeing behind one toggle" — and the parity test it shipped pinned `marksAtStake` ONLY (300.00 vs 300.00, exact). Nothing asserted anything about `projected`, and the file header stated the stronger claim as though proven. The decomposition: **pooling +8.853, clamp −1.016, sum 7.837 = exactly the observed gap.**
  - **Pooling is the big term and it runs one way.** `expectedMarks` is linear in marks but accuracy is a RATIO: pooling a chapter weights its subtopics by how much the STUDENT engaged with each, summing weights them by BANK SHARE. Pooling therefore spends a tested subtopic's accuracy across subtopics the student has never been shown — Permutation & Combination: 5 correct answers in 3 of 5 subtopics, awarded the full 10.53 marks. **69 of this student's 111 subtopics are untested against 13 of 31 chapters**, so the chapter grain was hiding the untested pool inside chapters it called tested.
  - **A blank counted as HALF a question, and that is right for the tracker.** Its data is INVIGILATED OMR — one hall, one clock, no retakes — where a blank means "could not do it under the same pressure as everyone else". A self-serve mock is not that: this student answered **35% of two papers at 79% accuracy**, cherry-picked, at home. Fixed by splitting into TWO scores rather than changing one: `weightedScore` (ABILITY, blanks at half, drives the mastery bar + weak/mastered bands + concept-graph focus) and `markScore` (MARKS, blanks in full, drives the projection and nothing else). **Measured before choosing** — moving the single score would have re-banded **18.2% of chapters across the 15 heaviest students (89 mid→weak, 53 mastered→mid)**, which is a different feature's calibration and was not what was authorised. The twin fix went with it: `wrongRate` now divides by REACHED too, because crediting a blank as a zero while charging the penalty at the answered-only wrong rate models two different students in one expression.
  - **`Math.max(0, …)` per row was worth 7.7 of the visible 94.** Three chapters whose own arithmetic predicted a LOSS were floored — Lines at −4.56, Definite Integration at −3.03 — and the card then ranked Lines as his **second-biggest opportunity at +13.7**, having erased the loss on the way. It is also not grain-invariant (`Σ max(0,x) ≥ max(0, Σx)`, so splitting a subtopic mechanically RAISES the projection), and it contradicts the skip weight: clamping assumes he would skip rather than lose marks while the half weight assumed he would convert his blanks. Moved to the headline alone. **Not inert there, which I assumed before measuring**: one production lane (72 answers at 17% accuracy) sums below zero.
  - **94 → 72**, against an actual mean of 75.03 and a like-for-like replay of 75.0. A guarantee was deliberately abandoned to get it: a chapter's number no longer survives a re-graining of the bank, and **it cannot** — grain-invariance and scoring a subtopic from its own questions are mutually exclusive once accuracy is a ratio. The degenerate case (bank subtopics matching none of the student's → a chapter projecting 0 against a non-null accuracy) is pinned by unit test AND asserted by `perf:smoke` against live data, where it reads **899/899 clean**.
  - **A fix I proposed and killed before writing it.** The intake rules discard a paper entirely when sitting 1 misses the 20% engagement floor and sitting 2 is a retake — which cost this student his only recent Maths data. Checking the premise first: **submitting a mock unlocks the full answer key for every question in the paper**, answered or not (`Review — all N questions`). He submitted after 73 seconds and restarted 8m24s later. The "hole" is the rule working; my fix would have admitted the most contaminated attempt on the page.
  - **nda-tracker carries all three defects** (`src/lib/analytics/projection.js` + `chapterStats.js`): same `Math.max(0, …)` per row, same half-weight skip, same pooled `totalProjected` beside an independently-built `subtopicBreakdown` — and its parity test likewise asserts `marksAtStake` only. It also has a fourth we do not: chapters with no taxonomy entry (`subtopicsUncovered`) contribute to the total while emitting zero subtopic rows.

- **2026-09-15 (sixth) — PRODUCTION INCIDENT: `/dashboard/students/[id]/performance` 500s on the heaviest student. The cause was not the exam the user clicked, not the render, and not the query. It was `next/link` prefetching the page's own filter pills.**
  - **The report was "it errors when I switch from NDA to CDS", and every part of that was a red herring.** The pure core builds all 18 lanes for that student without throwing; `renderToStaticMarkup` renders all 18 lanes' client components without throwing; both exams resolve through `buildLaneNav` identically. What the URL bar showed (`?exam=NDA`) was also misleading and is worth knowing: on a soft navigation the App Router commits the URL only AFTER the RSC payload arrives, so a failed render leaves the OLD url on screen. The user was looking at a failed render of `?exam=CDS` while the address bar said NDA.
  - **The evidence was in the logs, not the code.** 11:55 UTC: `rpc/get_student_performance` 24 calls, **18 of them 500** — and every other minute that day ran 1-11 calls with ZERO errors. Postgres logged exactly 18 `canceling statement due to statement timeout` in the same window. Nothing else on the project 5xx'd all day.
  - **Reproduced exactly, which is what turned a theory into a diagnosis.** The same RPC: sequential **523-757 ms**; **5 concurrent 0/5 fail; 9 concurrent 7/9 fail; 12 concurrent 12/12; 15 concurrent 15/15**, all `57014` at ~9.8 s. Production's 18-of-24 is 75%; the 9-way repro is 78%. The query is not slow — it is *fatal in a crowd*.
  - **The crowd is the page's own nav.** The exam and subject pills are QUERY-PARAM links on the SAME route, so there is no `loading.tsx` boundary for a prefetch to stop at and each prefetch is a FULL page render — and each render is that 1.27 MB RPC. This student's page carries 13 such links (2 exam + 10 subject + the Performance tab). The supporting counts in the same 3-minute window match link-for-link: `get_student_roster` 28 (the "← students" link), `/auth/v1/admin/users/<id>` 26 (`getStudentDetail`, which runs on both tabs), `student_profiles`/`entitlements`/`mock_attempts`/`user_activity` 26 each.
  - **Today's exam axis did NOT cause it — it slightly improved it.** The previous version rendered `lanes.map(...)` as one row: **18** pills for this student against 12 now. The defect has been there since the page shipped the same morning. Worth stating because the obvious inference from the timing is wrong.
  - **The roster is the same shape and worse**: `StudentRosterClient` renders one `<Link>` PER STUDENT with no pagination — 315 of them today, each pointing at a page that re-reads that student's whole profile.
  - **Fix: `prefetch={false}` on all 10 link sites across `/dashboard/students`**, pinned by `tests/dashboard-students-no-prefetch.test.ts`, which counts `<Link` against `prefetch={false}` per file rather than parsing tags — JSX attributes wrap across lines and contain `>` inside arrow functions, so a tag-matching regex is a probe that can quietly stop matching. Counts cannot drift silently.
  - **It also changed the work in flight.** The drill-down links approved the same session add ~15 more `<Link>`s to this page, all pointing at `/browse` — un-suppressed they would have built a second prefetch storm against a different heavy route. They ship with the prop from birth.
  - **Profiled while there, because "make it faster" was the tempting wrong fix.** End-to-end, median of 5: **SQL 503 ms (92%)**, download 29 ms, `JSON.parse` 5 ms, and the ENTIRE pure core — 18 lanes, 4,945 facts, both projection grains, time analysis, every audit — **7 ms (1%)**. Server-side the function is 367 ms / 62,269 buffers, of which `wt` (bank weightage, which scans **34,676 PUBLIC PYQs and does not depend on the student at all**) is the largest single piece and the per-question `options` answer-key lookup is 19,935 buffers run 4,945 times. **Shrinking the payload would buy ~34 ms of 544** and would NOT have prevented this: halving the cost moves the cliff from ~6 concurrent to ~12, and the page asked for 13. Caching `wt` is the real efficiency follow-up; logged, not done.

- **2026-09-15 (fifth) — the performance page's three list cards learn to DRILL DOWN, and the interesting part is that they do not all get the same link. The ask was three questions: "should we add links to subtopics?", "should we add an Open button to skipped as well?", "should we add link to projected subtopics?"**
  - **There are TWO links, and merging them under one button label is the trap the whole design turns on.** Link A — `/browse?extras=<ids>` — opens the exact questions THIS student got wrong or skipped: exact, personal, and empty by construction for a subtopic they never touched. Link B — `/browse?examId=…&chapterIds=…&subtopicIds=…` — opens the topic in the bank: always resolves, says nothing about the student. The audits and the chapter accordion take A, because a row only appears on them because a wrong answer or a skip put it there. The PROJECTION takes B, and the measurement is what settled it: the projected-score card is a marks-at-stake ranking derived from the bank's own weightage, so it deliberately ranks topics the student has never seen — **2,484 of its 4,939 subtopic rows across the 12 heaviest students have `judged === 0`**. The screenshot that prompted the question contains its own counter-example two rows down: *Properties of Definite Integrals — 0.0 of 4.3 marks*, ranked second precisely BECAUSE nothing has ever been scored there. An "open their mistakes" column would have opened nothing on half the card, and would have looked broken rather than empty.
  - **The skipped audit had no drill-down for one reason: the core collected `wrongIds` and not `seenBlankIds`.** Not a design decision — an asymmetry nobody had noticed. The Time analysis card shipped hours earlier is the argument for closing it: the heaviest student spent **44% of 26h 42m on questions they ultimately left blank**, a larger body of engaged-but-unfinished work than their wrong answers, and a wrong answer can be a misread where a skip is a declared gap. The new `seenBlankQuestionIds` carries the SAME exclusion the skip audit itself makes — seen-blank only, never never-reached — which is the four-state model earning its keep for the third time: an id list that quietly folded unreached questions in would hand a student a "revision set" that is really a record of where the clock ran out, under a card whose subtitle promises the opposite in so many words. `perf:smoke` now THROWS if any row's id list disagrees with its own count, because the badge reads the count and the href reads the list, and a mismatch renders as "7 skipped → opens five" with nothing anywhere reporting it.
  - **The chapter accordion needed links for a navigational reason, not a data one — it already had the ids.** A reader on *3D Geometry → Distance, Section and Collinearity in 3D — 3 wrong* had no way to open those three: the only Open button in the app for that subtopic was somewhere in the **14 pages** of the Wrong-answer audit below. The accordion is where you browse BY CHAPTER and the audit is where you read a RANKING; the same action has to be available in both. It links the COUNTS themselves rather than adding a sixth element, because that row already carries `3 wrong · 7 skipped · 63% of 8` and a button would wrap at phone width. The cap is deliberately NOT disclosed at this grain (the audit card below is where the full count lives) — a `34 wrong (50 max)` here costs more legibility than the case is worth.
  - **A latent lie fixed before it could tell itself: the Open label read the full count while the href sliced 50.** Measured across the 12 heaviest students, the worst subtopic holds **34 wrong and 33 skipped**, so it has never once been wrong — which is exactly the shape of defect that ships. `openLabel` now reads the cap (`Open 50 of 67`), and the cap exists because `extras` becomes a PostgREST `.in()` list carried in the URL, which answered a bare `Bad Request` at 833 ids elsewhere in this repo.
  - **Link B cost a taxonomy read, and it is deliberately NOT another column on the RPC.** `get_student_performance` returns taxonomy as NAMES — `dims.subjects/chapters/subtopics` are string arrays the facts index into — and that is the right shape for a payload already at 1,270 kB of which `facts` is 1,074 kB; a uuid per dim entry would grow it to serve a link. `taxonomyQuery.ts` reads ~30-120 rows for ONE subject instead, independent of how much the student has sat, and `taxonomy.ts` FAILS SOFT because every number on the page comes from the RPC: a broken taxonomy read must cost the links and nothing else. Names being the join key is a real coupling, and it is the same one `/guide` and `/notes` cross-links already accept — a chapter renamed since the attempt was sat loses its link, which is the intended failure, because a silently-wrong link is worse than an absent one. So `perf:smoke` REPORTS the resolution rate per lane rather than asserting it (a genuine rename is a fact about the bank, not a bug in this code). It read **100% on every lane at ship** — NDA Mathematics at 31/31 chapters and 111/111 subtopics, with no unresolved names anywhere.
  - **`topicHref` degrades one step at a time, and the middle case is not hypothetical.** Subtopic resolves → chapter + subtopic; subtopic does not → the chapter alone; chapter does not → no link. `(unclassified)` is minted by the RPC's own `coalesce(t.name, '(unclassified)')` and therefore has no id by construction, so without the middle rung those rows would fall all the way to nothing. What must never happen is the fourth option nobody proposed and everybody writes by accident: dropping the unresolved filter and linking to the whole unfiltered bank under a heading that names one topic, where the reader reads the destination as the thing they clicked.
  - **A NUL byte had been sitting in `compute.ts` since the first performance commit, making the file invisible to every text probe in the repo.** The lane key is `` `${a.examName}\u0000${subject}` `` — a correct and deliberate separator, written as a literal `0x00` rather than the escape. It compiled, typechecked, tested and shipped; `grep` and `ripgrep` classify a file containing one as BINARY, so `audit:text` and every other text gate here had been skipping that file in silence. Found only because a routine `grep` for `TimeAnalysis` answered `Binary file … matches`. Fixed as its own commit, byte-identical at runtime, with a comment saying why it is an escape so nobody simplifies it back.

- **2026-09-15 (fourth) — the projected-score card gains a SUBTOPIC grain (migration 0100), after a review of nda-tracker's version found its headline benchmark to be invented. The ask was "make projected score private" + "review how tracker's projected score works and identify gaps in bank".**
  - **(a) was already true, and saying so beat shipping a no-op.** The projected score exists in exactly one place in the bank — the Projected score card on `/dashboard/students/[id]/performance` — and that route's first statement is `if (!(await getSessionSuperadmin())) redirect("/browse")`. `getSessionSuperadmin` reads `platform_admins`, so an org ADMIN, a TEACHER, a student and anon are all bounced; the page is `force-dynamic` with `robots: {index:false}`. A grep of `src/` found the only other mentions of "projection" to be vector-projection maths in `/notes` and two prose comments. What was missing was not a gate but a PIN, so `tests/student-pages-superadmin-gate.test.ts` now asserts every page under `/dashboard/students` calls a superadmin guard, that the performance route in particular does not use `getSessionMember`/`requireEditor` (both of which admit a teacher), and that `ProjectionList` renders nowhere else in the app. It includes a test that the scan FOUND routes at all — an empty scan would otherwise pass every assertion — and it was fault-injected: swapping the guard for `getSessionMember` fails 2 of its 7 tests, and reverting passes all 7. A source scan cannot prove a guard WORKS, and the file says so: these are `force-dynamic` pages that `next build` never executes, this repo has no jsdom or Playwright, and an anon request to `/dashboard/*` is bounced by middleware before the page compiles. What it proves is that the guard is still THERE, which is the regression that would actually happen.
  - **(b) The tracker's benchmark line is not a cut-off, and it is wrong in the reassuring direction.** `ProjectedScoreCard.jsx` computes its `99 SSB / 150 merit / 201 rank` markers as `subjectMaxScore * 0.33 / 0.5 / 0.67` — three arbitrary fractions wearing authoritative names. Against the real figures in this repo's own `src/lib/exam/cutoffs/` (20 UPSC sittings, 2016-2025, shipped the day before), written cut-offs run **229-360 out of 900**, so the "merit" marker at 50% of the paper set (450/900) is HIGHER THAN EVERY WRITTEN CUT-OFF EVER PUBLISHED and "rank" (603/900) is far past it. Two category errors are stacked: the written cut-off is on the AGGREGATE of 900 (Maths 300 + GAT 600) and cannot be compared to one subject at all, and the real per-subject rule is a different thing entirely — `subjectMinimumPct`, 25% and **20% in four of the twenty sittings**, which on a 300-mark Maths paper is 75 marks. The student in the screenshot sits at 72/300, i.e. BELOW the subject minimum, while the card tells them they are approaching a line at 99. Recorded as a gap to close DIFFERENTLY rather than to copy.
  - **The subtopic level is worth taking, and we do it live where they cannot.** nda-tracker's `NDA_SUBTOPIC_SHARES` states its own source in its header — "PYQ Vault's NDA Maths taxonomy ... as of 2026-05-17" — so it is a hand-transcribed copy of THIS bank, frozen, covering one subject, and NDA Maths has since gone 2,160 -> 2,280. Migration 0100 adds one column to the weightage CTE's GROUP BY and derives it live for every subject a student has touched. The live derivation returns **111 subtopics for NDA Mathematics — the same count as their frozen table**, which is the cross-check that makes both look right. Chapter totals are SUMMED from the subtopic rows rather than returned alongside them (a pooled figure is derivable from per-row detail and never the reverse — the `question_item_stats` rule), and the parity is pinned two ways: a unit test feeding one row per chapter must leave every chapter number identical, and `perf:smoke` throws if any chapter's marks stop equalling the sum of its subtopics' against live data. The ranking is FLAT ACROSS CHAPTERS, which is the one design idea taken wholesale from their card — "which subtopic anywhere is worth the most" is the question a student has tonight, and a per-chapter ranking cannot answer it. Matching is on the (chapter, subtopic) PAIR, deliberately NOT their match-on-bare-name: `subtopics_chapter_id_name_key` makes subtopic names unique only WITHIN a chapter here, and their taxonomy is a flattened copy where that hazard does not exist.
  - **My pre-flight cost estimate was low by a third and the migration file says so.** I estimated ~9% payload growth from the re-grain; measured after applying, the weightage array goes 278 -> 1,257 rows and 22 kB -> 155 kB, which is **+133 kB = +11.7%** of the payload as it stood. `facts` remains 1,074 kB of the 1,270 kB total, so weightage is nowhere near the expensive part and the conclusion did not change — but the number in the file did. The version applied to production carries the pre-flight figure in its comment and the file carries the corrected one; the executable SQL is identical.
  - **The download is DESIGNED, not built** — deferred by the user until the subtopic rows have been seen in a browser. Sized first, because the sizing changes the design: top-10-subtopic wrong+skipped sets run **34 to 200 questions** and the full set reaches **817** (of which 707 are skipped, for one student's NDA Maths). So it cannot be a `/browse?extras=` link — this repo has already hit PostgREST's bare `Bad Request` at 833 ids, and the existing chip caps at 50 — and it cannot ignore the 200-question export cap. `seenBlankIds` does not exist yet either; only `wrongIds` is collected. Never-reached stays out, consistent with the skip audit's existing rule. And the 110-wrong-vs-707-skipped split means the artifact is a COVERAGE worksheet as often as a mistakes one, which the button has to say rather than let a teacher assume.

- **2026-09-15 (third) — the performance page gains an EXAM axis, PAGED list cards, and a TIME ANALYSIS section. Three asks, and the measurement changed the shape of all three.**
  - **(a) The exam filter is a DEFAULT fix, not just a row of pills.** Lanes are (exam, subject) sorted by answered-count, so on the heaviest multi-exam student the single row interleaves them — NDA·English, NDA·Physics, …, CDS·Chemistry, CDS·Physics, CDS·Biology, NDA·History, … across 18 pills — and you cannot scan one exam as a group. But the sharper finding was the DEFAULT: the page opened on whichever lane the student had answered most of, and **3 of the 12 production students who span more than one exam would land on the wrong exam** under that rule (their most recent sitting is a different exam from their busiest). The user asked for "default selected based on his recent exam attempt", which is exactly the fix. Selection moved out of the route — where it was an untested `lanes.find(...) ?? lanes[0]` — into `lib/performance/laneNav.ts` with 11 tests. Three rules are pinned there because each could plausibly have gone the other way: the exam ROW stays busiest-first and independent of selection, so it cannot reorder under the cursor that just aimed at it; the SUBJECT default stays busiest-first, because recency picks an exam but cannot rank subjects (one paper spans many at once); and a subject is resolved WITHIN the selected exam, so `?exam=NDA&subject=Physics` on a student whose only Physics is CDS falls back to a real NDA lane instead of rendering the CDS lane under an NDA heading. The row renders only above one exam — 112 of the 124 students with submitted attempts have sat exactly one, and a single-option filter is furniture. `summary.latest` gained `exam`, and it is the right source precisely because it is the latest COUNTED attempt: it has already survived the first-attempt-only and engagement-floor filters, so it can never name an exam with no lane.
  - **(b) I recommended against pagination and was overruled, correctly, on a point I had not weighed.** My analysis found the caps: wrong audit 12 of up to 69, skipped audit 12 of up to 106, projection **10 of up to 31 with no disclosure at all** — a card headed "Ranked by recoverable marks" quietly omitting 21 chapters, which is the one I still call a defect, because the headline total was summed over every row and so the number stayed right while the list lied. My recommendation was an expander rather than pages, reasoning that these lists are severity-ranked and the tail is the least actionable content. The user chose pages at 5 per item. Their framing is better for the reading it is actually for: an expander turns the tail into a wall you scroll past, while a page is somewhere you choose to go. Named up front rather than discovered later: 106 rows at 5/page is **22 pages**, so the pager is prev/position/next and not numbered buttons, and `PERF_PAGE_SIZE` is one exported constant. Client-side with no URL parameter, because the whole payload is already computed server-side — every hidden row is in memory, and a round trip would re-run a 1 MB RPC to fetch five rows it already had. The cost of that is stated in the component rather than left to be discovered: a page position is not shareable or restorable. The footers used to read "Showing the 12 worst of 106" over a link back to the PROFILE — naming the missing rows while offering no way to reach them. The chapter accordion pages too, at the same size, and that was the user's call over my recommendation: I argued it is the card you SCAN rather than step through (collapsed one-liners, weakest-first, 31 rows for NDA Mathematics), and they chose consistency — a card that pages while the one below it does not is its own kind of wall. Expansion is keyed by chapter NAME, so a chapter left open survives paging away and back.
  - **(c) The time card was only built after proving the field could carry it.** `time_spent_secs` is wall-clock dwell committed on navigation, which invites the assumption that it is idle-contaminated noise. Measured instead: it is populated on 49,372 of 52,949 answer rows, and across 300 submitted attempts `sum(ts) / (submitted_at − started_at)` has **median 0.95, p90 0.98, and never exceeds 1.01** (289 of 300 inside 0.5–1.05). The per-question timer PARTITIONS the sitting's clock rather than approximating it, which is what makes a share-of-clock readout meaningful at all. What it surfaces was invisible before: one student spent **20% of a 754-minute total on questions they ultimately left blank**, another 34%, and in the NDA Mathematics lane of the heaviest student, **39% of 225 minutes**. Median seconds on correct vs wrong runs 18 vs 24 on one student and 22 vs 17 on another — the direction varies per student, which is the argument for showing it per student rather than deriving a rule. And `medianSecs` was ALREADY computed on every chapter and subtopic row and rendered nowhere, so "slowest chapters, with the accuracy the time bought" cost nothing to add: `Permutation & Combination 170s at 100%` is time well spent, `Gravitation 67s at 18%` is a sink.
  - **Three decisions inside the time card that are about honesty, not display.** The four second-buckets sum EXACTLY to the total and are classified identically to `addToTally`, including the grace case — a page saying "654 left blank" in one card and excluding some of them from the blank share in the next would be describing two different papers, and `perf:smoke` now THROWS if the buckets ever stop partitioning. Every figure is a median, because production holds a single question at **6,131 seconds** and one such row moves a mean but not a median. And reached-but-zero-dwell rows — 6.8% of all answer rows — are excluded from every median and reported as `zeroDwell`: a row with no reading is a measurement gap, not a zero-second solve, the [[default-becomes-assertion]] shape. Excluding them was verified to be small before it was adopted (medians move 0–2s), which is also why the existing Coverage median could be switched to the same basis without inventing a second, disagreeing definition of "median per question". `timedCount` was added alongside it as the denominator that gates the slowest list, since one 600-second question is an abandoned tab and would otherwise top the ranking on every paper.
  - **What is NOT proven: the layout.** This route is auth-gated and `force-dynamic`, so `next build` never renders it, and an anon curl to `/dashboard/*` is bounced by middleware before the page compiles. The gate proves it typechecks, lints and builds; `npm run perf:smoke` proves the loaders, the nav default, the bucket partition and the paging arithmetic against real production payloads. Neither proves a single pixel, and the pager in particular is behind a click. That check was handed to the user rather than implied.

- **2026-09-15 (second) — per-student PERFORMANCE diagnosis at `/dashboard/students/[id]/performance` (migration 0099, superadmin-only): pacing, difficulty split, recency-weighted chapters, wrong/skipped audits, projection, concept-graph focus. nda-tracker's METHOD was worth importing; two of its three "imports" ran backwards.**
  - **Its weightage tables are hand-transcribed copies of THIS bank** (`ndaFreq.js` cites pyqvault.com), frozen at 2026-05-17 and stale since NDA Maths went 2,160 -> 2,280 — so weightage is derived live, and per-question marks come from the snapshot because MHT-CET's ZERO negative marking makes its hardcoded 0.33 penalty wrong for 4 of the 5 schemes in one payload. Only `CHAPTER_PREREQS` is a real import.
  - **FOUR response states, not three:** 240 of 606 graded attempts wrote a row for every question, so a missing row means NEVER REACHED — porting the tracker's skip audit naively reports "weak in Conics" for someone who ran out of time at Q80.
  - **Two defects the tests caught, both denominators:** a lost answer key put the question in the accuracy denominator (penalising the student for our defect), and a never-attempted chapter sorted as their WORST topic. Rows now carry `judged` + `thin` — the median attempt answers 36% of its paper, and "33% History" rested on 6 answers of 173.
  - **The admin attempt links were already dead** — `/mock/attempt/[id]/result` is own-row, so every row `/dashboard/students/[id]` rendered 404'd for the only people who could see it. Fixed with a superadmin route over an EXTRACTED `AttemptReviewList`: one renderer, two callers.
  - _(Digest-only: this entry was written as a digest in CLAUDE.md and archived here verbatim on 2026-09-16; there is no longer-form post-mortem.)_

- **2026-09-15 — `/dashboard/students` BECOMES AN ENGAGEMENT ROSTER: exam + time filters, sortable columns, filtered CSV export. Migration 0098 `get_student_roster()` + a pure core (`src/lib/students/roster.ts`, 32 tests) + `npm run students:smoke`. The request was "create a page to display this CSV"; the finding that shaped everything is that the CSV was the problem, not the missing page.**
  - **The source file was a lossy Excel export, and the loss is irreversible.** Every mobile in `generated-papers/nda-users.csv` had been rounded to 6 significant figures by Excel into sci-notation, and it COLLIDES: `9.16002E+11` appears six times, i.e. six different students' numbers flattened onto one value (123 filled -> 106 distinct). `%tage marks` was empty in all 217 rows — a column the header promised and no row delivered. Quoting would not have saved it; Excel coerces a quoted numeric-looking string too, so the export now writes `91 9876543210`, where the **space** is load-bearing because a cell containing one cannot be read as a number. The leading `+` of the display format is deliberately dropped: `= + - @` at the start of a cell is a formula-injection vector, and `name`/`city` are user-supplied (OAuth profile, onboarding free text), so those get an apostrophe guard. **The round-trip test was fault-injected** — reverting `csvMobile` to bare digits makes it fail — because an untested export guard is the one that silently stops working.
  - **It was also stale in a way that had already inverted its own primary sort.** 217 rows against **315 live students** (98 missing, 31%), and the `rank` column it was sorted by was wrong: Vinay sat at rank 1 with 28 submitted against Simran's 28, but live those read 32 and 33 — Simran leads. Vinay's `qs_answered` had nearly doubled (1,826 -> 3,569) in the days since export. A repo-wide search found **no generator script**, so the file was produced ad hoc and had no way to be refreshed; deriving it live therefore also created the repeatable derivation that never existed. Same shape as [[project-docs-staleness]]: a snapshot is an artefact, not a source.
  - **Not a new page — the surface already existed.** `/dashboard/students` was live and superadmin-gated, but thin (name / email / mobile / provider / signup date, no sorting, no filters, no metrics), with a per-student drill-down at `[id]`. Building a second page listing the same students would have duplicated it; the missing thing was the filter/sort/metrics layer, so the roster was extended in place and `listStudents`/`deriveStudents` retired (single consumer). `displayName`/`providerLabel` stay exactly as they were — the mocks and feedback admin readouts import them.
  - **The PostgREST 1000-row cap applies to a set-returning RPC, not just a table select.** `attempt_answers` is ~53k rows and `user_activity` ~12k, which is why the aggregate is in SQL at all rather than counted in JS. But returning a TABLE re-exposes the same cap on the way out, so `fetchStudentRoster` pages in 1000-row windows. At 315 students that loop is inert on the first iteration, and that is precisely the point — it cannot begin silently dropping students the month the roster crosses the cap.
  - **Absence is modelled as null everywhere, never as 0 or a zero date.** 176 of 315 students have no graded attempt and 76 have never taken a single learning action; both render "—" rather than 0%/epoch, and **sort LAST in both directions** so an ungraded student cannot top a descending score sort. "Never active" is its own filter bucket — the re-engagement list — rather than a silent exclusion, and the 59 students who never named a target exam get an explicit "Not specified" chip for the same reason. `last_active` is deliberately the newest LEARNING action (mock / notes / bookmark / activity event, 239 of 315 covered) and NOT `last_sign_in_at` (313 of 315): opening the site without doing anything is not engagement. `GREATEST` ignoring NULLs in Postgres gives that semantics for free.
  - **Two verification notes.** The permission lock was checked against a NON-EMPTY result — `service_role=true, anon=false, authenticated=false` while the function returns 315 rows; run against an empty table it would have returned 0 for every role and proven nothing. And the page is auth-gated `force-dynamic`, so `next build` never renders it and an anon curl is bounced by `src/middleware.ts` before the page compiles: `npm run students:smoke` drives the real loader + pure core against live data (that is why the query lives in `rosterQuery.ts`, injectable, with `admin.ts` as the `server-only` wrapper — the itemStats precedent), but **layout is owed to a browser** and was not claimed here.
  - **My own test fixture was wrong before the code was.** The `filterRoster` combined-filters test failed, and the implementation was correct: the row builder defaulted every fixture to `asha@example.com`, so a row named "Bilal" still matched a search for "asha" through its email. Fixed by deriving the default email from the row id so fixtures stay distinct. The reflex to suspect the code first is the wrong one when the probe is new — [[feedback-probe-must-reach-the-code]].

- **2026-09-14 (eighth) — THE SECOND `/blog` POST: NDA II 2026 GAT (Paper II) analysed against all 19 sittings. `_posts/nda-2-2026-gat-paper-analysis/` + a registry line + a line in `contents.ts` + an 11-assertion prod-contract suite. No routes, no nav, no sitemap edits — those derive from the registry, which is the first post's machinery paying for itself. Two findings shipped, one killed, one prose error caught before publishing.**
  - **THE OBVIOUS ENGLISH HEADLINE WAS MEASURING OUR OWN TAXONOMY.** The Grammar chapter runs 1.7 -> 16 q/paper across the decade, and it is tempting precisely because it is visible in `.xlsx`-sourced papers before 2026, which makes it look seam-proof. Reading actual stems killed it: the 2019 **Grammar** chapter contains Spotting-Errors-format questions ("a sentence with three underlined parts labelled (a), (b) and (c)"), the same format filed under **Spotting Errors** in neighbouring years. Spotting Errors and Fill in the Blanks decline over exactly the period Grammar rises, which is equally consistent with the 2026-05-18 NDA English Phase-D cleanup refiling old questions. The count series therefore partly measures our cleanup, and the magnitude is unusable. The generalisable rule: **a trend in a CHAPTER series is a claim about the taxonomy until you have read the questions.** The earlier post's difficulty seam was about WHO labelled; this is about WHEN the labels were rewritten, and no cross-source check catches it because every source was relabelled at once.
  - **Replacing the label probe with a TEXT probe found something strictly better.** Counting `%passive voice%` / `%indirect speech%` / `%word class%` over question text is immune to chapter labels, and it produced a presence/absence result rather than a ratio: **voice and speech transformation appears in ZERO of the 15 sittings from 2017 to 2024, and in ALL FOUR sittings since 2025.** That is a genuine syllabus change, it is checkable by any reader with the papers, and it is the sort of thing two-year-old coaching material does not cover — which makes it the most useful sentence in the post. A weaker adjacent claim (fill-in-the-blanks hitting zero in 2026) was DROPPED: the format has hit zero in five earlier sittings too, so absence in one year is not a trend, per the weak-signal rule.
  - **The History/Polity crossover is the post's other headline, and it clears the labeller seam by evidence rather than by argument.** History outnumbered Polity in **all 17 sittings from 2017 to 2025** — not usually, every single one — and in 2026 the two TIED in both papers (10-10 in April, 9-9 in September). The seam risk was real, because 2026-II's subjects were assigned by our ingestion agents while the other 18 came from spreadsheets. What settles it: **NDA I 2026 is `.xlsx`-sourced and shows the same tie**, so the convergence is present in a paper our classification never touched. The per-era table (History 16.0 -> 9.5, Polity 4.7 -> 9.5) is stated PER PAPER because the eras hold 6/5/4/2/2 papers, and the paper counts are computed in SQL for the reason the Maths post learned the hard way.
  - **A hand-typed comparative was wrong for the second post running.** The draft read "Physics was next" on difficulty; Physics is **third** by share (7 of 24 = 29%) behind History (3 of 9 = 33%), and leads only on the absolute count. Now derived from the table, with both the share ranking and the absolute-count leader named separately and the small-denominator caveat stated in the prose. Worth noting what the pattern is: in both posts every FIGURE was correct and the defect was in an asserted COMPARISON between figures — "fifteen chapters" last time, "Physics was next" this time. Numbers got a derivation discipline after the first post; comparisons did not, and they are the remaining soft spot.
  - **Difficulty is used, but only within the paper.** Unlike the Maths sitting, 2026-II GAT's 26 HARD is unremarkable against the decade's 11-29 range, so nothing looks wrong — but "looks plausible" is not "same rubric", and it is still the only GAT sitting with `derived_model` set. So the post compares subjects WITHIN this one paper (one reader, 150 questions, internally consistent) and makes no cross-sitting difficulty claim, and it tells the reader in plain words that this is our reading and not an official rating.
  - **Register deliberately changed from the sibling post.** The user's read of the Maths article was that the analytical sections sound *about* students while the exam-hall callout sounds *to* them, and that the second voice is the right one. This post is written in that voice throughout, uses Indian English ("appeared for" rather than "sat"), and carries one piece of arithmetic students can act on: at +4/-1.33 a blind four-way guess is worth +0.0025 marks (i.e. nothing), while eliminating one option makes it +0.45. Verified before publishing rather than asserted.

- **2026-09-14 (seventh) — `/blog` SHIPS AS A SURFACE, with one post: the NDA II 2026 Mathematics paper analysed against all 19 sittings in the bank. `/blog` (SSG index) + `/blog/[slug]` (SSG, `generateStaticParams`), a metadata-only registry at `src/lib/blog/posts.ts`, bodies as TSX under `src/app/blog/_posts/<slug>/`, `BlogPosting` JSON-LD, sitemap entries and a Footer link. 31 tests — 24 pure + 7 prod-contract. The request was "write a blog on Maths NDA 2 2026"; the two decisions worth recording are both about what was NOT published.**
  - **The most tempting headline available was an artefact of our own pipeline.** NDA II 2026 reads **15.0% HARD against NDA I 2026's 27.5%**, which reads as "the paper halved in difficulty" and would have been the strongest hook in the post. It is a **LABELLER SEAM**: all 18 earlier sittings took their `difficulty` from uploaded `.xlsx` spreadsheets, while 2026-II's was assigned by our own derivation agent (`questions.derived_model = claude-opus-5`). The shape is what settles it — **87 of 120 rated MODERATE (72.5%) when no other paper in the decade exceeds 58%**, and EASY at 15 is the lowest ever recorded. That is the signature of an agent defaulting to the middle bucket, not of a paper that changed character. Publishing it would have presented a property of our ingestion as a fact about UPSC. The exclusion and its reasoning are recorded in a comment block in `_data/stats.ts` rather than only here, because the next session to open that file will see the tempting numbers before it sees this log. Same shape as [[default-becomes-assertion]] and the half-period-cell lesson from the guide refresh earlier the same day.
  - **A whole section was cut for the PROVENANCE of its evidence, not its correctness — and the user made that call, correctly.** The draft included three questions (Q4, Q11, Q62) where a circulating answer key is wrong. The evidence is strong: the blind derivation was written **before** the key was seen, 117 of 120 agreed, all 3 disagreements resolved against the key, and there is no official UPSC key for this sitting nor one expected. The user's objection was that the key is a **private third-party document**. That is decisive in a way correctness is not: a reader cannot verify a source they cannot see, so the claim would rest entirely on our authority — the opposite of what the post is for. The neighbouring **defective-question** section survived exactly because its evidence is public. Q106's givens are mutually inconsistent (`P(A∩B)=P(A∪B)=1/2` forces `A=B`, contradicting `2P(A)=P(B)`, and the derived `k=2/3` implies `P(A)=1/3 < P(A∩B)`), and Q112 prints **both** standard inequalities reversed (Bonferroni and Boole), killable by the single counterexample `A=B=C, P=1/2`. Both were re-derived independently here before writing, and both rest on the printed booklet every candidate holds. **The generalisable rule: for outward-facing content, the test is not "is this true?" but "can the reader check it?"**
  - **The author stated a wrong number in his own draft, which is the whole argument for deriving them.** The prose read "fifteen chapters contributed two questions or fewer"; it is **twelve**. Caught by re-running the claim against the data rather than by re-reading the sentence. The fix was not to correct the word but to delete the capability: `chaptersAtOrBelow(2)`, `CHAPTERS_REPRESENTED` and `questionsIn(MID_WEIGHT_BLOCK)` are now derived from the same table, so the prose cannot disagree with the data. Above that, `tests/blog-nda2-2026-stats.test.ts` (prod-contract, 8 assertions) re-derives **every** figure the post quotes — chapter split, era drift, paper shape, baseline — from production, with a paged read because the 2,280-row corpus exceeds PostgREST's 1,000-row cap and a truncated payload would have produced confident wrong numbers. This is the `/notes` intro-count drift class, gated **before** the drift instead of after it.
  - **An arithmetic error in the analysis phase, caught before it reached the draft.** The first pass computed the 2017-19 per-paper baselines by dividing by 5 papers when the era holds 6, reporting Probability 10.4 and Statistics 11.4 instead of **8.7 and 9.5**. The direction of both findings was unchanged (and Probability's rise is in fact larger than first stated), but the figures were wrong. The correction was to compute paper counts **in SQL** rather than by hand, and `DATA_HANDLING_DRIFT` now carries `papers` per era as a stored, test-asserted field for the same reason.
  - **Two plumbing choices that diverge from the obvious.** (1) **Not in the nav.** `MobileTabBar` is pinned to exactly five role-independent tabs by an arity test — a constraint designed on measured evidence in the 2026-09-11 (third) entry — and `PrimaryNav` already carries 5-7. A sixth tab would have broken a deliberate constraint, so discovery is the Footer plus in-post cross-links. (2) **The sitemap reads the registry, not git.** The plan was to extend `scripts/seo/content-dates.ts`; that was dropped because a post **declares** `datePublished`/`dateModified`, those are test-validated, and they are the same dates the `BlogPosting` JSON-LD emits. A git-derived second date could disagree with the structured data and would move a post whenever someone fixed a typo in a code comment.
  - **Verified, and how.** `GATE_RESULT: PASS (prepush)`. Both routes are genuinely prerendered — `.next/server/app/blog.html` and `.next/server/app/blog/nda-2-2026-maths-paper-analysis.html` exist on disk, which is the only probe this repo trusts after the shell-component de-caching incident, since the route table prints `●` even when every prerender bailed. The cached artifacts were scanned for authed-only content: the single `@gmail` hit is the public `CONTACT_EMAIL` the Footer renders on every page including `/privacy`. The 8 apparent raw-LaTeX leaks in the HTML are the `text` prop serialised into the RSC flight payload for the `KatexRenderer` client island, not visible text. **Not verified, and stated as such: layout.** There is no jsdom, testing-library or Playwright here, so the tables at phone width and the KaTeX inside the question cards were handed to the user rather than claimed.

- **2026-09-14 (sixth) — the NDA guides refreshed for NDA II 2026: ALL TEN, not just Maths, because the GAT turned out to be PUBLIC. 32 principle + 186 concept tags written first, then every count, table and trend re-derived across 49 files.**
  - **The task arrived as "update the NDA maths guide" and the premise was wrong in the log, not in the bank.** CLAUDE.md recorded the 150 GAT rows as PRIVATE; they were PUBLIC, so all nine GAT guides were under-reporting too. Eight of ten subjects crossed the ritual's 5% refresh threshold. **A status line in our own docs is a claim — the DB is the evidence.**
  - **NOTHING was failing: prod-contract ran 24 files / 230 tests GREEN against a bank the guides mis-stated by up to 10%.** The integrity gates check each table against its OWN `OVERVIEW.totalQ`, so a whole-bank drift is perfectly self-consistent. `guide-marks` also coupled a PURE-ARITHMETIC test to live `MARKING.papers`, so an ingest broke a test of maths that was still correct; the fixture is now frozen and only the live-data invariants read live data.
  - **The regenerated 19-column `EXAM_MATRIX` reproduced all 18 pre-existing columns BYTE-FOR-BYTE**, which is what makes the new column trustworthy — the hand-typed decade and the live bank independently agree. By contrast `DRIFT_ROWS` did NOT reconcile pre-2026: principle tagging had continued past the 2026-05-17 snapshot and the table was never re-derived. The 4 subtopic-backed rows matched EXACTLY for 2017-2025, and that asymmetry is what localised the rot to the tag table rather than the corpus.
  - **Two headlines the September paper REVERSED, both from reading a half-year as a year.** Vieta's "plunged to 2 q/paper-set in 2025-26" was a one-year dip — 2026 closes at 5, inside its long-run baseline. Physics's "the paper hardened 22x, 2% -> 44% HARD" was 11 HARD in NDA-1's 25 questions; the completed year is 18 in 49 = 37%, i.e. ~19x. The hardening is real, the multiple was inflated. **A half-year column that LOOKS like a year is the most dangerous cell on a trends page.**
  - **A shell verification printed "OK" for all seven guides while computing nothing** — Git Bash has no `grep -P` and no `bc`, so every sum came back empty and `"" = ""` passed. Re-run in Python it found 2 real mismatches (Polity's wrapped chapter name, Current Affairs' decimal `pctHard`). **A probe that cannot fail is worse than no probe.**
  - _(Digest-only: this entry was written as a digest in CLAUDE.md and archived here verbatim on 2026-09-16; there is no longer-form post-mortem.)_

- **2026-09-14 (fourth) — THE TWENTY UPSC NDA & NA CUT-OFF PDFs EXTRACTED INTO A TYPED REGISTRY: `src/lib/exam/cutoffs/` carries all 20 sittings (I and II, 2016-2025, no gaps), backed by 34 tests and an in-repo evidence file. No page, no DB table.**
  - **Scope check first: nothing in the repo held cut-off data.** Every `cut.?off` hit was unrelated — geometry ("cut off by the chord"), photoelectric cutoff frequency, `safeSnippet`. Genuinely net-new, so no duplication risk and nothing to reconcile against.
  - **All 20 PDFs are pure text with ZERO embedded images**, verified per file before trusting any extraction. That matters because the alternative — a scanned table — would have made the whole corpus a vision job; the check cost one command and removed the question entirely.
  - **THE PER-SUBJECT MINIMUM IS NOT THE CONSTANT EVERYONE QUOTES.** "At least 25% in each subject" is repeated by every coaching site and is wrong for four of the twenty sittings: 2016-II, 2022-II, 2023-II and 2024-I published **20%**. It is therefore a stored per-sitting field, and the four are pinned BY NAME in the spec so a future "simplify this to a constant" refactor fails loudly rather than quietly making a fifth of the corpus wrong. This is the finding that most justifies keeping the data at all — a summary table copied from the web would carry the error.
  - **NDA II 2025 broke the one-cut-off-per-stage assumption, and that single sitting decided the schema.** It is the first to publish SEPARATE male and female cut-offs (304.90 / 358.84 written, 666.01 / 737.40 final) and the first with decimals. A `written: number` column cannot hold it; flattening to the male figure discards a 53.94-mark gap. So a cut-off is a LIST of `(audience, marks)` pairs — nineteen sittings carry exactly one `"all"` entry, the twentieth carries two, and the next split sitting needs no schema change. Note `"all"` is NOT a synonym for `"male"`: collapsing them would make a 2021 figure look gender-specific.
  - **`cutoffFor` falls back in one direction and THROWS in the other, deliberately.** Asked for the female cut-off of a 2021 sitting it returns the published figure, because UPSC applied one cut-off to everyone that year and returning `undefined` would make nineteen of twenty sittings look as though they had no female cut-off. Asked for a single `"all"` figure from a split sitting it throws, because there is no honest answer and inventing one — the male figure, or the higher of the two — is the exact flattening the `CutoffMark[]` shape exists to prevent. The caller renders both or picks one knowingly.
  - **Eight sittings publish no recommendation table at all** — 2016 I/II, 2017 I/II, 2018 I/II, 2019-II, 2020-II. UPSC adopted the "Recommendation Details" layout for the I-sitting in 2019 and for the II-sitting only in 2021. Those rows carry `recommended`/`vacancies`/`wings` = **null, not 0**; a 0 would assert that nobody was recommended, which is a different and false claim. The [[default-becomes-assertion]] shape again: store the absence.
  - **The wing table has three incompatible era-shapes, so it is stored WITH a flag that says so.** 2019-I, 2020-I and 2021-I print one Air Force line ("120 including 28 ground duties"); from 2021-II it splits into Flying / GD-Tech / GD-Non-Tech. `airForceShape` records `lumped` vs `split` so a consumer can refuse to compute a year-on-year delta across the seam rather than silently producing a nonsense one. The per-sitting wing rows are written out longhand rather than shared from a constant, because the figures drift in ways a shared default would erase — Navy's female allocation alone runs 3 → 12 → 6 → 5 across four consecutive sittings, and the Naval Academy was explicitly male-only in four of them (recorded as `female: 0` with the printed note, which is distinct from the `null` of a sitting that published no split at all).
  - **The provenance probe was FAULT-INJECTED before it was believed.** `sources.json` holds the extracted text of each PDF plus the SHA-256 of the file it came from, and a containment test asserts every claimed figure appears in its OWN source text. A green probe proves nothing until it has been shown to go red: flipping 2016-I's written cut-off 288 → 289 failed it, and flipping 2024-I's 20% → the commonly-assumed 25% failed it **twice over** — once on the name-pin, once on the source-text check, from two independent directions. Both reverted. The probe cannot prove a number landed in the RIGHT field; the hand-verified pins do that, and the two together are what the corpus rests on.
  - **Typecheck caught a defect in the test, not the data** — `writtenCutoffRange` returns `null` on an empty corpus (rather than the `{Infinity, -Infinity}` a bare `Math.min/max` would hand a caller to render), and the spec dereferenced it without narrowing. Worth recording because the null-return was itself a deliberate choice and the typechecker immediately made the caller honour it.
  - **Deliberately NOT built: a page and a DB table.** Twenty rows that change twice a year do not warrant a migration, RLS policies and a loader, and no surface was asked for. A public "NDA cut-off trends" page is the obvious next step if wanted — the data would support it, and the trend is real: the written cut-off peaked at **360 (2022-I)** and slid to **291 (2024-I)**, a 69-mark fall over two years, while recommended candidates rose 519 → 792 against near-flat vacancies. That contradicts the standard advice to target a flat 350.

- **2026-09-14 (third) — NDA II 2026 PAPER II (GAT) ingested: 150 q committed PRIVATE via a new `scripts/nda-gat/`, and Set D transcribed a SECOND time as a fidelity check that came back 134/134 with ZERO option permutations. The bank's other 18 GAT sittings all came from untracked `.xlsx`; this is the first with a source of record. Nothing is PUBLIC and no mock exists — the key is still to come.**
  - **NOT A FORK OF `scripts/nda-pyq`, and the criterion is the one cds-maths itself used.** That pipeline is Mathematics at MODULE level — one `SUBJECT`, one `SUBJECT_ID`, `QUESTIONS_PER_PAPER = 120`. A GAT paper carries NINE subjects and decides `subject` **per question**, which makes the catalog THREE levels — a TYPE change, so a re-export would not type-check. But the fork is small and that was measured rather than assumed: of the nine functions in the `cds-maths` pure core, **SEVEN re-export verbatim** (including `validateRows`, which already carries the duplicate-option, `content_hash`-collision, LaTeX-balance and pipe-table-separator gates, and `validateSets`), and only `validateCatalog` and `buildRecords` hard-code one subject — about 90 lines. **No shipped file was modified**, and the proof is that `cds-maths` and `cds-gs` keep all 104 of their tests green. `fidelity.ts` likewise IMPORTS `normText`/`scorePair`/`labelMap` from `nda-pyq/match-variant` (which guards its own `main`) rather than restating rules each earned from a measured failure.
  - **THE BILINGUAL RULE IS NOT A PARITY, and this is the fact that would have silently fed an agent Devanagari.** Part A (English, Q1-50) is printed in **ENGLISH ONLY** — it is an English test, so UPSC prints no Hindi counterpart — over six CONSECUTIVE pages 2-7. Only then does Part B alternate even=Hindi / odd=English. So the English pages are `2,3,4,5,6,7` and every ODD page `9…47`, 26 of the booklet's 46. The sibling Maths booklet is pure alternation, and carrying that assumption across would be wrong for the first six pages. Read off the footers page by page, never derived.
  - **`validateSections` is the one genuinely new gate, and it is not cosmetic.** `NDA_GAT_PAPER` declares two sections with HARD counts (english 50, gk 100) reconstructed by SUBJECT membership, so an English question mis-filed under Physics makes the sections 49/101 and the mock **fails to build with an error naming neither the question nor the cause**. The boundary is PRINTED on the page (`PART - A` p2, `PART - B` p9), so it is checkable against the source rather than inferred. It runs per-band in `check-bands` — where an agent can still fix its own band in context — as well as at merge and commit.
  - **THE FIDELITY PASS IS THE HEADLINE: 134 of 134 MATCH, 0 PERMUTED, 0 OPTION_MISMATCH.** Series D was transcribed a second time — terse stems, but **options read label by label** — and matched onto Series A by option TEXT. Two independent readings of two different photographs of two different booklets agree on option SET *and* label ORDER for every matched question, so **UPSC does not permute options between GAT series on this paper**. The defect it exists to catch is the one nothing downstream can see: the correct option's text landing in the WRONG LETTER's slot, which leaves a question that reads perfectly, passes every structural gate, and makes a blind derivation **confirm the wrong letter** — the mechanism that gave the sibling CDS English corpus 19 wrong keys while a full blind re-derivation returned `confirmed` on all 89 rows it saw.
  - **A PERFECT SCORE FROM A GREEDY MATCHER IS WORTH NOTHING UNCHECKED**, so the map was validated against two observations made BEFORE the tooling existed: an eye-check of Set A p4 against Set D p2 (done while still establishing the page layout), and the b4 transcription agent's independent block report (`A Q51-60 = D Q91-100`, `A Q61-66 = D Q76-81`). Both pass, the map is bijective, and every label map is the identity. **The map is a COMMITTED artifact keeping Series D's own numbering**, because a four-series solution document is wanted — the `nda-pyq` shape.
  - **THE MATCHER'S ONE REFUSAL WAS A NORMALISATION GAP, AND THE FIX BELONGS IN THE FOLD, NEVER THE THRESHOLD.** D-Q76 against base Q61 have byte-identical stems and options reading `\(45^\circ\)` against `45 degrees`; the imported fold reduces those to `45circ` and `45degrees`, so the option score was 0 and the pair fell under the floor. Lowering a floor that is protecting 133 other questions in order to admit one is how a wrong pairing gets in — teaching the normaliser a notation it genuinely did not know is not. A test pins that the four angles of that very question stay four distinct strings after the fold.
  - **SET D'S GAP IS EXACTLY Q21-36, and it is permanent.** Printed pages 4, 5, 34 and 36 are absent from that scan; 34 and 36 are Hindi versos and cost nothing, but 4 and 5 are Part A, which has no Hindi facing page to recover from. The 16 lost questions were pinned from the numbering jump (printed 3 ends at Q20, printed 6 opens at Q37) and corroborated by the `Directions` blocks either side. They cannot be cross-checked and **they will be a hole in any Series D solution document** until a more complete Set D scan turns up.
  - **SET A IS THE WEAKER IMAGE and the escape hatch was used exactly as designed.** Set A carries ~885x1184 real pixels per printed page against Set D's ~1150x1570, and two option blocks on printed p11 are backed by ~109x73 and ~85x24 real pixels — **measured, so zoom adds nothing**. They were closed from Set D under the rule that the MATCH must be established on independently legible content first, and the two values that came from Set D alone are flagged in the row. A later blind deriver then corroborated both on internal-coherence grounds it could not have faked: Q58's distractors are precisely the two physical readings of the stem plus the `mu = 2` arithmetic slip.
  - **THE RECONCILIATION WILL BE THE INVERSE OF THE MATHS ONE, and that is written into the config, the brief and the README before the key arrives.** On NDA Mathematics 2026-II all three key disagreements resolved AGAINST the key, because a maths answer is derivable from the printed page. **A GK fact is not** — "which committee recommended constitutional recognition for local bodies" has no derivation, only recall, where a single blind pass measures ~94% in this repo. So on the 100 GK questions the KEY is the stronger source and the default is to defer to it unless it is self-refuting; Part A (antonyms, PQRS, grammar) is genuinely derivable and gets the Maths treatment. Hence `merge-answers` prints the confidence split per SECTION rather than blended.
  - **THE CONFIDENCE SPLIT IS THE USEFUL PRODUCT, NOT THE ANSWERS: 127 HIGH / 19 MED / 4 LOW, 0 nulls — and all four LOW plus three MED sit in Q141-150.** That is not scatter. The paper's difficulty cliff lands exactly there: Q121-140 is near-verbatim textbook recall (19 of 20 HIGH) while Q141-150 is 2025-26 current affairs — a uranium supply agreement, an IBCA membership list, a Khelo India mascot. **When the key arrives the last ten questions are where the review effort belongs**, then the 19 MED rows, each of which names its runner-up and what would have to be true for it to win. The current-affairs deriver did what the brief asked rather than what looks confident, naming for each LOW exactly what it does not hold — which matters because a mislabelled guess does not cost one answer, it **corrupts the instrument**, since a HIGH disagreement with the key is later read as evidence the KEY is wrong.
  - **ROWS COMMIT PRIVATE AND THE GATE IS STRUCTURAL, PROVEN NOT ASSUMED.** `discoverSittings` filters on `visibility='PUBLIC'`, so the mock builder lists all 18 existing GAT sittings and does **not** list `nda-2026-sep-gat` — it cannot be published early by accident. That matters because `/mock` grades real students against a FROZEN score, so a later key fix would need every prior attempt re-graded by hand.
