Two further traps on the way: when several files failed at once my instinct was a wedged PowerPoint COM session, and only running a **known-good control alongside them** ([[probe-must-reach-the-code]]) proved the probe sound; and repeating the identical opens three times showed the failures were perfectly deterministic rather than flaky.
  - **Two more defects the RENDER caught after the tests were green:** tables inherited PowerPoint's default **blue banded** style (violating the white/black spec) → pinned to "No Style, Table Grid" with explicit white cell fill; and a long paragraph was **clipped behind a figure** because the line estimate under-counted, so the next shape was drawn over live text. That split the estimate in two — **`sizing` (accurate, picks the font) vs `layout` (deliberately pessimistic, decides where the next block starts)** — pinned by a test asserting `layout >= sizing` across the whole size x length grid. Fixing it then exposed a third: the figure took its natural height and pushed options (B)(C)(D) off the slide, so images are now budgeted against what the text leaves over, with a floor so a figure can never be squeezed to a sliver.
  - **Design calls worth not re-litigating:** a set's shared context is **REPEATED on every sibling slide** (a slide is shown alone, so a passage two slides back leaves the question unanswerable); `includeSourceTag` and `groupBySubtopic` are honoured (the latter as a section-divider slide) while `includeSolutions` is meaningless for a question-only deck; and the skeleton is hand-authored constants rather than a committed PowerPoint-generated blob, so the package stays diffable — PowerPoint is not available on the server anyway.
  - **Measured, not assumed:** 36,938 of 51,424 PUBLIC questions carry math, so LaTeX is the dominant case; MCQ stem+options is p90 = 406 chars, p99 = 676, and a 430-char stem with 4 options fits at 24pt with room to spare, so the ladder's tail is a genuine edge case. **200 questions build in ~495 ms / 2.25 MB**, far inside the route's 60 s `maxDuration`. Verified: gate PASS (0 statement timeouts), 631 prerendered `.html` (nothing de-cached), 37 new tests, and a deck built from REAL bank questions opening in PowerPoint across math, tables, figures, shared context, subjective and section slides. **Owed: the browser click-through of the new Slides button** — it lives in a Radix portal that does not exist until clicked, so the build proves it compiles, never that it lays out.
  - **Logged, not fixed:** `jszip` is a `devDependency` yet is imported by runtime server code (`docxBuilder` since the Word exporter shipped, and now this builder too). It works only because Vercel installs devDependencies and Next traces them into the function. In the SUGGESTIONS backfill ledger awaiting permission, since it is shipped code.

- **2026-08-18 — The Physics and Maths syllabus maps rendered a wall of "?" and "Part" where Chemistry rendered real verdicts. THREE different causes, none of them "Physics is less mapped": a mislabelling bug, a tautological column, and a derivation that could not emit `full`.** Opened by the user asking to align the Physics/Maths cell values with Chemistry's.
  - **THE DIAGNOSIS THAT SHAPED EVERYTHING IS THAT CHEMISTRY IS THE COARSER SUBJECT, NOT THE RICHER ONE.** Its 4,315 State-Board-spine rows are a CHAPTER-GRAIN stamp: sections 1.1, 1.2, 1.2.1 and 1.2.2 all carry the identical note ("Unit 1 Some Basic Concepts. 26 PYQs, 23 since 2023."), authored from a docx that no longer exists, with **no source of record**. Physics/Maths rows are per-section and traceable to an individually adjudicated `covered_by` pointer. So "align down to Chemistry's method" would have been a regression in rigour; the work went the other way — raise the two derived subjects where the evidence already supported it, and delete Chemistry's one information-free column.
  - **CAUSE 1 — every "Mixed" cell in both subjects was a mislabelled blank, and not one was genuine.** `rollUpChapterStatus` returned `"mixed"` whenever ANY concept was unassessed, while its own comment said "makes the chapter **unassessed**" — the intent was right and the return value was wrong. Splitting the two cases against the live bank: **genuine disagreements = Chemistry 6, Physics 0, Maths 0**, against 239 Physics and 259 Maths cells captioned *"concepts in this chapter differ — open the chapter"*. A reader who followed that instruction found blanks. **Chemistry hid it for a year by being 100% assessed** and so can only ever reach the genuine branch; the derived subjects exposed it the moment they landed. Same failure as `coverCellState`'s "no single section" (2026-08-14) and as an unruled pair defaulting to `full` (2026-08-04): the absence of a review borrowing the vocabulary of one. Now a fourth state, `"partly-assessed"`, checked BEFORE the disagreement test so absence outranks it — where both are true the weaker claim is the honest one, and it costs nothing, since both labels send the reader to the same detail view. It renders the SAME "?" glyph and the SAME colour as an untouched cell, deliberately: they are one thing to someone scanning the grid, and a distinct colour would become the sole carrier of the difference, which this table's own rule forbids.
  - **CAUSE 2 — the "State Board" column was the book ruled against itself.** All 863 Chemistry rows are `full` with one note: *"Baseline: this concept is a printed section of the MH State Board Std XI/XII Chemistry textbook."* It says the book contains its own sections. Physics/Maths had **no rows at all**, because `derive-board-status.ts` only iterates the exam spines plus NCERT and so never wrote a self-column — hence a wall of green in one subject and a wall of "?" in the other two. Dropped from the page via `EXAM_COLUMNS`. **The in-flight Word exporter had independently reached the same conclusion and kept its own copy of the filter**, so the reasoning moved into one shared constant both surfaces read. A RENDER decision only: the loaders still tally every exam, the 863 rows stay queryable, and it is reversible by one line. It does not preclude giving the column a real meaning later — *"is this section examinable in the HSC board paper?"* is a genuine question, now evidenceable from the mh-hsc-12 board PYQ corpus, and is a different column.
  - **CAUSE 3 — `full` was unreachable by derivation, and the exporter had already grown a workaround for it.** The script wrote `partial` for every cited section, reasoning that a pointer proves the exam asks SOMETHING there. Sound for a section with sub-sections; **unsound for a LEAF**, the finest grain the map has, where "part of it is required" is not a statement the map can express or a reader can act on — the hedge described the tooling's confidence rather than the syllabus. The tell that it had become a problem: `handoutVocabulary` existed solely to print "Yes" for `partial` on a derived subject, with a documented **cliff** waiting for the first real `full`. New rules: exactly-cited leaf → `full`; every direct child `full` → `full`; any other live citation → `partial`; old-syllabus-only → `not`; **uncited → still NO ROW**, the rule the whole map rests on.
  - **THE CHILD-CLOSURE RULE IS NOT COSMETIC, and simulating it in SQL first is what showed that.** Without it a parent sits `partial` above children that are all `full`, and the chapter roll-up reports that as a genuine disagreement — **a finding manufactured by the derivation rather than found in the data**. Simulated before any code was written it would have produced **179 such cells in Physics and 99 in Maths**; with the rule, both are **0**.
  - **Rendered cells, before → after** (chapter + section rows): Physics **Yes 0 → 616 · Part 616 → 0 · false Mixed 239 → 0**; Maths **Yes 0 → 260 · Part 260 → 0 · false Mixed 259 → 0**. **Row COUNT is unchanged** (1,346 and 903) — membership is identical and only the verdicts moved, which is the check that the new rules re-graded existing evidence rather than inventing any.
  - **THE GUARD BECAME DISCRIMINATING RATHER THAN BLANKET, which is what makes re-derivation safe to repeat.** It used to refuse on the mere presence of rows, so the designed workflow (re-run after new rulings) meant passing `--force` routinely — and `--force` is the one thing standing between a typo and Chemistry's 863 hand-authored rows. Rows the script wrote are now identified by the `Derived:` prefix they already carried and replaced freely; anything else still needs the flag. **Proven on live data rather than asserted**: Chemistry refuses (4,315 authored), Physics and Maths applied with no flag, and Chemistry was fingerprinted per (exam, status) before and after to confirm it never moved.
  - **A pre-existing gate failure was checked rather than inherited or blamed.** `npm run syllabus:audit` fails on `audit-directions` with 5 contradictions — all Chemistry, all the stale rulings the 2026-08-14 entry recorded as "left flagged rather than edited" (Classification of Solids, Types of Polymers). Chemistry was never written this session, so they cannot be from this work; they remain open.
  - **Em-dash-bearing text cannot be matched through `python - <<heredoc` on this box**: stdin decodes as cp1252, so an em dash typed into the heredoc never matches the UTF-8 one in the file. Edits were made by index-slicing with `\u2014` escapes, and every touched file was scanned afterwards for mojibake, control characters and U+FFFD (all zero). Another face of [[heredoc-backslash-eating]] — here the corruption lands in the SEARCH string, so it fails loudly instead of silently, but only because the script asserted its own match.
  - **Owed: the browser render.** `/dashboard/syllabus/[subject]` is auth-gated and `force-dynamic`, so the build proves it compiles and nothing headless proves it lays out — an anon curl is bounced by middleware before the route compiles ([[probe-must-reach-the-code]]). See [[syllabus-map]].
- **2026-08-18 — THE NCERT CLASS 11 MATHS BOOK IS COMPLETE: the remaining 10 chapters in ONE parallel run — 925 q, exam 234 → 1,159, all 14 chapters PUBLIC. 686 exercise rows diffed against the printed key with ZERO our-answer-wrong. The whole story is the BAND SEAM, and an OMML defect that is invisible on the web.**
  - **SCALE AND SHAPE.** 20 transcription bands, then 16 solution agents, then 10 cross-checks — ~46 agents. Bands were cut at BLOCK boundaries, never page ranges, and every big chapter was split only at an exercise boundary. Sets 226 · Limits 126 · Probability 105 · Straight Lines 94 · Trigonometry 83 · PNC 82 · Relations 76 · Linear Inequalities 59 · Statistics 45 · 3D Geometry 29.
  - **THE BAND SEAM IS THE WHOLE STORY, and only one of its three forms announces itself.** Blocks and pages do not coincide; the recurring case is the LAST WORKED EXAMPLE BEFORE AN EXERCISE, which bands to the exercise it PRECEDES while being printed atop the NEXT band's first page. Eight seams were caught: (a) **stranded** — Sets Eg.9-11, Straight Lines Eg.4-7 and Probability Eg.5-7 sat on one band's pages inside another band's ref namespace; (b) **truncated** — Statistics Eg.7 and Probability Eg.7 have their ENTIRE solution tail on the next band's page, so a page-scoped read ships a solution that reaches no answer while LOOKING complete; (c) **duplicated** — Trig Eg.9, Limits Eg.17/18, Straight Lines Eg.8. Only (c) is self-announcing, because `merge.ts` throws on a duplicate ref. **(a) and (b) are invisible to every gate and were caught ONLY by the instruction to report on territory you do not own** — the agents' own reasoning was that a duplicate is visible and a gap is not, which is exactly right. New `scripts/ncert/dedupe-bands.ts` resolves (c) and **REFUSES when the two copies disagree**, because two readings of one page is a finding, not a duplicate; proven on both paths against an injected fixture after seven quiet runs had failed to demonstrate it fires.
  - **THE DEFECT THAT MATTERED MOST WAS INVISIBLE ON THE WEBSITE.** 27 math zones across Sets and Probability were unconvertible to OMML: **a PRIME ON A PARENTHESISED GROUP CONTAINING `\cup` or `\cap`** — `(A ∪ B)'`. KaTeX renders it perfectly, so nothing on `/board` or `/browse` would ever look wrong; it surfaces only as raw LaTeX in a **teacher's downloaded Word answer key**. Measured against the real converter rather than guessed, and the measurement killed five candidate fixes: `^{c}`, `{(…)}'`, `\left(…\right)'` and `^{\prime}` **all fail too**, while a prime on a bare symbol (`A'`) is fine. **`\overline{…}` is the only passing form.** This is the same failure the Class-12 batch met on `(A ∪ B)'`, re-encountered on a chapter whose entire subject matter is set operations.
  - **AND FIXING IT EXERCISED TWO GUARDS AT ONCE.** The bad notation was in STEMS as well as solutions, and `content_hash` is stem-derived — so the two chapters had to be DELETED and RE-COMMITTED rather than edited (editing in place would leave stored text ≠ the hash's preimage, the [[reject-dont-normalise-when-hash-upstream]] shape). Re-commit minted fresh UUIDs, which left all 295 authored solutions pointing at dead ids — and **the ref→id PAIRING GATE refused every one of them rather than mis-attaching a single solution.** Remapped by `ref`, which survives a re-commit because it is provenance, not identity, under a guard that refuses unless every ref resolves to exactly one fresh row.
  - **FOUR BRIEFING ERRORS OF MINE, every one corrected by an agent reading the page.** (1) I told the Limits band to expect "Examples ~1-17"; it is **1-4**, because thirteen of those pages carry a SEPARATE stream, `Illustration 1..10`. (2) I called Limits p-04's `Summary` a probe artifact; it is **real** — that chapter has two. (3) I placed Straight Lines' §9.3 on p12; it **opens on p08**, which is why four Examples nearly fell between bands. (4) I told the Sets solution agent to expect the classic `n(A∪B)` counting word problems; **they do not exist** — the rationalised edition has no §1.11 and no Exercise 1.6, confirmed against the NCERT XI spine. Plus a scoping mistake made TWICE: passing transcription notes about defects on SOLVED rows into solution briefs whose dumps contain only EXERCISE rows, so Relations and Trigonometry were each told to expect misprints they could never see. Both grepped, found nothing, and said so.
  - **STEP-6: 686 rows diffed, 0 OUR-ANSWER-WRONG, 1 BOOK-KEY-WRONG** (851 and 2 across the whole book including the pilot). Two chapters ran at FULL coverage with no NO-KEY-ENTRY at all (PNC 53/53, Probability 93/93) because they contain no proof questions. The one key error is **self-refuting**: Trig `Misc Q8` prints sin, cos, tan of x/2 as 2/√5, 1/√5, **1/2**, but its own first two values divide to give 2, and sin/cos IS tan; it also fails the forward check, since `2t/(1−t²)` returns the given −4/3 at t=2 and +4/3 at t=1/2. Two further brackets: **PNC `6.3 Eg.13`, the book's OWN worked example, concludes `r = 8, 3` without rejecting `r = 8`** — inadmissible for `⁴Pᵣ` — though notably the printed ANSWER KEY does *not* repeat its own textbook's slip where the exercises pose the same shape; and Trig `3.3 Eg.17`'s stray `=` after "Prove that", which is also the sole `audit:text` DROPPED_SYMBOL hit (the rule is right that a bare `=` opens the zone; the cause is the printed page, so the bracket exists to stop someone "repairing" a faithful transcription).
  - **FIVE FLOATING-POINT FALSE ALARMS, each of which would have flipped a correct answer**, and none acted on: a boundary evaluating to `−5.55e-17` instead of 0 (reading as endpoint-excluded); a ratio computing as `0.04000000000000001` instead of exactly 4% (reading as qualifying); a range scan returning exactly `1.0` at x = 1e9 when `f(x) = 1 − 1/(1+x²) < 1` strictly; a limit returning `3.9999999977` at 40 dps through catastrophic cancellation, converging to exactly 4 at 200 dps; and a scan "finding" solutions at every very-negative integer through a degenerate absolute tolerance. **Floating point is the a-CAS-returning-something-is-a-question rule in another dress.** Standing practice now: exact `Fraction`/`BigInt` for any boundary or equality test, and compare distances as SQUARES so `√20` vs `2√5` cannot false-alarm.
  - **VERIFICATION THE AGENTS IMPOSED ON THEMSELVES**, worth recording as the bar: Statistics **mutation-tested its own probe** — corrupting a cell in each of four table families to confirm it fired, on the reasoning that a clean run which cannot go red proves nothing — and computed every variance two ways with an assert between them. PNC generated all **34,650** distinct MISSISSIPPI permutations, all **907,200** EXAMINATION permutations beginning with A, and all **2,598,960** five-card hands. Probability enumerated all **5,461,512** five-marble hands. Trigonometry tested **239 points at 40-decimal precision at deliberately awkward angles** (0.31, 0.73, 1.19 rad — never 0 or π/4, so no convenient-angle coincidence could pass a false identity). One cross-check proved a key block's END by checking the PDF's **page count** rather than trusting blank space.
  - **A PARALLEL-RUN HAZARD:** one agent's scratch checker was **silently overwritten in the shared scratchpad by a concurrent agent's script** and unknowingly reported on a DIFFERENT chapter. It caught the discrepancy itself and re-ran under a unique filename. With ~46 agents sharing one scratchpad this is live; later agents were told to namespace their scratch files. Related: `git add -A scripts/ncert` swept an agent's in-flight probe into a commit — `.gitignore` now covers `_tmp_*`/`_validate*`/`data/_*`, though staging explicit paths is the real fix.
  - **Two judgement calls settled identically and recorded so they are not re-litigated:** the ten Limits `Illustration N` items and an unnumbered Statistics step-deviation demonstration are NOT ingested. Both are worked items with complete workings — but **the book gives neither a number**, so no honest provenance ref exists and `Eg.6b` would fabricate one. Reversible, with the natural ref shape noted in config.
  - **Rationalisation gaps found, beyond those already recorded:** Linear Inequalities' own §5.1 still promises two-variable inequalities the edition removed and cites "Section 6.2" from the pre-renumber book; 3D Geometry sets **three of its four Miscellaneous questions** requiring the section/centroid formulas it no longer teaches; Limits sets four requiring the chain rule it never develops; Sets has lost §1.11 and Exercise 1.6 entirely. Where a chapter sets a question it cannot support, the solution SAYS SO in its opening sentence rather than pretending.

Rather than default the value, the **export was REMOVED so the typechecker enumerated all 12 call sites** (the technique the syllabus loaders used when `subject` became required). Forking was rejected on evidence already in this file: `apply-errata`'s MCQ mirror hole was fixed in `mh-sb-11` while "the identical hole is confirmed live in `scripts/stateboard`" — a fork means applying every future fix twice. It now reports BOTH classes in one run, sectioned by exam id (a chapter NAME does not identify a class: Relations and Functions, Probability and 3D Geometry exist in both), and prints an explicit "0 flagged items" for an empty class, because **a missing section reads as "not checked" while a zero reads as "checked and clean"**. (3) **The text layer is arithmetically lossy**: `√` occurs ZERO times across all 14 chapters, a Conic Sections radical extracting as `2 2 ( ) x – a y +` with the sign gone and terms reordered ⇒ VISION ONLY, already the pipeline's mode.

A function `await`ing Postgres burns no CPU, so *every* SQL-side remedy — the 2.1 s query, the 378 daily statement timeouts, the retry loop — moves that line by approximately nothing. Explanations offered and killed, in order: **row growth** (correlation only — `db_health` starts 2026-08-07 and `pg_stat_statements` was reset 2026-08-09, so nothing can show per-call latency across the Jul 28 step; untestable, retracted); **DB latency** (arithmetically impossible — 1,317 successes × ~1.5 s + 352 timeouts × 3 s ≈ 51 min/day against a 17 min/day chart, a component cannot exceed its total); **a 3× retry amplifier** (refuted by the gap distribution between cancellations — a 3-attempt retry lands cancels ~3.25 s and ~3.75 s apart and **that band is empty**, 133 of 149 gaps are >15 s). - **2026-08-13 — A false alarm in the health tracker led to the two real costs left on this database: the homepage was uncached (38 min of DB time in 4 days) and `question_kind` was missing from every index (`/browse` 1,986 → 5.3 ms).   - **THE WARNING WAS THE TRACKER MISREADING ITS OWN NOTES.** It reported 113 MB spilled with "only 0.9 MB" accounted for — while **177 MB sat in the same `queries` array it was reading**. Four of the six spilling queries were first-seen, and the coverage rule dropped every first-seen row. (0.9 MB is exactly the two surviving rows' deltas — confirmed arithmetically, not inferred.) **The fix could not be "include new rows":** an existing test rightly defends against a newly-COLLECTED query laundering months of lifetime history into one window, which is what 0070 caused when 100 queries appeared at once. The discriminator used instead is a **physical bound, not a heuristic — no single query can have spilled more IN THIS WINDOW than the whole database did.** Under the bound a first-seen figure is credible; over it, it is provably lifetime and still ignored. The defending test passes unchanged.
  - **A MONITOR SET AT THE SAME POINT AS THE AUTOMATIC REMEDIATION CANNOT CARRY INFORMATION.** The dead-row rule warned at 20%; autovacuum fires at `50 + 0.2 × live` = 9,415 rows on `questions`, and the rule fired at 9,365 — **the same point**. Its message even said "autovacuum usually clears this on its own", true by construction. It had never fired in eleven snapshots, across a healthy sawtooth of 7.7 → 18.3 → 7.2%. Raised to 35%, where firing means autovacuum is genuinely losing. Filed as rule 8 of [[monitor-threshold-calibration]].

The July sweep fixed `AppHeader`; **a fix to a shared component does not cover a page that reads cookies directly.** Now behind `unstable_cache` (anon client ⇒ cache-legal). Verified on a production build: **5 loads → 12 DB calls instead of 60**, counts matching the bank exactly, cache-miss and cache-hit renders identical, and the signed-in redirect confirmed by hand. **Only the DB half is cached** — registry order, flags, hrefs and the notes lookup stay outside, so a new exam appears on the next deploy rather than waiting out a 24-hour entry. The trap that shaped the payload: **`unstable_cache` serialises its result and a `Map` serialises to `{}`** — cache one and every card silently prints "0 questions" with no error; entry arrays are used instead, pinned by two tests.

That is the distinction: an **Index Scan + Filter is vacuum-proof** (the heap visit is the filter), while an **Index Only Scan + heap fetches is exactly what vacuum fixes**. The index converted one into the other, and only then did `VACUUM (ANALYZE)` pay: coverage **67.4% → 100%**, dead rows 17.5% → 0%, heap fetches **13,092 → 0**, 705 → 228 ms. Vacuuming first would have bought ~16% and looked like a dead end.

Same lock cost, worse lock, and only an `EXPLAIN` estimate instead of live traffic. Also unresolved: 100% coverage will decay under ingestion (which is why 0076 tracks it), and the 80% threshold is set from a single reading, so it may prove too chatty. Incidentally: the **largest chapter is now 664 PUBLIC questions** (was 531 six days earlier) against the tracker's 800 warn and the PostgREST 1000 cap.

New `chapterOverride` carries the move: the compilation files a question by the section it was typed into, so a stem that acquired an integral sign from its neighbour acquired that neighbour's chapter too.

A fix whose `from` equals its `to` is now refused outright: one shipped as a silent no-op because it was built with `.replace()` against a needle a shell layer had mangled, and it passed every check while correcting nothing. A known MCQ whose options were lost is refused rather than shipped as free-response — a silent format downgrade invisible in every count. And `commit.ts` NAMES every row the exam-scoped `content_hash` absorbs into an existing textbook row, because in a PYQ ingest a silent `skipped=1` is indistinguishable from a question that was never on the paper.
  - **The extractor's own output was wrong in five ways that only showed once rows were live**, all found by `audit:text`: pandoc's default markdown emits "simple tables" (a dashed grid nothing here parses) for five probability-distribution tables — switching to GFM pipe tables then exposed that `collapseSpaces` joined every newline, and **a pipe table IS its line structure**; escaped `\<`/`\>` on every p.d.f. support interval; a flattened fill-in blank shipping as `\:`; a lone `\` before the board's internal-choice `OR`; and three lost superscripts shipping as literal `x2`. Changing the extractor invalidated every adjudicated fix and the guard refused them all — correctly — so they were migrated by applying the same artifact rules to both `from` and `to`.
  - **All 317 rows were deleted and re-committed rather than edited**, since `content_hash` covers the stem; the wipe asserts its own scope first because the textbook corpus shares these chapters. Verified per chapter by reading back FROM the database: 15/15 clean, `audit:text` clean on all five classes, `board:lint` green, 5 circuit figures attached. See [[mh-hsc-12-pyq-ingestion]].

- **2026-08-11 — Local database backups shipped (`npm run db:backup`, pure core + 20 TDD cases, Windows task every Monday 11:00) — the project had NO backup mechanism of any kind.**
  - **WHY IT WAS NEEDED, stated as an audit rather than a feeling.** Much of the bank is reproducible from the repo — 1,433 tracked data JSONs, 88 JEE paper files — but **zero `.xlsx` are tracked**, so the NDA + MHT-CET corpora (~14,000 q, the two oldest subjects) have no source of record here at all; the 13-subject taxonomy cleanup was done as **inline SQL in chat** ("no scripts", per the workflow note above), so 513 chapters + 4,941 subtopics exist only as rows; and the ~235 wrong-key flips were applied to rows, some mirrored back to source and some not (the `scripts/stateboard` MCQ mirror hole in the backfill ledger is a live instance). On top of that ~15,500 operational rows — `paper_questions` 3,431 · `attempt_answers` 7,756 · `user_activity` 2,090 · `question_reviews` 1,312 · `student_profiles` 98 — have **no source anywhere**.
  - **THE THREAT MODEL IS OUR OWN SCRIPTS, NOT SUPABASE, and that decided the design.** This log is a list of near-misses from bulk writes: the unscoped NCERT prune that would have deleted the whole Physics spine (2026-08-03), `derive-board-status` that would have destroyed 4,315 hand-authored rows without its `--force` guard (2026-08-05), `scan-flip` publishing two withheld Maths rows (2026-08-01), the review-dump that silently destroyed filled-in verdicts (2026-08-11). Every one was caught by a guard or by luck. So the highest-value invocation is **by hand before a risky script**, and the weekly cron is the safety net — not the other way round.
  - **TWO ROUTES ELIMINATED, both by testing rather than reasoning.** (1) **The Supabase CLI shells out to DOCKER** — `supabase db dump` returns `LegacyDockerRunError`, and Docker Desktop (multi-GB + a background VM, on a drive with 15 GB free) is the wrong price for a weekly backup. (2) **A hand-rolled TypeScript export was the tempting zero-install option and is the wrong tool**: reading tables through PostgREST inherits the 1000-row cap that has bitten this codebase five times — **silently**, producing a backup holding 2% of the bank that looks fine — and it **cannot reach the `auth` schema at all**, so all 102 accounts would be absent and every row keyed to them would restore orphaned. pg_dump reads from one snapshot, fails loudly, and covers `auth`. Verified: `auth.users` is in the dump.
  - **The CLI dry-run was still worth running, for two things it printed.** Supabase's **own pg_dump flag set** (the authoritative list of schemas their tooling omits, now the basis of `EXCLUDED_SCHEMAS` — kept as a DENY list so a new custom schema is backed up rather than silently dropped, the `needsBuild` polarity argument); and the fact that the CLI **provisions a temporary `cli_login_postgres` role**, so it needs no database password. **Caveat worth knowing: `--dry-run` prints that role's live password to the console in plain text** — never paste its output anywhere.
  - **The direct DB host is IPv6-ONLY** (`db.<ref>.supabase.co` publishes AAAA and **no A record**). It works on the current network and will fail with a confusing connection error on any network without IPv6; the session pooler is the IPv4 fallback, with a different username format. Checked before writing a line of the script, which is the only reason it wasn't discovered at 11:00 on a Monday.
  - **A REAL BUG IN MY OWN RETENTION CODE, caught in self-review before it shipped.** `--keep=abc` parses to `NaN`; `Math.max(1, NaN)` is `NaN`; `slice(0, NaN)` is `[]` — so the naive version marked **every backup for deletion** on a typo, in the one function whose entire job is deciding what to delete. Now every degenerate limit (NaN, Infinity, 0, negative, fractional) resolves towards keeping MORE, and the CLI rejects a garbage `--keep` loudly. Two sibling safety properties are spec'd: it never returns a file whose name it cannot parse (so a stray in `backups/` is not its business), and retention is by RUN so a dump and its manifest can never be separated. See [[destructive-default-fails-safe]].
  - **VERIFIED, not asserted.** 24 MB in 16 s; the archive read back through `pg_restore` as **85.3 MB of SQL, 71 COPY blocks**, with `questions` **45,351** and `auth.users` **102** matching the live counts exactly. **The size reconciles completely** — 169 MB on disk − 58 MB of indexes (derived data, rebuilt on restore, correctly never dumped) − 11 MB page/TOAST overhead = **89 MB heap → 85.3 MB as SQL → 24 MB at compression level 9 (3.6×)**. A truncated dump would show as wrong row counts, not as a small file.
  - **REGISTERING A SCHEDULED TASK IS NOT PROOF IT RUNS.** Fired it through the scheduler: `LastTaskResult 0`, a third dump written, `backups/last-run.log` appended by `weekly.cmd` (a scheduled run's console output otherwise goes nowhere). `-StartWhenAvailable` is the load-bearing flag — without it a sleeping laptop skips the week silently.
  - **My own failure-path probe never reached the failure path.** Running with a deliberately wrong password dumped production successfully, because every script here loads `.env.local` with `override: true` and the file beats the environment. Recorded in the runbook; the rejection path is therefore proven **by construction** (`fail()` exits before the pruning block) and by unit test, **not empirically** — stated as a gap rather than papered over. See [[probe-must-reach-the-code]].
  - **Scope deliberately NOT taken:** encryption (a mitigation for uploading somewhere shared — these stay local), an off-machine copy (the user's call; `C:` already holds the only copies of the source PDFs and Excel uploads, so that exposure predates this), and a restore rehearsal into the test project (it would copy production PII into a second Supabase account and clobber the test fixtures). Runbook: `scripts/backup/README.md`. See [[local-database-backup]].
- **2026-08-11 — BLIND re-derivation of two LWS papers (180 q): 176 agree · 4 disagree · 3 wrong keys corrected — and the one that mattered was invisible to a read-through.** The user asked for the solutions of the 120-q NDA Maths Full Mock + the 60-q Properties-of-Triangle/Inverse-Trig/Trig-Equations paper to be reviewed. Done twice: first a read-through (`solution_audit`), then a genuinely blind pass via agents.
  - **THE READ-THROUGH found 2 wrong keys and 1 broken solution**, each with a distinct tell. **Q941** ("variance of 2,4,6,8") was keyed 8 while **its own stored solution derives 5** — a key/solution contradiction. **Q2017** (shortest distance between two lines) was keyed (2,3] while the true value is **1.7263 ∈ [1,2)**, and the tell was that the solution *never computed anything* — it said "the printed solution evaluates ≈ 2.7". **A solution that cites an authority instead of deriving is unverified by definition.** **Q51** (relation "x−y zero or irrational") had the right answer and a solution that was visible failed scratch work: four attempted counterexamples, every one of which SATISFIES transitivity, then "the standard result is…". Rewritten with one that works (√2, 0, √2−1: two irrational steps whose difference is 1).
  - **THE BLIND PASS found a third — and this is the whole argument for keeping the two methods apart.** **Q1217**: option B lists **only VALID** solutions of `tan((π/2)sin θ) = cot((π/2)cos θ)`, so nothing about it reads as wrong. It is wrong by **OMISSION** — missing every odd multiple of π, since θ=π satisfies the equation (`tan 0 = 0 = cot(−π/2)`) while the π/2 branch it excludes is inadmissible anyway. Complete set `θ = rπ` matches no option ⇒ **D**. My read-through checked that π/2 was inadmissible **and stopped there**. A `solution_audit` cannot reach this class by construction, which is exactly why 0075's `METHOD_STRENGTH` refuses to let a read-through excuse a blind pass.
  - **THE BLIND PASS ALSO RE-PROVED THE MORNING'S WORK.** Three separate agents, each seeing only stem+options, independently returned **Q941→D**, **Q2017→C** and reproduced the **NDA 2023-I two-triangle ambiguity** from scratch. Those three corrections had rested on my own derivation alone; they no longer do. **Independent confirmation is worth as much as the find** — it is the difference between "I checked it" and "it was checked".
  - **THREE DEFECTS, SOURCE-ADJUDICATED, AND THEY HAD THREE DIFFERENT OWNERS** (booklets located via `scripts/practice/config.ts`, all with usable text layers): **Q2666 was OURS** — the ingest dropped "The minimum value of", leaving a stem naming no quantity; printed key (a) already matched, stem restored. **Q2526 is the SOURCE's** — the booklet genuinely prints both `[-1,∞)` and `(-1,∞)`, and BOTH are true (strict monotonicity does not require f′>0 at an isolated endpoint), printed key (d) retained with a note saying plainly that a student answering (a) is not wrong. **Q761 is the SOURCE's** — it prints `a=1/3` and `c=4/12`, the same number, both distractors, printed key (d) matches. **The lesson: a defect report is a HYPOTHESIS ABOUT WHOSE DEFECT IT IS, and only the source settles it** — the same rule that fired that morning when I called the NDA 2023-I question defective before checking and was rightly challenged.
  - **ALL FOUR DEFECTS WERE `practice` ROWS; NOT ONE WAS A PYQ.** They came from the vision-ingested practice pipeline ([[practice-pdf-vision-ingestion]]). That matters for what to review next: papers hold **1,843 practice questions vs 1,211 PYQ**, and the 2026-07-25 `audit:keys` sweep sanitised only the STRUCTURAL class (solution-contradicts-key · duplicate options · not-exactly-one-correct). **Q1217 is none of those** — coherent solution, distinct options, exactly one flagged correct, key still wrong. That *stealth* class has never been swept, and this pass found it at ~1 per 180. Prioritise practice-heavy papers; the estimate rests on one sample, so measure two more before committing to a bank-wide sweep.
  - **A COLLISION IN MY OWN TOOL, same family as the dedupe lesson written hours earlier.** `reviews:paper` used `paper:<id>` as the run label **regardless of method**, so the blind rows collided with the morning's `solution_audit` rows on `(question_id, run_label, hash)` and **118 confirmations were silently discarded** — only Q1217 survived, because flipping its key changed the hash. The tell was again a count that had no business being what it was ("0 recorded | 118 already on record"). Now method-qualified. New tooling: `diff-blind.ts` (prints disagreements as a **work list, never a verdict**) and `triage-dump.ts`, which **refuses to run against a blind dump** — it would otherwise flag all 120 rows `NO_SOLUTION`, and a probe that fires on everything buries its one real hit. Agent derivations are committed under `scripts/reviews/data/blind/` as the auditable artifact.

- **2026-08-11 — Review provenance now EMITS ITSELF: nine pipeline scripts record as they run, `*.errata.json` backfilled (+114), and the two surfaces that were doing the most review work with the least record — printed papers and report triage — got CLIs (migration 0075).** Follows the 0074 ship + backfill below. Table now **952 rows / 943 questions**.
  - **THE QUESTION THAT FOUND THE BIGGEST GAP was the user's: "there are papers in the paper section — how are their reviews handled?"** Answer: they weren't. **50 papers · 3,431 placements · 3,054 distinct questions · ZERO rows** — more than 3× everything the backfill recovered, and it is the review that runs most often (read the solutions before printing). Both now have CLIs (`reviews:paper`, `reviews:resolve`), and the route's private recorder MOVED into the shared `emit.ts` so the two cannot drift.
  - **MIGRATION 0075 adds `solution_audit`, and the reason is that the distinction is LOAD-BEARING, not descriptive.** A pre-print review is usually a read-through of the stored solution; a blind re-derivation is a different animal. Labelling the first as the second would overstate evidence *inside the audit trail* — the failure this table exists to prevent, one level up. What makes it more than a label: **it decides what a later pass may SKIP.** A question confirmed by blind re-derivation is done; one confirmed by a read-through must still be shown to a blind pass, because **a stealth wrong key survives a read-through by construction** (the 2026-06-03 audit's central finding: most of its ~235 flips were solutions that were internally consistent and simply wrong). Proven live on a 60-q paper: after two read-through confirmations a second read-through skipped them (58 left) while a blind pass still showed all 60. `METHOD_STRENGTH` + `classifyForReview` (TDD) carry it; a known defect **outranks a skip**, because before printing "this question has a known defect" is exactly what the reviewer needs.

Report triage derives `confirmed` only from `wont-fix` on an answer-affecting category (unambiguous: a claim was rejected, so the answer stands) and otherwise requires an explicit pick.
  - **THREE DEFECTS FOUND BY USING THE TOOLS, NOT READING THEM** — each invisible to the gate. (1) The paper dump omitted `context`, so set-based questions ("Consider the following for the next two items…") read as unanswerable — **it nearly produced a false defect report on the very first run**, and only checking the DB stopped it. (2) **Re-dumping silently destroyed filled-in verdicts** — I did exactly that to my own work; it now refuses without `--force`. (3) `reviews:report` crashed with `Bad Request` the first time its coverage section met real data: **`.in()` with 833 uuids exceeds the PostgREST URL limit — paging a RESULT (1000) and chunking a FILTER (~200) are different limits and only one of them is 1000.**
  - **A REAL FINDING ON A PAPER ABOUT TO BE PRINTED, and the user's push-back is the lesson.** Reviewing 3 questions of an NDA paper surfaced that Q36's solution opened "From Q35" while Q35 was not in the paper. Chasing it showed the underlying **NDA 2023-I Q35/Q36 pair is under-determined**: `sin A = √3/2` admits **A = 120°** as well as 60°, giving a genuine triangle (√3,1,1) that satisfies every printed condition, with perimeter **√3+2 — printed option (b) of Q35** — under which Q36 flips from (c) to (d). **I asserted "the source is defective" BEFORE verifying it, and was right to be challenged**: the documented rule here is that the bank-side is the ~80% default suspect and a stem must be source-verified before the source is blamed. Rendered `Maths_2023_NDA1.pdf` p.13 and read it — our stem is word-for-word faithful, nothing dropped — then confirmed the ambiguity with a **brute-force numeric scan that found both branches without being pointed at a second one**. That last number is the result: across every recorded review, not one "our answer was wrong" finding survived adjudication, so the Decisions-log claim that source keys fail far more often than our answers now stands as data rather than prose.
  - **RESOLUTION WAS 100%, which is why this was worth doing at all.** All 566 ref-only rows resolve via `(source_file, question_number)` — verified unique — and all 278 id-bearing rows point at live questions; 844/844 → 833 distinct, every one PUBLIC. The per-file counts reconcile *exactly* against the Decisions log (mh-ssc-10 gives 279 AGREE / 14 BOOK-WRONG / 0 ours-wrong; NCERT gives 2 book-key errors across ~256 exercise questions), which is the best available evidence the ref mapping is right.
  - **THE DEFECT, and it is the transferable part: the dedupe constraint resolved a genuine disagreement by `readdir` order.** NCERT `Ex 7.8 Q13-22` sit in TWO overlapping agent batches of one cross-check that **disagree on all ten** — `integrals.ex678` says CANT-READ-KEY ("the reprint lists Ex 7.8 answers 1-12 only"), `integrals.ex8910` says AGREE *and transcribes a concrete printed key for every one*, having found them under the old Ex 7.9 numbering exactly as the other batch guessed they might be. Same question, same `run_label`, same hash ⇒ `UNIQUE (question_id, run_label, reviewed_content_hash)` collapsed each pair and kept whichever file the OS listed first — **the weaker verdict, on all ten**. Caught only by re-checking a number I had already called "benign" (844 rows → 834 written, 10 deduped). **A dedupe key silently picks a winner; if the rows it merges can DISAGREE, that is an adjudication being made by file order.** Now `findVerdictConflicts` blocks a conflict *within* one run, while a disagreement *between* runs still lands — that is real history, not a conflict. Adjudicated all ten to `confirmed` (7 keys match verbatim; Q16 distributes to ours, Q17 is term order, Q20 is `4/π−2√2/π = (4−2√2)/π`, each checked by hand): **evidence beats absence of evidence.**

Mapping it would have inverted the record. Same for an mcq-verify row disagreeing with the live key: either the key was fixed later or the question is defective and the official key was deliberately kept, and guessing between them is not available. **13 adjudications live in `scripts/reviews/backfill-overrides.json`**, each citing its Decisions-log date; a stale entry that matches nothing is a BLOCKING error, so the file cannot rot.
  - **Prose is never a source.** Only committed machine-readable artifacts are read. A `*.crosscheck.json` row carries a ref, a verdict and a derivation written by the pass that did the work; a Decisions-log paragraph re-read by an LLM is a plausible reconstruction, and this table exists precisely so a reconstruction and a record stop looking alike. Hence `source='backfilled'` on all 834.

So the fingerprint means "as at backfill": drift after this run is detected normally, drift before it is undetectable by construction. The alternative (a sentinel) would mark all 833 permanently stale and make the report's stale section useless on day one.

Coverage lands at CBSE Class 12 Maths **53.6%**, MH-SB-11 7.8%, MH-HSC-12 7.0%, MH-SB-9 4.9%; everything else reads 0, meaning *not recorded*. See [[question-review-provenance]].

- **2026-08-11 — Review provenance shipped (migration 0074 + `npm run reviews:report`): the bank can now say which questions nobody has checked.** Prompted by the question "we review question solution — do we maintain record of it?". The audit found the answer is *partly, and not queryably*: the Decisions log carries the narrative (Phase 7 of `/solution-cleanup` mandates an entry), `question_reports` covers inbound student reports, and three in-band markers cover slivers — `derived_model`/`derived_at` on 1,093 of 44,220 rows, 533 `pyq_note` provenance clauses, 206 `[Textbook…]` errata brackets. Nothing recorded *this question was reviewed, by this method, with this verdict*.
  - **THE DISTINCTION THAT MADE IT TRACTABLE: provenance of CONTENT was already shipped five times over — provenance of REVIEW never was.** `derived_model` (0040), `source_file`/`pyq_note`, the `[Q# · month · year]` student citation, written-paper slot provenance, sync metadata (0010) all answer *where did this come from*. None answers *who checked it and what did they conclude*. `derived_model` is the near-miss and is still upstream of verification — it says an LLM wrote this solution, not that anyone confirmed it. That is exactly why 1,093 rows carry it while ~9,546 questions are described as audited: two different facts, never stored in the same place.
  - **A REGISTRY WAS THE OBVIOUS ANSWER AND WAS REJECTED.** The `src/lib/relevance/config.ts` precedent (reviewed scope in TS, exceptions in the DB) works for the syllabus-fit screen because ~95% of questions pass, so only the failures carry information. Solution review is the inverse: **the per-question verdict is the expensive artifact and it already exists** — a blind re-derivation agent judges every question and today that judgement is flattened into a paragraph and discarded. Three concrete failures decided it: the scope unit is not stable (chapter for `/solution-cleanup`, `source_file` for JEE, bank-wide for a probe, single-question for report triage — one registry axis cannot hold all four); a chapter marked reviewed in May silently claims every question uploaded into it since (the [[default-becomes-assertion]] shape); and a registry cannot carry a verdict, so the moment you want one it has become a table with extra steps.
  - **`reviewed_content_hash` is the load-bearing column, and it came from re-reading 0040's own comment** ("so staleness is detectable"). A review describes the question AS IT WAS; without the fingerprint a confirmed row keeps asserting itself about text that has since been repaired. Two corollaries the implementation forced: a corrective script stamps the hash the row holds **after** its own edit (the edit is the review's own output — stamping the pre-fix value would make every fixed row born stale), and an unknown current hash counts as STALE, never fresh.
  - **Append-only is not ceremony — the NCERT Integrals cross-check already produced an overturned review.** An agent recommended flipping our (A) to match the printed key; source-verification reversed it (the agent had `options:[]` from a dump bug; the page shows our (A)=6 is right and the NCERT key is wrong). An UPDATE erases both the reversal and the reason — which is the single most valuable line in the record, and the thing [[audit-probe-symmetry]] keeps re-learning. Current belief = newest row per question, not the only row.
  - **TWO THINGS DELIBERATELY GET NO ROW, for the same reason.** A HELD key dispute in `grounding/commit.ts` is a flag, not a verdict — the adjudication that follows (`apply-key-fix.ts`) is what concludes one. And **a structural probe pass (`audit:keys`) records nothing**: it checks three defect shapes and is blind to a plain wrong key, so stamping every scanned row `confirmed` would turn ~40k unexamined questions green — precisely the failure that shipped 169 false coverage verdicts on the exam spines. Only an adjudicated flag earns a row.
  - **Report triage never infers a verdict from a status.** "wont-fix" on an answer complaint IS unambiguous (a reporter said the answer was wrong, we rejected the claim ⇒ `confirmed`) and is derived without asking; "resolved" is ambiguous — flip, repair, or rewrite — so it records only if the admin picks one, and the picker is offered only for answer-affecting categories. The server re-derives this from the **stored** category and never trusts the client, or a caller could stamp `confirmed` on a question nobody adjudicated. Fixed a pre-existing no-op on the way: the reports "Save note" button called `apply(currentStatus)`, which the same-status guard swallowed — so notes had never saved.
  - **Pilot scope (user's call): `scripts/grounding/*` only** — the run-label convention is easier to change before five callers depend on it. Read surface `npm run reviews:report` (coverage by exam/subject · per-run correction rate · stale reviews), counts from the `get_chapter_facets` aggregate on the **anon** client so RLS scopes them to PUBLIC, never a row-derived `.select()`. First run against prod: **40,720 PUBLIC questions, 0 recorded**, and the report says in those words that a 0 means *not recorded*, not *unexamined*. **Backfill deliberately NOT done** — and the good news found while scoping it is that **53 machine-readable review artifacts are already committed** (37 `*.mcq-verify.json` carrying real question ids, 16 `*.crosscheck.json` carrying `ref` + verdict + derivation). Those are parseable evidence; Decisions-log prose is not, and reconstructing from it would put a plausible guess where the table promises a record. Hence `source: 'live' | 'backfilled'`. Verified: 42 unit + 6 RLS integration tests, full gate PASS, 625 prerendered `.html` (no de-caching), advisors show only the expected `rls_enabled_no_policy` INFO. **Owed: the signed-in browser click-through of the triage verdict picker** — `/dashboard/reports` is auth-gated `ƒ`, so the gate proves it compiles, not that it lays out.

  - **THE EXPENSIVE LESSON — plan transcription bands from a `Solution :` SCAN, never from section banners.** A banner scan (`SOLVED EXAMPLES` / `EXERCISE N.M`) sees only the BOXED blocks, but this book embeds worked examples with printed solutions directly in the theory, and those are `solved` rows too. Ch.5 carries **29** `Solution :` markers of which only ~18 are in banners. Consequence: **four separate "belongs to nobody" gaps** across Ch.1 and Ch.5 — `1.1 SolvedEx.8`'s solution tail, the whole octagon example `1.2 SolvedEx.6`, ~11 theory-embedded §5.1/§5.2 examples, and `Ex 5.2 Q9`. Every one was recovered ONLY because agents were told to REPORT on territory they did not own; that instruction turned out to be doing more work than the boundaries themselves. Now codified in `scripts/mh-sb-11/README.md`: scan for solution markers → cut bands at BLOCK boundaries (never page breaks) → name the split point in both prompts → theory-embedded examples get SUB-SECTION-scoped refs (`5.1.6 SolvedEx.1`) so they cannot collide with the boxed block's bare `<N.M> SolvedEx.<n>`, which the book reuses.
  - **`Ex 5.2 Q9` is the judgement call worth keeping:** skipped by the transcriber under the brief's "skip Activity boxes" rule, but it is a NUMBERED exercise question merely tagged `[Activity]`, with 8 determinate sub-answers. The rule targets open-ended classroom tasks with no determinate answer. Ingested as 8 set-siblings. **And the book's own pre-filled row in it is WRONG** — it marks `a+b even` on ℕ as NOT transitive, when that relation is congruence mod 2, i.e. an equivalence relation. The single cell the book fills in as its worked example teaches the wrong answer.
  - **Two more substantive book errors, both verified by the maintainer rather than taken on an agent's word:** (a) Angle answers "ratio of radii" with the ratio of the ANGLES, **twice** (60:75→4:5 and 65:110→13:22, where equal arcs make radius inversely proportional to angle, so 5:4 and 22:13) — two independent agents each found one, and only seeing them together identified it as a systematic slip rather than a typo; (b) `5.1.6 SolvedEx.1(c)` derives `(x−4)/(x−3) ≤ 0` correctly then prints the `≥ 0` region, so x=3.5 satisfies the inequality yet is excluded and x=5 fails yet is included.
  - **`apply-errata.ts` MCQ mirror hole CLOSED — the same defect this session found sitting live in `stateboard`.** The mirror tested `typeof hit.solution === "string"`, which is false for an MCQ fragment row (an MCQ carries a key, not a solution), so the bracket landed in the DB only and the next re-commit would revert it. It now CREATES the field and warns loudly when a bracket fails to mirror anywhere. Sets' `Misc I Q9` bracket would otherwise have been lost. The identical hole is confirmed live in `scripts/stateboard` (3 of its 76 brackets, all MCQ rows) — logged in the SUGGESTIONS backfill ledger with a 360, awaiting permission since that is shipped work.
  - **Also banked:** an authoring agent caught its own **id permutation** (rows shifted onto neighbours' ids) via a `ref`→`id` pairing diff — an id-SET check passes such a shift perfectly, since it is a permutation, not a loss. `SOLUTION_BRIEF.md` now requires diffing the PAIRING, not the set.

Same failure as Class-9 Real Numbers; recorded in `config.ts`, the README and the transcription brief so a later chapter cannot quietly reach for `dump-text.ts`. Generalises: *a text layer that renders prose perfectly can still be arithmetically lossy — measure a glyph you KNOW is on the page before trusting it.*

Both answer-key errors are *self-refuting on the page* (Ex 2.1 Q3 prints `cos 4° > 0` AND `cos 4° < 0` in one line; the Misc II table prints `tan 315° = −1` beside `cot 315° = 1`) — I re-read both pages myself and checked all 90 cells of the two answer tables, finding exactly the one flagged error. `board:lint` · `audit:text` · `audit:keys` clean; full gate PASS.

(2) **`merge.ts` globbed every `<id>.*.json`** and ingested `blind.mcq-verify.json` as "10 questions" — only a coincidental duplicate ref in `errata.json` stopped 10 garbage rows entering the source of truth. Both now exclude scratch artifacts BY NAME. **Shared lesson: an allow-by-exclusion glob over a directory that also holds generated dumps is a silent-corruption hazard, and it fails OPEN.** (3) A Class-9 theory erratum rode along in the copied `errata.ts` and was appearing in the Class-11 publisher report.

Caught only by reading the stored rows back. *Verify LaTeX by inspecting what landed in the DB, not by whether the writer reported success.*
  - **`tests/exam-context.test.ts` pinned "Std 11 resolves to null — no Class 11 corpus" as an HONEST GAP**, which this change intentionally falsified. Before editing I confirmed `stdsForBoard`/`getExamForBoardStd` have **no consumers** in `src/` or `scripts/` (a forward-looking written-paper-picker API), so nothing suddenly offers Class-11 papers. Remaining scope: 17 chapters ≈ 1,500-2,300 q, best ordered by measured MHT-CET weightage (Trig-I 99 · Limits 93 · Trig-II 90 · Determinants & Matrices 50 …). See [[mh-sb-11-ingestion]].

- **2026-08-09 — Sitemap `<lastmod>` made TRUE per URL (migrations 0072 + 0073), and the three canonical-less pages closed — prompted by a Search Console "Duplicate without user-selected canonical" email whose real content was somewhere else entirely.**
  - **THE EMAIL WAS ABOUT 1 PAGE. The coverage export said the thing worth reading: 20 indexed, 942 "Discovered – currently not indexed", 13 crawled-not-indexed, 3 blocked, 3 redirects, 1 duplicate.** Most of the investigation went into modelling a *mass*-duplication mechanism (`/login?next=` variants, the 72 chapter-slugs repeated across exams) before the export arrived and showed the count was one. **The generalisable error: an alert's severity is DATA, and it was one click away in the tool that sent the alert.** Get the magnitude before modelling the mechanism — see [[diagnose-from-data-not-assumptions]].
  - **The 1 duplicate page, identified by exhaustive audit of the live site:** `/login`, `/signup`, `/pricing` were the ONLY public 200-routes with no canonical, and `/login` + `/signup` are `"use client"` pages whose server HTML is an empty shell — **278 visible characters, 0 `<h1>`, 0 `<form>`, 0 `<input>`, byte-identical to each other** (`BAILOUT_TO_CLIENT_SIDE_RENDERING`). Identical content + nothing declaring a canonical is exactly this GSC reason. **The cause of the missing canonical is structural: a `"use client"` module cannot export `metadata`** — hence new `login/layout.tsx` + `signup/layout.tsx` carrying `robots: { index: false, follow: true }` (nobody searches for a sign-in form), and a canonical on `/pricing`, which stays indexable. `/login` also left the robots.txt Allow list — **deliberately still crawlable, because a Disallow would PREVENT Google from seeing the noindex.**
  - **THE REAL FIX — `<lastmod>` was a single build clock stamped on 984 of 988 URLs.** `sitemap.ts` read `const now = new Date()` once and reused it at 33 of its 34 sites, so every deploy announced that the entire site had changed — including the ~54% of pushes that touch only docs or ingestion scripts. Google discounts a lastmod it learns not to trust, and with 942 URLs queued that date is the ONLY lever for saying "this chapter is the one that changed". Now: **397 landing pages carry `max(created_at)` of their own chapter's PUBLIC questions; 93 notes/guide chapters carry their `_data` directory's git commit date; index/hub pages carry the newest of their children; only genuinely-aggregate pages (home, `/browse`, `/questions`) keep the build date.** Live result: **40 distinct lastmod days, up from 4 — with 0 of 397 landing pages falling back.** Pure core `src/lib/seo/lastmod.ts` (12 TDD cases; the load-bearing one is that ancestor matching is SEGMENT-WISE — a naive `startsWith` would hand `/guide/nda-maths-advanced` the date of `/guide/nda-maths`). Also removed from the sitemap: `/login` (now noindexed) and `/guide` (a 307 to `/guide/nda` — listing a redirect asks Google to index a page that does not exist; it was one of the 3 "Page with redirect"). **`/guide` was deliberately LEFT a 307 rather than promoted to a permanent 308** — a 308 is aggressively cached and hard to reverse, and the file's own comment says `/guide` becomes a real exam picker once a second exam ships.
  - **MIGRATION 0072 WAS WRONG AND 0073 REPLACES IT — the failure mode is the lesson.** 0072's aggregate was bank-wide: `max(created_at) … group by chapter_id` over every PUBLIC pyq row. Measured on prod it walked **25,026 rows for 6,144 buffers in 5,430 ms**, because `questions_question_kind_idx` is `(org_id, question_kind)` and carries neither `chapter_id` nor `created_at`, making every row a heap fetch. At 5.4s it sat right at the anon statement timeout and **failed INTERMITTENTLY** — a standalone probe returned all 421 rows while the same call from the running app was cancelled. **The bug was invisible because the call site destructured `{ data }` and dropped `error`**: JEE Mains, MHT-CET and MH-SSC-10 silently fell back to the build date, i.e. the exact defect being fixed, reintroduced through a swallowed error. Caught only by noticing that the exams which resolved were precisely the practice-only ones. **An index was the obvious fix and was rejected**: `questions` is the most heavily written table here and this project has already spent a session tracing disk-IO exhaustion to write amplification — paying a permanent write cost on every ingest to speed a read that happens once a day behind an `unstable_cache` is the wrong trade. Instead the aggregate is **scoped to one subject** (0073), riding the existing `questions_filter_idx` and joining the per-subject `Promise.all` that was already there: **88.7 ms for the largest subject, ~61× faster, no new index, no extra round-trip**, and a slow subject can now only cost its own dates. The error is logged rather than swallowed. **Two rules banked: measure before indexing (the 2026-08-01 lesson, reconfirmed — but note it cut the OTHER way this time, and only the measurement distinguishes the two cases); and a best-effort lookup must still SURFACE its error, or its failure mode is indistinguishable from the bug it fixes.**
  - **En route, the JEE subject-name trap fired again**: a first EXPLAIN filtered `subjects.name='Mathematics'` and returned 0 rows — JEE's subject is **`Maths`** — producing a meaninglessly fast plan that would have "proved" the query was fine. A measurement over an empty set is not a measurement.
  - **Not the problem, and worth recording so it is not re-investigated:** the 398 `/questions` landing pages are correctly built. Uppercase paths, trailing slashes and arbitrary query strings all resolve to a self-canonical clean URL; 72 chapter-slugs repeat across exams but on distinct URLs each carrying its own canonical. **And the 942 "Discovered – currently not indexed" is not a defect at all** — it is crawl rationing for an 11-day-old set of pages on a low-authority domain (~20 impressions/day). No configuration change manufactures crawl demand; this work makes the crawl budget land on the right pages once it arrives.

- **2026-08-09 — The unattributed disk spill traced to SUPABASE'S OWN METRICS EXPORTER, not to any app query; clearing `pg_stat_statements` (4,868 entries → 7) STOPPED IT COMPLETELY — ~13 GB/day to zero; migration 0071 turns the store's size into a watched gauge.** The 2026-08-07 tracker had been warning `spill-unattributed` — 8.5 GB written in a 16-hour window with only 8 MB attributable — and this session chased it down.
  - **THE FINDING: the thing doing the spilling is the thing that measures spilling, and it excludes itself from measurement.** The culprit is `postgres_exporter` (Supabase's Prometheus collector, running as `supabase_admin` on a connection open since 2026-07-28). It reads the ENTIRE `pg_stat_statements` store once a minute to build its metrics; the store had grown to **4,868 entries carrying 3.8 MB of query text against `work_mem` of 2,184 kB**, so every scrape sorted more than fitted in memory and spilled **5,802,298 bytes — byte-identical every time — twice a minute, around the clock**. That is ~13 GB/day on a **164 MB** database. Its own queries are absent from `pg_stat_statements`, which is exactly why three separate query-level investigations found nothing.
  - **Ruled out by measurement before accusing anything** (each cheap, each decisive): every tracked query moved <1 MB and none went backwards between snapshots; `dealloc` was only 12; `pg_cron` is not installed; `track = 'top'` does not hide nested statements (their usage rolls up). What finally named it was `log_temp_files`.
  - **The diagnostic, and the permission wall in front of it.** `log_temp_files` cannot be set from SQL here — the `postgres` role is **not** superuser on Supabase (`ALTER DATABASE … SET` → *permission denied*), a limit I asserted a plan around before checking. The working route is the **CLI**: `npx supabase --experimental postgres-config update --project-ref <ref> --config log_temp_files=4MB --no-restart` (flags go AFTER the subcommand; the API rejects a bare number — `4MB` is accepted because it is a string). Applied by config **reload**, no restart, no dropped connections; reverted the same way after ten minutes. Read-only alternatives failed and are worth recording: `pg_ls_tmpdir()` polling caught **nothing** in 25 s because each file lives well under a second, though the filename carries the owning PID and would have identified it instantly on a hit.
  - **The fix is a one-liner, and it was total.** `pg_stat_statements_reset()` took the store **4,868 entries / 3,800 kB → 7 / 5,611 bytes** and evictions 12 → 0. **Spill went to ZERO**: `temp_files` and `temp_bytes` are cumulative, and 56 minutes after the reset both stood exactly where they had 5 minutes after it (5 files / 26 MB) — across a window that included a full `prepush` (690-page build + ~2,800 tests). At the old rate that window should have produced ~80 files. ~13 GB/day → 0.
  - **AN INTERIM CONCLUSION OF "IT HALVED" WAS WRONG, AND THE WAY IT WAS WRONG IS THE LESSON.** It was measured over **5.4 minutes** — below the tracker's own `MIN_RATE_WINDOW_HOURS` floor, i.e. a window this very codebase already refuses to extrapolate from; the caveat was even stated and then the conclusion drawn anyway. The 5 files it saw were almost certainly **self-inflicted**: `npm run db:health` plus a verification call to `collect_db_health()` plus several `pg_stat_statements` scans, each of which spills ~5 MB by design (documented in [[db-health-tracker]]). **When measuring whether an intervention worked, the diagnostic tooling is part of the system under test** — either idle out the window or use probes that cannot spill (`pg_stat_database` alone is safe; anything touching `pg_stat_statements` is not). The "files arrive in PAIRS" observation was real; the inference built on it — that only one of each pair was the store read — did not survive a longer window.
  - **A number this file has been quoting is wrong by an order of magnitude, and the shape of the error is the lesson.** The 2026-08-05 entry called the `/browse` wide-sort "99.4% of the entire database's temp writes". It was 99.4% **of the `pg_stat_statements`-tracked subset** — and that subset is only ~10% of reality: **114 GB tracked vs 1,145 GB in `pg_stat_database`**. So ~90% of this database's spill has always been invisible to statement-level attribution. The `/browse` fix was still real and is confirmed dead (those ten retired query shapes read 0 calls / 0 bytes across a full window), but it was the largest thing we could SEE, not the largest thing there was. **Corrected in the Recurring-pitfalls bullet.**
  - **Migration 0071 folds the lever into the tracker** (`statements_tracked` / `statements_max` / `statements_evictions` + `statement-store-full` at 80%/95% and `statement-store-evicting` at any eviction). Rationale: the cost scales with the store's SIZE, the store refills in ~3 months (over half its entries were one-off ingestion/audit queries run exactly once — 2,615 of 4,865), and without a gauge the next session would simply repeat this whole investigation. Eviction earns its own rule because what a full store discards is **this tracker's own input**, so the reports silently under-count. Columns are **nullable on purpose** — the 20 pre-0071 snapshots have no reading, and a `DEFAULT 0` would render as a healthy 0% measurement that was never taken. Gauges deliberately survive a stats reset (they are the reading that tells you whether to reset again), which is asserted by test.
  - **Verification:** 52 dbhealth tests green (9 new flags + 4 new delta), full `prepush` PASS, **624 prerendered `.html`** on disk (the [[shell-component-decaches-site]] check). The reset also exercised the tracker's own refusal path end-to-end — the next report declined to measure the window, naming the reset, instead of printing a negative delta.
  - **CLOSED — no residual, no support ticket.** The 56-minute zero-delta window settles it; nothing further to diagnose. What remains is maintenance, now automated: the store refills in ~3 months (2,615 of 4,865 entries were one-off scripts run exactly once), and 0071's `statement-store-full` warning is what will say so. Should the spill ever return, the recipe that named it in one pass is in [[db-perf-diagnosis]].

- **2026-08-07 — Database health tracking shipped (migrations 0069 + 0070, `npm run db:health`, daily GitHub Action) — and the investigation that motivated it CLOSED with the opposite answer to the one assumed** (merge `da90f24`, full gate green + a second independent pass by the pre-push hook).
  - **THE PROBLEM, stated once so it stays stated: every Postgres load counter is CUMULATIVE with no time dimension.** `pg_stat_statements` will say a query has spilled 1,129 GB since the stats were reset (2026-05-08); it cannot say whether any of that was today. That is not academic — after the `/browse` wide-sort was fixed on 2026-08-05 there was **no way to confirm from the database that the spill had stopped**, because the lifetime total keeps the old number forever. Two snapshots subtract to a real rate; one snapshot cannot. Everything else here follows from that.
  - **The `/notes` question, answered by measurement, and the answer is "do nothing".** `loadWorkedExamples` is the highest-volume query left (1,041,940 calls). Two complete builds, both exit 0: **cold (`.next` deleted) = 437 calls ≈ 3.6 MB; warm (cache intact, 690/690 pages, 624 `.html`) = ZERO.** Next's fetch cache spans builds, so `unstable_cache` would buy nothing locally or on Vercel. **The user's proposal to inline the examples into the page was declined on correctness, not effort**: the bank changes constantly (~235 wrong keys flipped, solution-cleanup sweeps, stem repairs), so a frozen copy would keep teaching a superseded answer with no lint catch, and RLS withdrawal (a flawed question set PRIVATE) would stop working. If ever wanted anyway, the right shape is a generated snapshot + a drift probe — never hand-inlined content. Only cold CI builds still pay (~437 calls), judged not worth a `.next/cache` CI step: ~100–250 MB/month against an 11.48 GB read, and caching build inputs slightly weakens the gate.
  - **The "unexplained 8,600 calls/day gap" was an ARTIFACT of the measurement window, not a mystery.** The 91-day window starts 2026-05-08 — the project's beginning — and for most of it EVERY page was dynamic, because the `AppHeader` de-caching bug was not fixed until 2026-07-29. The 11,479/day average therefore describes a period dominated by an already-fixed defect. **Generalisable: a lifetime average is not a current rate, and the older the window the more it describes history you have already repaired.** En route I proposed a ×3-builds-per-push explanation and had to withdraw it — arm 2 showed local and Vercel builds are warm, so only CI is cold.
  - **Attribution was VERIFIED, not assumed** — I suspected `/browse`'s two-phase fetch shared the query shape and was wrong: the 1M-call statement selects exactly `loadWorkedExamples`' column list (name-only joins, no `image_url`/`set_id`/`question_format`), while `queryQuestionsByIds` selects wider and is a different queryid. Checking cost one query and would have invalidated the whole analysis if skipped.
  - **The design centre of the tracker is REFUSAL: it never reports a number it cannot stand behind.** Three ways the subtraction lies, each yielding `null` or an explicit flag rather than something plausible — (1) `pg_stat_statements` reset (cumulative deltas null, point-in-time gauges still valid); (2) a single query entry evicted and re-created, counters restarting while the global reset timestamp does not move (`suspectedReset`, under-count disclosed); (3) **the window too short to extrapolate — measured, not hypothetical: two snapshots two seconds apart reported "268 GB/day" from 7 MB of real activity**, most of it the collector's own query.
  - **TWO RULES CAME FROM FIRST CONTACT WITH REAL DATA, and both refuted the plan.** (a) **Collecting queries by LIFETIME rank misses exactly what the tool is for** — the first run showed 29 MB of database spill with nothing in the list to explain it, because a query that starts misbehaving today has a small lifetime total by definition. 0070 records every query that has *ever* spilled (rare: 100 of 4,477), plus a `spill-unattributed` rule, since silence when the database spills and no tracked query accounts for it reads as "all clear". (b) **Per-call spill alone is unusable** — the widened collector produced 20+ warnings, every one a hand-run analysis query that executed ONCE and spilled ~5 MB. Volume is what made `/browse` an incident, so a query must also clear a total-for-the-window floor. **The general lesson: a monitoring threshold cannot be calibrated from first principles — it has to meet real data before it is trustworthy, and the first contact usually shows it is too noisy, not too quiet.**
  - **Also corrected a number this file has been quoting:** the largest chapter is **531 PUBLIC questions**, not 346, against the PostgREST 1000-row cap. The 346 counted PYQs only; the cap applies to whatever a `.select()` returns, so 531 is the honest distance — ~2× away, not ~3×. **(Stale again as of 2026-08-17: Worksheets `Vectors` is now 664, so the headroom is ~1.5×. Re-measure rather than quoting either figure.)**
  - Scope discipline: **report-only, no alerting** (thresholds nobody has calibrated against a week of real data should not page anyone), and the collector's own cost (~2.7 s, ~8 MB spill per run) is documented rather than optimised. 33 TDD cases; the gate earned its keep by catching a fixture field that vitest alone passed over. Runbook `scripts/dbhealth/README.md`. **First genuine 24-hour window lands the morning after ship — that is when "did the /browse spill actually stop?" finally becomes answerable.**

- **2026-08-07 — Three database performance fixes (migrations 0067 + 0068 + the `/notes` chapter-landing count), merged separately.**
  - **0068 — the optional-parameter anti-pattern, and it is worth recognising by sight.** A `language sql` body with `where (p_x is null or col = p_x)` is planned ONCE, generically: the planner cannot prove the parameter non-null, so every predicate is demoted to a filter and the index is unusable. Proven with `EXPLAIN (GENERIC_PLAN)` — **Seq Scan cost 7,941 vs 541** for the same query with literals. Fix is `plpgsql` + `RETURN QUERY EXECUTE … USING` (a one-shot plan). **`plan_cache_mode` does NOT fix it** (tested, no effect). `public.match_chunks` (0040) is the only other function in the schema carrying the pattern; left alone deliberately — 2 calls ever, ~1 ms, the tutor that would consume it was never built.
  - **0067** indexes the `/notes` subtopic counts and rewrites `get_pyq_years` as a loose index scan.
  - **The `/notes` chapter landing fetched ONE ROW PER QUESTION** (`.select("subtopic_id").in(...)`) and tallied in JS to render about five integers — 9,858 bytes for 170 rows on NDA Maths Matrices, on all 83 chapter landings, every build. Now aggregates through the existing `get_subtopic_facets` RPC: **9,858 → 423 bytes, same numbers**, no new migration. **The correctness fix is worth more than the bytes**: the old query inherited the PostgREST 1000-row cap, so once a chapter crossed 1000 PYQs the weightage counts would have silently UNDER-reported. **The trap avoided**: `get_subtopic_facets` is CHAPTER-scoped and returns every subtopic, where the old query asked only for notes-REGISTERED ones — passing it straight through would have inflated a number the page renders, so `subtopicCountsFromFacets` narrows it back and that is the first thing the tests assert. Two siblings deliberately NOT changed: the concept-tags tally (a fifth the payload, nowhere near the cap) and the `head: true` drill count (0-byte body, 0.181 ms after 0067 — caching it would buy a staleness contract for no gain).
